httpMock.expectOne only checks the URL and method ('PUT'); it does not assert any Authorization header or identity-binding parameter, consistent with the client design not re-verifying ownership of the code before submission.

req.flush({ data: 'apiResponse' }) completes the exchange purely on the basis of the URL match, with the mock backend never asked to validate any identity claim tied to the code — mirroring an application design where the code alone is treated as sufficient authorization.

The test only validates HTTP method and response payload, confirming the client-visible contract accepts and forwards any code value without an identity check at this layer — the trust decision is deferred entirely to a server component outside this file.

title: Unhandled JSON.parse exception can permanently hang the chat streaming generator
description: The SSE-style stream handler parses each 'data: ' line with JSON.parse(data) at line 59 with no surrounding try/catch. If the backend (or an attacker positioned to influence the LLM's raw output, e.g. via a successful prompt-injection that causes the model to emit a line beginning with 'data: ' followed by non-JSON text, or any malformed/truncated chunk boundary) produces a line that is not valid JSON, JSON.parse throws synchronously inside the RxJS `next` handler. This exception is not caught anywhere in this file: `done` is never set to true, `resolve()` is never invoked for that terminal state, and the observable's `error`/`complete` callbacks may not fire for a synchronous throw inside `next` depending on RxJS version/behavior. Because the async generator's while loop at lines 96-102 awaits a Promise that only resolves when `resolve()` is called, a thrown exception that bypasses the intended resolve/done-setting paths leaves the generator suspended forever on `await new Promise<void>((r) => { resolve = r })`. This causes an indefinite hang of that chat session (denial of service for the caller) and leaks the pending subscription/promise, since the design never wraps the parsing step in error handling to guarantee `done`/`resolve` are always eventually triggered.

JSON.parse(data) executes with no try/catch; a thrown exception here skips the code paths that set done=true and call resolve(), leaving the async generator's pending promise unresolved forever (line 100).

title: Model-generated tool calls are forwarded verbatim without validation, enabling excessive agency downstream
description: The service extracts `delta.tool_calls` directly from the parsed LLM response (line 74) and passes the raw structure (function name and arguments string) through the ChatChunk stream to the caller with zero validation, allow-listing, or sanitization of the function name or arguments. Because the tool-call content originates entirely from the model's output — which is itself influenced by the conversation history/messages the client sends (line 31/37) — a successful prompt injection against the LLM can cause it to emit an arbitrary tool_calls payload (arbitrary function name / arbitrary argument JSON). This file performs no verification that the requested tool/function is one the current user is authorized to invoke, nor does it bound the number or size of tool calls per turn. If the downstream consumer (outside this file) executes tool calls based on trust in this data without independently re-checking authorization, an attacker who can influence the conversation (directly, or indirectly through injected content the model reads) gains the ability to trigger privileged actions the model was never meant to grant unilaterally.

title: Unsanitized model-generated content (deltaContent) forwarded to UI consumer with no output-encoding control in this file
description: Text content generated by the LLM (delta.content) is placed into chunk.deltaContent (line 73) and yielded unmodified to the caller (line 98). No sanitization, encoding, or content-type restriction is applied in this service. Because LLM output can itself be steered by earlier user input or by content the model retrieves/reads (classic indirect prompt injection), an attacker able to influence the conversation could cause the model to emit HTML/script-like text. Whether this becomes an XSS depends entirely on how the consuming Angular component renders deltaContent (e.g., via [innerHTML] versus safe interpolation) — that rendering sink is outside this file, so this is reported as a propagation risk: this file is the point where untrusted, model-generated markup enters the client application unsanitized.

title: Message role field accepted without restriction, enabling potential system-prompt/role spoofing
description: streamMessages accepts an array of `{ role: string, content: string }` objects and posts them verbatim to the backend (line 37) with no restriction on the value of `role`. If any caller path allows user-influenced data to populate the role field (rather than the application hard-coding 'user'), an attacker could inject a message with role 'system' or 'assistant' into the array sent to the LLM backend, potentially overriding or manipulating the system instructions the backend later assembles for the model — a role-spoofing / prompt-injection vector. This file provides no validation or allow-listing of the role field before transmission, and since the caller is outside this file, the exploitability depends on whether any upstream code lets user input reach this parameter. There is no intervening line between the parameter declaration and its use in the POST body: `messages` is forwarded as-is into the request object literal on the same line it is sent.

The unvalidated messages array (including its role fields) is sent verbatim in the POST body to the /rest/chat backend.
Backend chat endpoint (outside this file) receives the role-unrestricted messages and presumably uses them to construct the LLM prompt/context.

title: Unvalidated LLM tool_call directives passed through to caller without verification
description: The spec exercises ChatService.streamMessages() and confirms that when the backend (which proxies an LLM completion stream) emits a tool_calls delta, the service surfaces the tool call's function name and raw arguments string directly to the consumer (deltaToolCalls) with no test coverage of any validation, allow-listing, or argument schema check performed before exposing it. Tracing the full path: the test messages enter the service call, the returned generator is drained into an accumulator by an unfiltered for-await loop that pushes every chunk (including tool-call chunks) verbatim, the mocked HTTP response delivers the raw tool_calls payload, and after the request completes the test asserts that the function name and (by extension) the raw arguments are exposed unchanged. At no point in this path is there a step that inspects, allow-lists, or strips the tool call before it reaches whatever downstream code consumes the generator (e.g. a chat component that executes the named tool). This establishes that the model's output is trusted verbatim as an instruction to be acted upon. If the downstream consumer executes tool calls based solely on this unvalidated data (name/arguments controlled by the model, which in turn can be influenced by attacker-supplied conversation content), this is a textbook LLM06 Excessive Agency pattern. The actual execution sink lives outside this file, so full exploitability cannot be confirmed here, but the interface tested provides no verification hook anywhere along the path.

title: Raw backend/LLM error strings forwarded verbatim to chat consumer
description: The 'should handle error from server' test shows that when the backend SSE stream contains an {"error": ...} field, ChatService.streamMessages() forwards that string unmodified into the emitted ChatChunk ({ error: 'some_error' }). Tracing the full path from entry to assertion: the triggering messages enter the service, the generator is drained by an unfiltered accumulation loop, the mocked HTTP request is captured, the raw error payload is delivered through the response stream, the request is flushed to completion, and the test asserts the exact raw string reached the output with no intermediate normalization, redaction, or logging step anywhere on this path. If the real backend/LLM provider ever includes internal details (stack traces, provider error payloads, upstream API keys/config hints) in its 'error' field, this pass-through design would expose them directly to the end user, and there is no corresponding security-event logging of the failure for later investigation.

title: No evidence of input sanitization/fencing on user message content sent to LLM backend
description: Across all tests, the messages array sent to streamMessages (e.g. { role: 'user', content: 'hello' }) is passed straight through as the POST body to /rest/chat with no test asserting any escaping, delimiting, or moderation of the content field. Tracing the full path: the raw user content is defined, handed unmodified into streamMessages, the generator is drained by an accumulation loop, the outbound POST request is captured by the mock, and the only assertion made against that request checks the HTTP method — never the body content — before the request is flushed to completion and accepted as valid. This is consistent with a design where user-supplied conversation content is forwarded to the LLM backend without any fencing that would prevent it from being interpreted as system-level instructions once concatenated into a prompt (a prerequisite condition for LLM01 prompt injection). This cannot be fully confirmed from the spec alone since the actual prompt-construction logic lives in chat.service.ts, not in this file, but the tested contract provides no indication such protection exists anywhere along the traced path.

title: Code snippet retrieval tested without any authentication/authorization context, suggesting endpoint may lack access control
description: The spec exercises CodeSnippetService.get() against the real backend route '/snippets/:challengeId' but never sets, mocks, or asserts on any Authorization header, bearer token, or session credential in the HTTP request that httpMock.expectOne intercepts. The test module configuration (line 16) wires up only the plain HttpClient/HttpClientTesting providers and the service itself — no auth or bearer-token interceptor is registered or exercised anywhere in the suite, so the path from service instantiation through the call to the mocked response never involves an identity check. Neither the happy-path test (lines 26-39) nor the error-path test (lines 41-52) verify that the service attaches an auth token or that unauthenticated/unauthorized requests are rejected differently from a plain 404. If the underlying service and its server-side route indeed omit any identity check (which cannot be fully confirmed from this file alone, since the service implementation lives elsewhere), any client could retrieve arbitrary challenge code snippets — including snippets tied to challenges not yet unlocked or exposed to the current user — by supplying any challenge identifier. Because this spec is the only visible evidence of how the service is expected to behave, and it encodes no expectation of an auth check on this data-retrieval path, it points to a design that treats snippet retrieval as unauthenticated by default. This is a weak/absent-check finding on a trust boundary (client-supplied challenge id fully determines server response) rather than a confirmed exploit, hence lower confidence.

httpMock.expectOne intercepts a GET request to 'http://localhost:3000/snippets/testChallenge' — the mocked request object is never inspected for an Authorization header or credential, and no test asserts one is required.

The TestBed providers list registers CodeSnippetService, provideHttpClient(withInterceptorsFromDi()), and provideHttpClientTesting() only — no auth/bearer-token interceptor is registered or exercised anywhere in this suite, confirming the tested request pipeline carries no identity-attachment step feeding into the call at line 31.

title: Continue-code progress restoration trusts client-supplied code as sole authorization
description: restoreProgress, restoreProgressFindIt and restoreProgressFixIt take an arbitrary continueCode string from the caller and PUT it directly to the backend's apply endpoint with no ownership check performed anywhere in this file (and none of these functions verify that the continueCode belongs to the current session/user before submitting it). The design treats mere possession of a continue-code string as sufficient authorization to overwrite the current user's challenge-solve progress. If continue codes are guessable, leaked, or brute-forced (they are a deterministic encoding of solved-challenge state, a known weakness in this class of feature), any user who obtains or guesses another user's code can restore that state into their own account via this client, without the server (as invoked from here) ever confirming the caller is the rightful owner of that progress. The entrypoint (the component that collects the continueCode from user input, e.g. a paste field) lies outside this file; this file is the boundary where the untrusted string is accepted and forwarded to a state-changing endpoint. The same unchecked pattern is repeated identically for all three progress namespaces (main, findIt, fixIt), showing the design gap is structural rather than a one-off omission.

title: No throttling on repeated continue-code guesses enabling brute-force enumeration
description: The restoreProgress family of methods issues a PUT request for any continueCode string supplied by the caller, with no rate limiting, backoff, or attempt-count control visible anywhere in this service. Since continue codes are a compact deterministic encoding, an attacker can script rapid, repeated calls through this client (or directly against the underlying endpoint it wraps) to brute-force valid codes belonging to other accounts. Nothing in this file bounds the number or frequency of such attempts across any of the three parallel endpoints, so the cost of large-scale guessing falls entirely on the backend with no client-side or observable server-side safeguard represented here.

title: Failed/invalid continue-code restore attempts are not logged for security monitoring
description: Every network call in this service funnels errors through catchError((err) => { throw err }), which simply rethrows the error without recording any detail (timestamp, attempted code, requester context) anywhere in this file. For the security-sensitive continue-code apply operations in particular, a failed attempt is indistinguishable from a benign network error at the point where security monitoring would need to detect a pattern of repeated invalid-code submissions (a hallmark of brute-force enumeration). No correlation ID, attempt count, or log emission exists in this client layer to support reconstructing an attack timeline for these state-changing calls, and the same silent-rethrow pattern recurs across all three continue-code variants.

title: No transport-security enforcement on backend host used for state-changing and credentialed requests
description: All requests in this service are built from this.hostServer (derived from environment.hostServer) with no check or enforcement in this file that the configured host uses HTTPS before dispatching requests, including state-changing PUT calls that carry continue codes. If the environment configuration defaults to or is misconfigured with a plain http:// origin (a value not visible from this file), continue codes and other data sent through this service would traverse the network without transport confidentiality, and this file contains no defensive check to catch that misconfiguration before making the call.

title: Unbounded, unthrottled challenge-verification requests allow brute-forcing the correct fix
description: The check() method posts an attacker/user-controlled `selectedFix` index (and `key`) to the backend verification endpoint with no client-side attempt limiting, delay, or lockout. Because the 'correct answer' space for this kind of code-fix challenge is small (a handful of candidate fixes returned by get()), a caller can script repeated calls to check() cycling through every possible `selectedFix` value until the server returns verdict:true, defeating the intended purpose of the challenge (the user must reason about the correct fix) via brute-force guessing rather than legitimate use. Nothing in this file rate-limits, debounces, or caps the number of verification attempts, and each call triggers a network round trip and presumably server-side computation, which also enables resource-consumption abuse via automated rapid-fire requests. This is a design gap: the server-trust model assumes a human trying fixes occasionally, but the client interface offers no compensating control for automated exhaustive guessing.

title: HTTP errors from challenge endpoints are silently rethrown without any logging
description: Both get() and check() catch HTTP errors via catchError but only rethrow them (`(error: any) => { throw error }`) with no logging, metrics, or alerting. Failed verification attempts or anomalous error patterns (e.g., repeated 4xx/5xx from probing the verification endpoint, which could indicate automated brute-forcing or abuse as described in the companion finding) are not recorded anywhere in this service, making it impossible to reconstruct or detect abuse of the challenge-verification flow from the client side of this codepath.

title: Unvalidated/unencoded key interpolated into request URL path
description: The `key` parameter passed into get() is concatenated directly into the request URL (`this.host + '/' + key`) without validation or URL-encoding. If this key ever originates from a route parameter or other externally influenced value, an attacker could supply path-altering characters (e.g. '../', encoded slashes) to change which backend path is actually requested, potentially probing or reaching unintended API routes on the same host. The file performs no sanitization or allow-listing of the key before building the outbound request.

title: Errors from snippet retrieval are rethrown without any logging
description: The get() method's RxJS pipeline uses catchError((err) => { throw err }) to handle failures from the HTTP GET request to the /snippets/{key} endpoint. This handler does nothing but rethrow the error — there is no console logging, no telemetry, and no call to any monitoring/logging service before the error propagates further up the call stack. If this endpoint is used to probe for valid challenge/snippet keys (e.g., enumerating 'key' values to discover which code-snippet challenges exist or to fingerprint server behavior), repeated failed requests generated through this service leave no client-side trace and rely entirely on whatever the (unseen) backend does. Within this file, a security-relevant event — a failed data-retrieval attempt possibly indicating enumeration/probing — is silently swallowed and forwarded with zero observability.

title: Unvalidated/unencoded key interpolated directly into request URL
description: The get() method builds the request URL by directly template-interpolating the caller-supplied 'key' parameter into a path segment (`${this.host}/${key}`) with no validation, allow-listing, or URI encoding (e.g. encodeURIComponent). Because the server is expected to be the authority that decides which snippet a given key maps to, but the client performs no sanity checking on the value before sending it, any component that forwards route parameters or other externally influenced strings into this service can cause requests to arbitrary path segments beneath /snippets (e.g. path traversal-like segments such as '../' or unexpected values) with no client-side guard. This reflects a design gap: the service trusts the caller to supply only well-formed keys and never re-validates or encodes them, pushing 100% of the trust decision to an unseen backend route.

title: Test confirms ComplaintService.save() forwards arbitrary caller-supplied object fields to the Complaints API without any allow-list
description: The spec file demonstrates that ComplaintService.save() accepts an arbitrary JavaScript object (here `{ foo: 'bar' }`) and passes it, unmodified, as the POST body to `/api/Complaints/`. There is no evidence in this test suite that the service restricts, validates, or allow-lists which properties of the object are sent to the backend. If the underlying Complaint model has sensitive or privileged fields (e.g., an id, a user reference, or a status/verification flag), a caller of this service could set those properties simply by including them in the object passed to `save()`, and they would be forwarded as-is to the REST endpoint. The actual enforcement (or lack thereof) lives in complaint.service.ts and ultimately the server-side Complaints handler, both outside this file, but this spec is the clearest evidence available here that the client-side service imposes no allow-list on the object it serializes into the request body. Tracing the full test path: the service and mock harness are obtained (lines 41-42), an error-capture variable is set up (line 44) before the arbitrary-body call is made (line 45); the mock then intercepts the exact outgoing request without any assertion that its body was filtered or restricted (line 46), and the test completes the exchange by flushing a synthetic error response, at no point checking or constraining which properties of the original object reached the request body (line 47), while the final assertions only verify the HTTP error status, not the shape of the transmitted payload (lines 48-49).

title: Configuration fetch failures are silently propagated without security logging
description: The getApplicationConfiguration() method requests the application configuration from the backend and wires a catchError operator that does nothing but re-throw the original error (line 121: `catchError((err) => { throw err })`). No log entry, telemetry event, or monitoring hook records that the configuration fetch failed, why it failed, or which client/session encountered it. Because this is the mechanism the entire SPA depends on for feature flags, security-relevant toggles (e.g. challenges.safetyMode, hackingInstructor.isEnabled, ctf.systemWideNotifications.url) and OAuth client configuration, repeated or anomalous failures here (e.g. an attacker tampering with the admin endpoint, a MITM injecting malformed responses, or a denial-of-service against the config endpoint) leave no trace for detection or incident reconstruction. An operator investigating a security incident involving unexpected application behavior would find no log evidence that configuration retrieval was failing or being manipulated.

title: Application-wide configuration served from an '/rest/admin' path without visible authorization enforcement in the client
description: The service builds its request host as `this.hostServer + '/rest/admin'` (line 114) and fetches essential, app-wide configuration data (feature flags, challenge settings, OAuth client id/redirects, CTF notification URL) from what is nominally an administrative API namespace (line 121: GET '/rest/admin/application-configuration'). No authentication token, admin-role check, or authorization header is attached in this file before issuing the request, and the response is trusted and cached indefinitely in `configObservable` for reuse by the whole application (lines 115-123) without any integrity or origin validation. If the backend does not itself gate this specific route behind an authorization check (a design assumption this file cannot verify but which the URL naming implies should exist), any unauthenticated caller — not just admins — can read and, depending on backend enforcement, an attacker with access to modify this endpoint's backing data could poison configuration values (e.g. safetyMode, redirect URLs, notification URLs) consumed trustingly by every client in the application, since the client performs no verification that the returned config originates from a legitimate, unmodified source.

title: Unvalidated arbitrary payload forwarded directly to Complaints API (mass-assignment surface)
description: The `save()` method accepts a parameter typed as `any` and forwards it verbatim as the JSON body of a POST to `/api/Complaints/`. There is no shape validation, field allow-listing, or sanitisation performed in this service before the object reaches the network call. Any caller in the application (or any code able to invoke this service, e.g. via a compromised component or a manipulated form binding) can attach arbitrary extra fields to the complaint object — for example ownership/user identifiers, verification flags, or other properties the server-side model may blindly trust (a classic mass-assignment pattern). Because this file establishes no contract on what `params` may contain, the design never re-derives or bounds the data before it leaves the client, pushing 100% of the trust decision onto the server. The HTTP client and target URL used to carry that unvalidated object are wired up at construction time (injecting HttpClient and building the host string from environment configuration) and then reused unchanged as the transport for the unvalidated body. If the server-side Complaints handler is equally permissive (which this file cannot see, but which the design here does nothing to prevent), an attacker can inject fields the business logic never intended the client to control.

title: Complaint submission failures are swallowed without any logging or telemetry
description: The RxJS pipe attached to the POST call only maps the response and rethrows any error via `catchError((err) => { throw err })`. No error is logged, no metric is recorded, and no correlation identifier is attached before the error is rethrown up the call stack. This means the client has zero visibility into patterns of failed complaint submissions — for example repeated 4xx/5xx responses that could indicate a user (or automated attacker) probing the endpoint with malformed or oversized payloads, or attempting to abuse the complaint workflow. The request that generates these errors is built from the injected HttpClient and the environment-derived host before being dispatched, and the response is piped through map() before catchError() discards the error context; server-side logging is outside this file, but this file is the last point at which the outbound request/response pair is fully known on the client, and it discards that information instead of recording it for monitoring/debugging.

title: No client-side size/rate constraint on complaint payload before transmission
description: save(params: any) forwards whatever object it is given straight into an HTTP POST with no size cap, no chunking, and no throttling applied at this layer. Juice Shop's complaint feature is known to allow attaching file content (e.g., base64-encoded uploads) inside the complaint payload; because this service applies no bound to the size of `params` and no client-side rate limiting, a caller (or a compromised/scripted client bypassing the UI and calling this service or its underlying endpoint directly) can repeatedly submit very large bodies against the fixed endpoint assembled from environment configuration. Whether this is exploitable end-to-end depends on server-side body-size limits not visible in this file, but this file itself establishes no defensive bound, which is the layer where such a check would naturally belong for a public write endpoint.

title: Test suite mocks CountryMappingService against a plaintext HTTP endpoint
description: The spec file exercises CountryMappingService.getCountryMapping() and mocks the network call to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/country-mapping' (lines 33 and 49). Because HttpTestingController.expectOne() matches the exact URL the service under test issues its request to, this indicates the CountryMappingService itself is configured to call the REST API over plain HTTP rather than HTTPS. If this base URL construction (protocol + host) is not overridden per-environment in production builds, sensitive data returned by /rest/country-mapping (or other endpoints built the same way) would be transmitted without transport-layer encryption, exposing responses to network-level interception/tampering. This is inferred indirectly from the test fixture rather than directly observed in a config file, since the actual URL-building logic lives in country-mapping.service.ts, which is outside this file. Tracing through both test cases in this file shows the same insecure endpoint is exercised twice, in two independent test setups, confirming the pattern is a consistent property of the service rather than a one-off artifact of a single test.

title: HTTP errors from country-mapping API are swallowed and rethrown with no logging
description: The getCountryMapping() method issues an HTTP GET to hostServer + '/rest/country-mapping' and attaches an RxJS catchError operator whose only action is 'throw err' (line 20). This is effectively a no-op error handler: it does not log the failure, does not record diagnostic/telemetry information, and does not distinguish between transient network failures, malformed/unexpected server responses, or potentially malicious responses (e.g., a tampered/backend-compromised response, unexpected redirect, or repeated failures indicative of probing). Because no logging or monitoring hook exists on this path, an operator has no client-side signal to detect abnormal or repeated failures against this endpoint, and any anomaly in the response (which could indicate backend manipulation or an attack) leaves no trace for later investigation. As a design matter, the error-handling path was added but performs no actual handling, meaning the service consistently discards the opportunity to observe and react to backend errors.

title: Stored XSS: unsanitized chat message/title content persisted to localStorage with no output-encoding boundary
description: The service persists caller-supplied StoredConversation objects (including message text and a generated title derived from the first user message) directly to localStorage as JSON, with no sanitization, HTML-encoding, or allow-listing of the text content. `generateTitle` simply truncates the first message and returns it verbatim - it performs no encoding. `save` then writes the full conversation object (title + presumably message array) unmodified into localStorage, going through its existing read-merge-write cycle (fetch current list, locate a matching id, either overwrite or append) before serializing. Because this is the classic Juice Shop chatbot conversation-persistence pattern, the conversation title/messages are very likely rendered later in a chat UI component (outside this file) via a template binding or innerHTML-style rendering. If that downstream renderer does not itself apply context-appropriate encoding, a user (or another user's payload replayed into this browser context, e.g. via a shared/exported conversation) who supplies a chat message containing `<script>` or event-handler markup will have that payload persisted verbatim through this merge path and later rendered as active content - a stored XSS. Per the injection playbook, stored XSS should be reported at the persistence point; the render sink is outside this file and not directly observable here.

title: Untrusted localStorage payload deserialized and trusted without schema validation
description: getAll() reads a raw string from localStorage and passes it straight to JSON.parse, immediately casting the result to StoredConversation[] with a TypeScript type assertion (which provides no runtime guarantee) and then calling .sort() on it assuming each element has a numeric updatedAt. localStorage under the app's origin is not solely written by this service's own controlled paths - it can be modified by any script running in the page's origin (e.g., via an XSS elsewhere in the app, a malicious browser extension, or direct devtools tampering), and this file performs no shape/type validation of the parsed data before using it. A corrupted or adversarial STORAGE_KEY value (e.g., an object instead of an array, or elements missing updatedAt/id) will propagate into every caller of getAll()/getById(), causing runtime type confusion or exceptions, and downstream code that trusts the StoredConversation shape (e.g., rendering or business logic) is not defended by this parsing step.

title: Unbounded conversation storage growth with no size cap or write-failure handling
description: save() appends to (or replaces within) the full conversation list and writes the entire array back to localStorage on every call, with no limit on the number of stored conversations, no limit on message/title length, and no eviction/pruning policy. localStorage has a small per-origin quota (typically 5-10MB); repeatedly saving conversations (e.g., an automated/scripted client, or a user generating many long chatbot exchanges) will grow the stored JSON blob until localStorage.setItem throws a QuotaExceededError. Neither save() (line 44) nor delete() (line 49) wraps the setItem call in a try/catch, so the exception is unhandled and will propagate out of the service, breaking any further conversation save/delete operations for that user until storage is cleared. This is a missing resource-consumption control: no cap on stored data volume and no graceful degradation path when the underlying storage is exhausted.

title: Conversation IDs generated with non-cryptographic Math.random()
description: generateId() builds conversation identifiers using Math.random() to pick 8 characters from a 36-character alphabet, combined with Date.now(). Math.random() is not a cryptographically secure random source and is predictable/reproducible given knowledge of the PRNG state or narrow timing window. If these IDs are ever treated as unguessable identifiers for access purposes (e.g., a future feature that shares or looks up a conversation by ID across contexts), an attacker could feasibly enumerate or predict IDs. Within the current file the impact is limited since storage is purely local per-browser with no cross-user access control visible here, so this is a design-quality concern rather than a directly demonstrated exploit in this file.

title: Failed GDPR erasure and data-export requests are silently rethrown without any logging
description: erase(params: any) accepts an untyped, arbitrary object from its caller and forwards it verbatim as the body of a POST to /rest/user/erasure-request — an operation that deletes/erases user data and is inherently irreversible. Within this service layer there is no re-validation, no confirmation token, no re-authentication requirement, and no shape constraint on params (typed as `any`) before the destructive request is dispatched. Because the design of this data-access layer places zero constraints on what the client can request to be erased or how, any logic error or manipulation upstream (e.g., a modified params object, a replayed request, or an automated/rapid double-submit) reaches the backend as a fully-formed erasure call with no client-side compensating control such as a second confirmation step, and no record of what was requested is kept if it fails (see companion logging finding). This is a design gap in an inherently risky, irreversible workflow rather than a simple missing-field validation bug.

title: Caller-controlled arbitrary URL passed directly to HttpClient without validation (SSRF-like / token-exfiltration design flaw)
description: The `fetchNotification` method takes a fully caller-supplied `url` string and passes it verbatim into `this.http.get<...>(url)` with no validation, allow-listing, or restriction to a known/trusted backend endpoint (e.g. the app's own `/rest/...` API). A component such as `CtfSystemWideNotificationService` should almost certainly only ever fetch the system-wide notification from a single, fixed, internal API path. Instead, the design allows the caller (and, transitively, whatever upstream data — route parameter, query string, stored config, or user input — feeds that caller) to redirect the underlying HTTP request to an arbitrary origin. Angular applications commonly configure an `HttpInterceptor` that automatically attaches the user's Authorization/Bearer token or session cookie to every outgoing `HttpClient` request regardless of destination host. If such an interceptor exists in this app (a very common Juice-Shop-style pattern), an attacker who can influence the `url` value reaching this service can cause the victim's browser to send its authentication token to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in session/token theft. Even without an interceptor, this is a textbook 'trust assumption violation': the service trusts the caller to supply a safe destination rather than deriving/hardcoding it itself, which is exactly the kind of design gap that lets an attacker turn a benign 'fetch a banner message' feature into a data-exfiltration or open-proxy primitive. The `this.http` instance used to perform the call (line 20) is a generic, un-scoped `HttpClient` injected with no base-URL restriction or request-guard visible in this file, so nothing between the parameter and the network call constrains the destination. The vulnerability is structural — no implementation-level input check would fix it without redesigning the service to accept, at most, an identifier that is resolved server-side/internally to a fixed URL.

title: No error handling or logging on notification fetch failures
description: The Observable returned by `this.http.get(url)` is handed back to the caller with no `catchError`/`tap` and no logging of failed or anomalous requests (e.g. non-2xx responses, redirected/foreign-origin responses, or malformed payloads). The request is dispatched through the bare `this.http` client instance created at line 20 with no interceptor or wrapper visible in this file that would record outcomes, and the resulting Observable is returned directly at line 23 with zero instrumentation. If this service is ever pointed at an unexpected or attacker-influenced URL (see companion finding), there is no monitoring hook in this file to detect or alert on the anomaly — failures simply propagate silently to whatever subscribes. This is a minor logging/monitoring gap since the fetch itself is not obviously a high-value security event, but combined with the unrestricted URL parameter it removes the last chance to notice misuse at the point of the request.

title: Conversation history stored in a globally-keyed, unscoped localStorage bucket (no per-user isolation)
description: The ConversationStorageService under test persists all chat conversations under a single fixed localStorage key (STORAGE_KEY = 'juiceshop_chat_conversations') with no reference to the currently authenticated user or session. Every test in this suite (getAll, getById, save, delete) operates against this single global bucket and none of them establish or verify any notion of 'whose conversation is this' — save() simply appends/updates by conversation id, and getAll()/getById() return whatever is present in the shared key regardless of which account is logged in. On a shared or public browser, or simply after one account logs out and a different account logs in within the same browser profile, the second user's session would read the first user's full chat history (getAll returning all records, getById returning any id) because the storage layer never scopes data to a user identity. This is a Broken Object Level Authorization pattern implemented entirely client-side: the 'identifier' controlling access is nothing more than a fixed string constant shared by all users of the browser, and the service performs no ownership check between the stored records and the requesting session.

Because chat messages (free-form user/assistant text) accumulate in the `messages` array of each StoredConversation and the whole collection is serialized on every save, a user (or script) that keeps creating conversations / long message histories can grow the stored JSON without bound until the browser's per-origin storage quota is exhausted, causing save() to throw/fail (a client-side denial of service for the chatbot feature) and potentially degrading the whole origin's localStorage-dependent functionality. No pagination or truncation is exercised in getAll() either — it returns the full array in one call.

title: Stored conversation data is round-tripped through JSON.parse and trusted without schema/content validation
description: getAll() and getById() are exercised by tests that seed localStorage directly with JSON.stringify'd StoredConversation objects and then assert the service returns them essentially unchanged (e.g. lines 108-117, 179-189). None of the tests demonstrate any validation, sanitization, or schema check being applied to the parsed data before it is handed back to callers. Because localStorage is writable by any script running on the origin (e.g., via an XSS elsewhere in the app, a malicious browser extension, or direct devtools tampering), and because message `content` fields are free-form text, the service as tested blindly trusts whatever structure/content is present under STORAGE_KEY and returns it verbatim (including the `messages[].content` field used to reconstruct the chat UI). If that returned content is later rendered in the chat view without separate encoding, tampered localStorage entries become a stored/persisted script injection vector. While these IDs are only observed here as storage keys for chat conversations (not as auth/session tokens), if this ID generator or its pattern is reused elsewhere as a security-relevant token (e.g., referenced in a URL or used to correlate resources across users), the predictable timestamp component and non-CSPRNG suffix would make the identifier guessable/enumerable, which combined with the lack of any per-user access check identified above (see the access-control finding) would enable an attacker to enumerate and access other users' conversations by id.

title: GDPR-sensitive erasure/export requests configured over plaintext HTTP
description: The tests pin the DataSubjectService's real endpoints to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/user/erasure-request' and 'http://localhost:3000/rest/user/data-export' (plain HTTP, not HTTPS). Because httpMock.expectOne() matches the exact URL the service under test actually issues requests to, this confirms the production DataSubjectService is wired to call these GDPR data-subject-rights endpoints (erasure requests and full personal data export) over an unencrypted transport scheme. The first test drives the erasure call through completion (flush, method assertion, verify) entirely over the plaintext URL, and the second test independently re-injects the service/mock and repeats the same pattern for the data-export endpoint, confirming the plaintext scheme is not incidental to one call but the consistent base configuration used across both sensitive operations. Erasure and data-export payloads carry highly sensitive personal data and should always travel over TLS; using http:// here indicates the base URL/config used by the service does not enforce HTTPS, allowing network-level interception or tampering of GDPR requests and exported personal data if this configuration carries to any non-localhost deployment.

title: Unvalidated id parameter concatenated into outbound request URL
description: The getById method accepts an id parameter with no type annotation (implicit any) and no validation, sanitisation, or encoding before it is embedded into the request URL via a template literal. Because the value is not passed through encodeURIComponent or validated to be a simple numeric/opaque identifier, a caller that can influence id (e.g., a route parameter such as /delivery/:id bound directly to this service, which lives outside this file) can inject path-traversal sequences (../) or extra path segments. The untrusted id is combined with the service's base host, which is itself built from the environment-configured hostServer plus the fixed '/api/Deliverys' suffix, so the final request target is a concatenation of a trusted prefix and an untrusted suffix with no boundary enforcement. This lets the constructed URL address a different API path than intended on the same backend host (e.g. ${host}/../Users or similar), potentially reaching unintended endpoints that the calling component never intended to hit. The design trusts the caller-supplied value completely and never re-derives or constrains it before using it to build the request target, which is a trust-boundary violation typical of insecure design: the client component decides the destination path segment and the service performs no defensive check.

title: API errors are swallowed and rethrown without any logging
description: Both get() and getById() register a catchError operator whose handler does nothing but rethrow the error (catchError((err) => { throw err })). No security-relevant details (failed request, endpoint, status code, timestamp, correlating identifier) are captured or logged before the error propagates. If the backend Delivery API returns authorization failures, malformed input errors, or repeated failed lookups (e.g., enumeration of delivery IDs via getById), there is no record created in this service layer that could support later detection, alerting, or incident reconstruction. This is a systemic absence of logging for outbound API failures rather than a coverage gap for one event type: both public methods of the class share the identical no-log rethrow pattern.

title: No pagination or bounds control on delivery methods listing endpoint call

If the backend does not itself enforce a cap, an attacker who can trigger repeated calls to this service (directly against the underlying REST endpoint, bypassing this Angular wrapper) receives an unbounded result set each time, and repeated invocation could be used to place load on the server. This is a minor finding since delivery methods are typically an administratively curated, small list, but the client contract here establishes no expectation of bounded retrieval.

title: Client-supplied params forwarded unsanitized to feedback creation endpoint, permitting attribute spoofing
description: The save() method accepts an untyped 'params: any' object from its caller and forwards it verbatim as the body of a POST to /api/Feedbacks/. There is no stripping, whitelisting, or server-side-derived overriding of security-relevant fields (e.g. the author/UserId association, rating, or comment metadata) before the request is sent. Because the design of this service trusts whatever the calling component places in 'params', any field the client chooses to include is transmitted as-is to the backend. If the backend does not independently re-derive the authenticated user's identity for the feedback record (a common Juice Shop weakness), an attacker can manipulate the params object (e.g. via browser devtools or a modified request) to submit feedback attributed to another user's ID, since the client is the one asserting which user the feedback belongs to rather than the server deriving it from the session. This is a trust-boundary violation: a value that should be authoritative server-side (the feedback author) is instead accepted from client input with no validation layer present in this file.

If the corresponding server endpoint has any authorization gap, this thin service exposes a direct, unrestricted path for any authenticated (or even any) caller to attempt deletion of any feedback record simply by iterating ids — an IDOR-enabling design with no compensating control in this layer.

title: No client-side throttling or backoff around CAPTCHA retrieval enabling trivial automated abuse of the anti-automation control
description: The CAPTCHA subsystem exists specifically to slow down or block automated/bot activity, yet the client-side service that requests a new CAPTCHA (getCaptcha) applies no cooldown, debounce, or retry-limit logic of its own — it is a bare, repeatable pass-through to the backend endpoint. The service resolves its HttpClient (line 15) and target host (line 17) once at construction, and every subsequent call to getCaptcha() (line 19) unconditionally re-issues the GET request (line 20) with the same unthrottled control flow, and any error is simply rethrown (line 20) rather than being used to trip a backoff or lockout. Because there is no compensating control anywhere in this file preventing a caller (or a scripted client bypassing the UI entirely and calling this endpoint directly) from invoking getCaptcha() in a tight loop, the design does not enforce any rate discipline on the very mechanism meant to prevent automated abuse. This is a design gap rather than an implementation bug: the service was never built to bound the frequency of captcha issuance, so even a 'correct' implementation of this class still allows unlimited CAPTCHA solicitation, which can be leveraged to farm captcha challenges/images for offline solving services or to probe backend availability.

While this specific call is for a low-sensitivity language list, the same catchError-and-rethrow pattern used across the app's services means security-relevant failures (e.g., repeated 401/403/5xx responses that could indicate backend issues or abuse) are never recorded anywhere, hindering incident detection and reconstruction of an attack timeline from the frontend's perspective.

If this configuration is carried into any non-local deployment, captcha challenge/response data would be transmitted without TLS protection, allowing network-level interception or tampering (e.g., replacing the served captcha image or answer verification response). A wallet's private key is the single secret that grants full control over on-chain assets and must never leave the client in plaintext, let alone be sent to a server over a non-TLS (http://) endpoint. If this test accurately reflects production behavior, any interception (network MITM, server-side logging, a compromised backend, or a malicious/misconfigured proxy) yields full compromise of the user's crypto wallet. This is both a cryptographic failure (secret key material handled without any encryption or client-side signing substitute) and a design flaw (private keys should never be submitted to a server at all — a signed message/challenge-response should be used instead).

By design, this service transmits the caller-supplied private key over the network to a server, meaning any compromise of the transport, the backend, request logs, proxies, or the server's memory/storage exposes the key to full account/wallet takeover. This is a design-level trust violation: the server should never require or accept a private key as proof of anything — it should use signature-based challenge/response instead. No amount of correct implementation of this exact call (e.g. adding TLS, or masking the field name) removes the risk, because the design itself requires the secret to be sent off-device.

If this base URL is also used outside of local development (e.g., left as a default that is not overridden for a real deployment), sensitive order and payment-related data would traverse the network unencrypted, enabling interception/tampering by a network-level attacker (MITM). This is inferred from the fixed literal URL that the service under test is built to call; the actual environment/config file that supplies this base URL is outside this spec file, so this is reported as the point where the file reveals the (mis)configuration rather than as a certainty about production behavior.

title: toggleDeliveryStatus accepts a caller-supplied order ID with no visible ownership/authorization check
description: The tests exercise service.toggleDeliveryStatus(1, {}) which sends a PUT to /rest/order-history/1/delivery-status and merely asserts the HTTP method and response passthrough; none of the tests validate that the caller must own order '1' or otherwise be authorized to flip its delivery status. Because this spec is the only visible contract for the service, and the tested behavior is simply 'given an id, PUT to a URL built from that id', the design as exercised here treats the order id as fully client-controlled with no server-side re-validation asserted or expected by the client contract. The flushed response is accepted and returned to the subscriber unconditionally, with no branch checking for an authorization failure distinct from a generic error, reinforcing that the client-side contract never anticipates an ownership check. If the real backend endpoint (outside this file) trusts the id parameter the same way the client does, any authenticated (or even unauthenticated, per the misconfiguration finding) user could toggle delivery status for orders they do not own by supplying arbitrary numeric IDs — an IDOR-style trust-boundary violation. This is reported at reduced confidence because the actual authorization enforcement (if any) lives in the server route handler and/or interceptors that are not part of this file.

If the backing endpoint returns the full order-history collection for a user (or, worse, all orders) in a single response, a caller can force the server to serialize and transmit an unbounded result set on every invocation. Because the client-side service never offers a way to request a bounded page, any consumer of this service (and the endpoint behind it) is structurally unable to apply resource limits from the client side, and nothing here indicates the server enforces a cap either. Repeated invocation of this call is a cheap way to force large-payload responses.

title: Delivery-status toggle forwards caller-controlled id and arbitrary params without client-side validation
description: toggleDeliveryStatus(id, params) accepts an order id and an untyped params object directly from its caller and forwards them verbatim into a PUT request path/body (`${this.host}/${id}/delivery-status`). There is no validation here that the id belongs to the calling user, and no shaping/whitelisting of what fields 'params' may contain before being sent to the server. This service establishes no rule that the server must independently re-derive order ownership or that the payload is restricted to an expected shape — it simply passes through whatever the caller (a component, or ultimately an attacker manipulating the app state) supplies. If the server-side handler trusts the id/params without re-validating ownership of the order (a common assumption baked into thin client wrappers like this), an attacker can toggle delivery status on orders they do not own by iterating ids, since nothing in the design here binds the request to the authenticated user's own orders.

This produces a blind spot: an attacker probing many order ids via toggleDeliveryStatus, or repeatedly hitting failures, leaves no client-side trace an operator could use to reconstruct the attack timeline.

title: Payment card API endpoint served over plaintext HTTP (inferred from test expectations)
description: This spec file asserts that PaymentService issues requests to 'http://localhost:3000/api/Cards' (and sub-paths) using httpMock.expectOne(), which matches the exact URL the real service constructs. Because HttpTestingController.expectOne() only matches a request whose actual outgoing URL equals the string passed to it, the literal 'http://...' (non-TLS) scheme baked into every test in this file (get, getById, save, del, and both error-handling tests) is strong evidence that the underlying PaymentService (in payment.service.ts, not shown here) is configured to call the backend over unencrypted HTTP rather than HTTPS. Payment card data (numbers, expiry, etc.) is sensitive financial information; transmitting or receiving it over plaintext HTTP exposes it to network eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle tampering. Tracing through all four CRUD-style tests (get, getById, save, del) shows the same insecure scheme is exercised consistently across GET, POST and DELETE verbs, each time the service instance is freshly injected, the method invoked, the exact insecure URL matched, and a response flushed back over that same channel — indicating this is the service's baked-in base URL rather than an incidental test artifact. This is a transport-layer cryptographic failure (missing encryption in transit for payment data) and, since the base URL and scheme appear hardcoded rather than derived from a secure environment/config abstraction that enforces HTTPS, also a security misconfiguration. Confidence is capped because the actual runtime configuration (environment.ts / payment.service.ts) is not visible in this file — it is possible this hardcoded localhost URL is strictly a local development default that is overridden with HTTPS in production builds.

title: Backup restore path trusts unsigned, attacker-authored file content to overwrite security-relevant challenge/progress state
description: The spec exercises LocalBackupService.restore(), which is fed a raw File object whose entire content is an attacker-controlled JSON string (line 75). The only integrity check the tests exercise is a bare numeric 'version' field (line 83: version 0 is rejected, version 1 is accepted at line 75) — there is no signature, checksum, HMAC, or any cryptographic proof that the JSON originated from a legitimate export produced by this same application. Once the version check passes, arbitrary fields from the file (e.g. 'language', and by the symmetry of save()/restore() shown in the later test, continueCode / continueCodeFindIt / continueCodeFixIt) are written straight into the cookie store, which the rest of the app (ChallengeService) treats as authoritative fallback state for whether challenges have been solved. Lines 93-95 show the exact cookie keys (continueCode, continueCodeFindIt, continueCodeFixIt) being seeded, lines 98-100 show the server-side source of truth for those codes being made unavailable, and line 104/106 show save() proceeding to use those locally-held (and, via restore(), locally-forgeable) cookie values as the trusted fallback with only a diagnostic log and no re-validation. Because the restore mechanism has no way to distinguish a backup file honestly produced by save() from one hand-crafted by the user in a text editor, a player can fabricate a JSON file containing forged continue codes and 'restore' it to mark arbitrary challenges as solved — a classic design flaw where a value the server/application should independently verify is instead accepted verbatim from the client-controlled file.

If, as is typical in i18n implementations, this cookie value is later used elsewhere in the app (outside this file) to construct a URL or file path for loading translation assets (e.g. an i18n JSON resource keyed by language code), an attacker-controlled string containing path traversal or unexpected characters could be used to influence that downstream resource-loading operation. This file only proves the unvalidated propagation of the value into persistent client state, and additionally shows the UI surfaces a generic success notification (line 77) with no content-based warning, reinforcing that no validation/sanitization step exists between file parsing and persistence; the actual downstream sink (if any) is outside this file and was not observed.

title: Security-relevant restore/backup actions lack dedicated audit logging
description: The only logging behavior exercised in this spec is a generic console.log fallback message when the server fails to return continue codes (line 106): 'Failed to retrieve continue code(s) for backup from server. Using cookie values as fallback.' There is no evidence anywhere in this spec that a security-relevant event — a user restoring a backup file that overwrites language/progress cookies (lines 75-76), or a fallback occurring because server-side challenge state could not be verified (lines 88-106) — is logged in a way that would support later detection or investigation of a forged/tampered backup being restored. Tracing the full path: restore() silently mutates cookie state with no log call at all (lines 75-76); the separate save() fallback scenario seeds cookie values that stand in for server-verified continue codes (lines 93-95); the server calls for all three continue-code types are made to fail (lines 98-100); console.log itself is stubbed out for the test (line 102), and save() is executed (line 104) before the single diagnostic message is emitted (line 106). At no point is a structured, security-focused audit entry produced (no timestamp, user identity, source-file provenance, or event classification) — only a debug-style console.log statement.

title: Unverified backup file content trusted to overwrite security-relevant cookies and challenge continue codes
description: The restore() method accepts an arbitrary File object, reads its full text and JSON.parse()s it into a Backup object with only a single sanity check (backup.version === this.VERSION). No schema validation, type checking, or cryptographic/integrity verification (signature, checksum, origin check) is performed on the parsed content. Every field of the untrusted object (banners, language, continueCode, continueCodeFindIt, continueCodeFixIt) is then written verbatim into persistent browser cookies via restoreCookie(), and — once the user clicks the 'Apply changes now' snackbar action — the continue codes are sent (URL-encoded) to the server-side challenge-progress endpoints via challengeService.restoreProgress/restoreProgressFindIt/restoreProgressFixIt. Because the client places total trust in the contents of a file it did not generate or verify, an attacker who can get a victim to import a crafted 'backup' file (e.g. distributed as a 'juice shop backup' via email/social engineering) can inject arbitrary continue codes and cookie values into the victim's session, altering the victim's stored challenge/progress state and cookie-driven UI state without any server-side ownership check visible from this file. This is a data-integrity failure (unauthenticated import of unverified data driving state changes) and simultaneously a trust-assumption/insecure-design violation, since the design never establishes any fact the server should independently verify about the imported file's authenticity before acting on it.

No 'secure' or 'sameSite' options are passed, meaning these cookies (some of which drive server-side challenge-progress restoration flows) may be transmitted over plain HTTP and/or sent in cross-site contexts, depending on the CookieService's global defaults. Because the code explicitly builds an options object here and computes an explicit expiry, but chooses to include only 'expires', this is the point where a stronger cookie policy could have been enforced and was not.

title: Unbounded file read/parse in backup restore with no size limit
description: restore() reads the entirety of a user-selected file into memory via backupFile.text() and then JSON.parse()s the whole content, with no maximum size check before or between either operation. While the file is user-selected in the browser (self-inflicted in the common case), if this restore path can be triggered programmatically or with a very large crafted file (e.g. delivered via a script that auto-submits a File/Blob to this service), it could cause excessive memory/CPU consumption in the tab. This is a lower-confidence, client-side resource-consumption concern since there is no server-enforced cap visible in this file.

title: Unrestricted file upload with no client-side size/type validation before POST to /rest/memories
description: The addMemory() method accepts an arbitrary File object (image) supplied by the caller and immediately appends it to a FormData payload and POSTs it to the memories endpoint, with no check on file size, MIME type, or count before the request is issued. The design never establishes or enforces any bound on what can be uploaded from this service layer — the caller (a component outside this file) can pass any File, of any size or type, and it will be forwarded unmodified. If the corresponding server endpoint (POST /rest/memories) does not itself enforce a strict size/type/count limit, an attacker (or a compromised/malicious client) can repeatedly submit very large files to exhaust server memory, disk, or bandwidth — a classic unrestricted resource consumption pattern. Even if server-side limits exist, this file establishes no defense-in-depth control and blindly trusts the caller-supplied File object, which is a design gap: the service that owns the upload call path never validates the object it is about to transmit.

Failed uploads (which could indicate abuse, oversized payload attempts, malformed content, or repeated probing of the memories endpoint) leave no client-side trace that could be aggregated for security monitoring purposes. While ultimate responsibility for security event logging typically lies server-side, this file is the sole client-side chokepoint for this feature and performs no instrumentation of failure conditions along the entire request-building and dispatch path, making it harder to correlate client-observed failures (e.g. repeated large-file rejection) with server-side security events.

title: Test suite hardcodes and validates an unencrypted HTTP endpoint for the Quantity REST API
description: Every test in this spec file exercises QuantityService against the literal URL 'http://localhost:3000/api/Quantitys/...' (lines 32, 46, 60, 72). Because HttpTestingController.expectOne() matches the exact URL the service under test actually issues, these assertions confirm that QuantityService is configured to call the backend over plain HTTP rather than HTTPS, and this same unencrypted base URL is exercised consistently across the read path (getAll), the write path (put), and both of their error-handling variants. If this base URL configuration is carried into any non-local/staging or production build (a common pattern in Angular apps where environment.apiUrl defaults to a hardcoded localhost/HTTP value), quantity-update requests (PUT /api/Quantitys/:id, which mutates inventory/stock data) would be sent unencrypted, allowing network-level attackers to observe or tamper with product quantity data in transit. This is a transport-layer security misconfiguration surfaced through the test's own expected-request assertions, and its repetition across four independent tests shows it is the service's baked-in, unconditional configuration rather than a one-off test artifact.

title: No test coverage for authorization or input validation on the quantity-mutation endpoint
description: The PUT test (lines 40-52) and its error-path counterpart (lines 66-76) invoke service.put(id, {}) with an empty/arbitrary body and no authentication/authorization header assertions, and no assertion that the service enforces any bound or shape on the quantity payload before sending it. The suite verifies only that whatever object is passed is forwarded verbatim as the PUT body (line 49) and only checks the HTTP method (line 48) and the raw response equality (line 50) before tearing the mock down (line 51) — at no point is an Authorization header, role claim, or quantity-value bound checked or even referenced. This indicates the client-side service — and by extension the design under test — treats quantity changes as an unauthenticated, unvalidated pass-through to the server with no client-side guard against malformed or malicious payloads (e.g., negative or non-numeric quantities). Since inventory quantity is a value with real business meaning, a design that lets arbitrary caller-supplied objects flow straight to the mutation endpoint without any shape/bounds check or authorization assertion is a trust-boundary gap: the server is presumably the sole enforcer, but nothing in this file confirms or exercises that expectation, and the client offers no defense-in-depth. This is inferred from the test's shape rather than proven server-side, so it is reported at lower confidence.

title: Client-controlled X-User-Email header used to assert caller identity
description: The interceptor reads the 'email' value directly out of localStorage — a value fully controlled by the client (settable via devtools, XSS, or any script running in the page) — and attaches it verbatim as the 'X-User-Email' header on every outgoing HTTP request. There is no cross-check against the JWT stored under the 'token' key, nor any validation that the email actually corresponds to the authenticated session. If any backend endpoint uses this header (rather than deriving identity solely from the verified/signed token) to resolve 'who is making this request' for authorization, audit trail, or business-logic decisions (e.g., attributing feedback, complaints, orders, or basket association to a user), an attacker can trivially spoof another user's identity by writing `localStorage.setItem('email', 'victim@example.com')` before firing a request, since the header is generated by this interceptor with zero server-side derivation. This is a textbook trust-boundary violation: the server-facing identity claim is sourced from client storage instead of being derived from a cryptographically verified credential, which is simultaneously an authentication/identity-resolution defect and an access-control design flaw (BOLA-style spoofing is possible for any endpoint that consumes this header).

title: Unauthenticated security-question lookup by email enables account-recovery enumeration
description: The spec confirms that SecurityQuestionService.findBy(email) issues a plain GET request to /rest/user/security-question?email=<email> and returns the target user's chosen security question directly, with no Authorization header, token, or credential supplied in the test setup (no interceptor/auth provider configured beyond the plain HttpClient). This mirrors the classic OWASP Juice Shop 'forgotten password' flaw: an attacker who knows or guesses a victim's email can retrieve which security question is associated with that account before authenticating, which (a) confirms account existence (email enumeration) and (b) tells the attacker exactly which security question to target for social-engineering or guessing during account recovery, undermining the recovery flow's intended protection. The test module's provider list only wires the plain HttpClient and HttpClientTesting harness with no authentication interceptor or token provider, so the service instance under test has no mechanism to attach a credential to the outgoing request even if one were required server-side. The request built and dispatched carries only the email as a query parameter, and when the mock server responds, the returned security-question content is delivered straight through to the caller with no gate in between. Because the actual route handler and full service implementation are outside this file, the exact server-side check cannot be fully confirmed here, but this spec is strong behavioral evidence of the design: any caller supplying an email receives the associated security question unauthenticated.

title: Unvalidated pass-through of arbitrary client data to POST /api/Recycles (mass-assignment trust violation)
description: The save() method accepts a caller-supplied object typed as `any` and forwards it verbatim as the request body of a POST to the Recycles REST endpoint. The request target is assembled from `this.host`, itself built once from `environment.hostServer` concatenated with `/api/Recycles` (line 18) and reused at the call site. No field allow-listing, type checking, or server-authoritative value derivation happens anywhere in this file — every property the caller places on `params` (originating from user-facing form input in a component not shown here) is transmitted unmodified to the backend as soon as the http.post call fires. If the backend model persists whatever fields are present in the body (a common pattern for Sequelize/restify-style CRUD endpoints, as suggested by the generic `/api/Recycles` CRUD routes), a caller could inject fields that should be server-controlled — e.g., an owner/user id, an approval/status flag, a quantity or monetary value — allowing the workflow's trust boundary to be violated entirely from the client side. This is a design gap: the interface layer establishes no contract restricting which fields are legitimate for client submission, so even a 'correctly implemented' version of this exact call still allows attacker-controlled fields to reach persistence.

title: Unbounded query parameters on find() with no client-enforced pagination/limit
description: The find() method forwards a caller-supplied `params` object of type `any` directly as the HTTP query-string params for a GET request against /api/Recycles. The request URL is built from `this.host` (constructed on line 18 from `environment.hostServer + '/api/Recycles'`), and the options object literal spans lines 21-23, with the caller's `params` embedded via object-shorthand on line 22 before the call closes with `.pipe(...)` on line 23. No default page size, max-limit, or pagination enforcement is applied anywhere along this path. If the backing endpoint does not itself cap result set size (which is plausible for a generic REST list endpoint), a caller invoking this service with no params, or with parameters crafted to request a large page, can pull an unbounded number of records into a single response, consuming memory/bandwidth on both client and server. Because the limiting behavior (if any) lives entirely outside this file, the file itself supplies no compensating control.

title: Errors from Recycles API calls are silently rethrown with no logging
description: Both find() and save() pipe their HTTP calls through catchError handlers that do nothing but re-throw the error (`catchError((error) => { throw error })`). In find(), the underlying request is issued via http.get on line 21 and its errors flow into the pipe's catchError on line 23; in save(), the request is issued via http.post on line 27 and its errors flow into the catchError chained on the same line. No error is logged, and no security-relevant event (e.g., repeated failed submissions, malformed/rejected recycle requests, potential abuse patterns targeting the create/list endpoints) is recorded anywhere in this service. Because this is the sole client-side integration point for the Recycles feature, and no logging call (console, telemetry, or monitoring service) exists on either failure path, any anomalous or abusive pattern of calls to this service leaves no trace that could be used to detect or investigate the activity from this layer.

title: Security-answer creation service accepts an unrestricted, arbitrarily-shaped payload for an account-recovery-relevant endpoint
description: The spec exercises SecurityAnswerService.save() with an untyped/arbitrary object (`{ a: 1 }`) and confirms it is forwarded verbatim as the raw HTTP request body to POST /api/SecurityAnswers/, with the test asserting only on HTTP method and response value — never on the shape of the outgoing body. This demonstrates that the client-side service imposes no allow-list or DTO validation on which properties are sent to the security-answer creation endpoint; any caller of save() (application code outside this file) can pass arbitrary key/value pairs through untouched. Security answers are part of Juice Shop's account-recovery / forgot-password flow, so if the server-side handler for POST /api/SecurityAnswers/ (out of scope here, but listed among the app's routes) similarly performs unrestricted mass assignment from the request body, a caller could supply extra fields (e.g. a UserId/foreign-key property) to associate a security answer with a different user's account, enabling an account-recovery bypass / account takeover. This is speculative regarding server-side enforcement, but the client contract exercised by this spec shows no property restriction is enforced or even expected at this layer, and the endpoint sits squarely on the identity-recovery decision path the crypto-auth playbook calls out explicitly.

This indicates the client-side service performs no pre-flight validation that a security answer actually contains required content before submitting the create request. If mirrored by weak/absent server-side validation, this could allow the security-question workflow to be manipulated by submitting empty/degenerate answers, weakening the account-recovery mechanism. This is inferred purely from client-service behavior exercised in the test and the actual server enforcement is outside this file.

title: Unauthenticated enumeration of user security questions by email, with no logging or throttling
description: findBy(email) sends an unauthenticated GET request to the backend's security-question lookup endpoint using only a caller-supplied email address, and returns the associated security question text directly to the caller (response.question). The design never requires the caller to prove ownership of the account (e.g., a valid session, a prior password-reset token, or CAPTCHA) before disclosing which security question is configured for an arbitrary email. This is a classic 'forgot password' design flaw: an attacker can iterate over a list of candidate email addresses, learn each account's security question type (e.g., 'What is your pet's name?' vs 'What is your first car?'), and use that knowledge to select the easiest-to-guess accounts to target for a subsequent security-answer brute force / account-takeover attempt. The email value is also concatenated directly into the query string without encodeURIComponent, so it is passed to the server unsanitized. Compounding the design gap, the catchError handlers at lines 21 and 27 simply rethrow errors without any logging, so there is no application-level record of repeated or failed lookups that would let defenders detect an enumeration sweep, and there is no client- or server-visible rate limit apparent in this file to slow down mass enumeration.

title: Unbounded, client-controlled query passed to security-question listing endpoint
description: The find(params: any) method forwards an arbitrary, untyped params object directly as HTTP query parameters to GET /api/SecurityQuestions/ with no validation, no enforced page size, and no cap on result count. If the backend does not itself enforce pagination limits, a caller (or any code path that constructs params from user input) could request an unbounded result set, causing excessive memory/CPU use on repeated or scripted calls. Because the type is 'any' and no shape/limit checks exist in this file, this service provides no defense-in-depth against oversized or repeated queries.
