title: Unvalidated caller-supplied string used directly as i18n translation key with unencoded fallback rendering
description: The public `open(message, cssClass)` method accepts an arbitrary string and passes it straight into `TranslateService.get(message)` as a translation lookup key, with no validation, allow-listing, or type check on its shape. The entrypoint to this file is external — any component throughout the Angular app (including code that surfaces server-derived error text, HTTP error bodies, or other externally influenced strings) can call this method with attacker-influenced content. The tainted 'message' value is forwarded unchanged into the `subscribe({...})` call at line 19, which registers two branches: a 'next' success handler and an 'error' handler. When resolution of the translation key fails, execution proceeds into the 'error' branch defined at line 26, which is the decision point that routes the still-unvalidated original 'message' value directly to display rather than performing any sanitization or re-validation. That branch then calls `this.snackBar.open(message, 'X', {...})` at line 27, displaying the raw, unmodified caller-supplied string to the user, again with no sanitization or encoding step performed anywhere in this file — it relies entirely on downstream framework behavior (Angular Material's snack bar template) to be safe. Because this file performs no validation of the untrusted string at any point along entry (18) → lookup (19) → failure branch selection (26) → direct display (27), it is the point in the codebase where an unsanitized, potentially attacker-influenced value is handed to two different interpretation/rendering paths without an intervening check.

If failures are triggered by malformed or unexpected 'message' values being passed into this shared, application-wide service (for example, because an upstream caller is feeding it unexpected or manipulated content), there is no record produced anywhere in this file that such an event occurred, which removes the ability to detect anomalous or abusive call patterns to this widely-used UI utility from logs.

title: Order tracking endpoint has no client-side ownership/ownership-token enforcement, enabling order ID enumeration (IDOR by design)
description: The find method accepts an arbitrary string params from its caller, URL-encodes it, and issues a GET request to /rest/track-order/{params} with no additional binding to the requesting user's identity, session, or an unguessable/opaque order token. Order tracking in this style of feature is typically implemented so that any authenticated (or even unauthenticated) client can retrieve tracking details for any order ID it can supply, since the service performs no local validation that the ID belongs to the caller and passes through whatever value it receives verbatim. If order IDs are sequential or otherwise predictable, an attacker can iterate over IDs to pull other customers' order/tracking data - a trust-boundary violation where the server is expected, but not demonstrably designed here, to re-verify ownership rather than simply returning whatever order matches the supplied identifier. Because the authorization decision (if any) happens entirely server-side and is invisible from this file, the client offers no compensating control (e.g. requiring a per-order secret/token alongside the ID) for what is otherwise a mass-enumerable primary key lookup exposed directly to the caller.

While server-side logging is out of view, this file represents the only client-side hook where such security-relevant failures pass through, and it performs no logging, counting, or reporting of the error before propagating it - meaning a pattern of abuse against the order-tracking endpoint (enumeration, scraping) would produce no client-observable audit trail from this service.

title: No authentication credentials attached to Socket.IO connection
description: The service opens the Socket.IO connection (both branches at lines 22-24 and line 26) without attaching any authentication token, session identifier, or user credential to the `io()` call (e.g., via the `auth` option or a query parameter). Socket.IO's own auth mechanism (`io(url, { auth: {...} })`) is available but unused. As a result, any code path that relies on this socket for real-time features (chat, notifications, order updates, etc.) has no way for the server to bind socket events to an authenticated identity unless the server independently re-validates every incoming event payload. If the corresponding server-side handlers trust the socket connection implicitly (a common pattern paired with an unauthenticated client socket like this), any anonymous client can open a connection and send/receive events meant for authenticated users, because the client never establishes who it is at the transport layer. This is a design gap: the file establishes the trust boundary (the socket channel) without ever deciding to authenticate it, leaving that decision entirely — and silently — to whatever server code happens to be reached. Tracing the full construction path confirms neither branch (the same-origin branch nor the external-hostServer branch) ever supplies credentials, so the gap is structural, not an omission on one code path only.

description: The service creates the underlying Socket.IO client and immediately hands it out via the public `socket()` accessor (line 31-33), but never registers listeners for security-relevant connection events such as `connect_error`, `disconnect`, or `reconnect_failed`. There is no logging, telemetry, or error surfacing anywhere in this file. If the socket handshake is rejected (e.g., due to a bad/expired token check on the server, a CORS rejection, or a forced disconnect after detecting abuse), the client silently drops the event with no record — nothing is logged to the console, sent to a monitoring endpoint, or otherwise surfaced. Walking every statement of the constructor (lines 20-29) confirms this is not a gap on only one branch: neither the same-origin path nor the external hostServer path, nor the wrapping runOutsideAngular call, nor the constructor's closing lines ever attach a listener, so the entire object lifecycle from creation to hand-off at socket() is unobserved.

title: Socket.IO client transport security not enforced (protocol inherited from configurable host)
description: When `environment.hostServer` is not '.', the client connects with `io(environment.hostServer)` (line 26) with no explicit `secure: true` / transport restriction and no validation of the scheme embedded in `environment.hostServer`. Socket.IO derives ws vs wss from the URL passed in; if this configuration value is ever set to (or defaults to) a plain `http://` origin — for example in a staging/misconfigured deployment — the client will silently fall back to unencrypted WebSocket/polling transport, exposing all events (which may include chat content, order data, or session-linked information) in cleartext. title: Order tracking lookup by opaque ID with no ownership/authentication check
description: The spec exercises TrackOrderService.find(), which issues a GET to /rest/track-order/:id and simply resolves whatever the backend returns as the tracking data (line 31-35), and on a 404 only checks the HTTP status (line 44-49). Tracing the full path of the call: the test invokes find() with only a bare order-ID string (line 31); the mock expectation matches the outgoing request purely by URL, with no Authorization/session header asserted as part of the match criteria (line 32); the backend response is flushed and accepted unconditionally as the trusted payload (line 33); the test then only verifies the HTTP verb used (GET) rather than any authorization mechanism attached to the request (line 34); and finally the flushed data is asserted to be returned to the caller as-is (line 35), confirming that nothing in the observable request/response cycle constrains who may retrieve tracking data for a given order ID. If the corresponding backend endpoint authorizes purely on knowledge of the ID string rather than verifying that the requesting user owns the order, any caller who can guess or enumerate an order ID (order IDs here are low-entropy, partially sequential strings like '5267-...') can retrieve another customer's order/tracking details. This is a trust-assumption violation: the client supplies an identifier and the server is trusted to return the right data without re-deriving whether the caller is entitled to see it.

description: The tests assert the service issues requests to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/track-order/...' (non-TLS) rather than an https:// endpoint, and this holds across both the success and error paths, indicating it is the service's fixed/base-URL behavior rather than a one-off. Because HttpTestingController.expectOne matches on the exact URL the service under test constructs, this confirms the service is wired to communicate with the backend over unencrypted HTTP. If this base URL configuration also reflects (or defaults to) the production wiring, order-tracking identifiers and returned order data would traverse the network unencrypted, exposing them to interception or tampering by a network-position attacker. title: Hardcoded absolute backend URL (localhost:3000) revealed in service under test
description: The spec asserts that VulnLinesService.check() posts to the absolute, hardcoded URL 'http://localhost:3000/snippets/verdict' rather than a relative API path or an environment-driven base URL. This confirms the underlying service (vuln-lines.service.ts, not shown here) hardcodes a development-only host/port. If this hardcoded value ships to production builds (or is not properly overridden per-environment), it can cause the app to send challenge-verification requests to the wrong/unreachable host, silently fail security-relevant functionality, or — if an attacker controls a local listener on port 3000 in a shared/dev environment — allow interception or spoofing of verdict responses. This is a configuration-management defect: connection endpoints should be sourced from environment configuration, not hardcoded literals baked into the client bundle. The same literal URL is exercised and confirmed a second time in the error-handling test, showing it is a fixed value used consistently across all call paths rather than a one-off test artifact.

title: No verification that failed challenge-verification requests are logged or monitored
description: The error-handling test (lines 34-44) simulates a failed request to the snippets/verdict endpoint (a security-relevant operation — verification of a submitted coding-challenge 'fix') and only asserts that the HTTP status code is propagated to the caller. There is no assertion, mock, or expectation involving any logging/monitoring call (e.g., a logging service, analytics, or audit trail) being invoked on failure. Walking the full error path — service/httpMock setup, error variable declaration, the failing call, the mocked network error, and the final assertion — shows every step deals only with propagating the raw HTTP error to the subscriber; at no point is a security-relevant logging or alerting side-effect exercised or verified for this failure, even though repeated failed verdict submissions could indicate an attacker probing/brute-forcing challenge answers.

title: 2FA temporary token persisted in browser localStorage
description: The spec file's own test setup reveals how the underlying TwoFactorAuthService constructs its verify() request: it reads a 'totp_tmp_token' value directly out of window.localStorage (see the test seeding `localStorage.setItem('totp_tmp_token', '000000')` before calling `service.verify(...)`), and the resulting HTTP request body contains that value as `tmpToken`. This shows the real service stores a short-lived, security-sensitive authentication artifact (the token proving the user has already supplied a correct password and is now completing step 2 of login) in localStorage rather than in memory, a short-lived sessionStorage entry, or an httpOnly cookie. localStorage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the page's origin, so a single XSS vulnerability anywhere in the SPA (or a malicious/compromised third-party script) can read this token and complete the second factor without ever seeing the user's password, or replay/exfiltrate the token. localStorage entries also have no built-in expiration, so unlike a short-lived in-memory value the tmp token can linger indefinitely across tabs/reloads if the flow is abandoned, widening the window during which it could be stolen and used to finish the TOTP challenge. This is both a weak choice of storage for an authentication-bearing token (crypto-auth: the mechanism that ties a completed password check to the pending TOTP step) and a design decision that trusts client-side, script-accessible storage for a value that gates authentication outcome (insecure-design).

trace.description: Test seeds localStorage key 'totp_tmp_token' with a value, mimicking what the real TwoFactorAuthService does after a successful password login pending 2FA — it persists the temporary token to browser localStorage rather than an in-memory/session-scoped store.
service.verify('123456') is invoked; the implementation (outside this file) must read the tmpToken back out of localStorage to build the verification request.

httpMock.expectOne intercepts the outgoing POST to /rest/2fa/verify; at this point the tmpToken value read from localStorage has already been forwarded, unmodified, into the live HTTP request object's body, making it visible on the wire/in the request payload.

The captured HTTP request body is asserted to equal { tmpToken: '000000', totpToken: '123456' }, confirming the localStorage-resident tmpToken is transmitted as-is to complete the second authentication factor — any code able to read localStorage (e.g. via XSS) can obtain and replay this value.

title: Password change credentials transmitted in URL query string via GET
description: The changePassword() method builds the change-password request as an HTTP GET with the current password, new password, and repeated password concatenated directly into the URL query string (`?current=...&new=...&repeat=...`). Sending credentials as URL parameters instead of in a request body means the plaintext password values are written into browser history, are stored in proxy/CDN/webserver access logs, may be cached by intermediate infrastructure, and can leak via the Referer header if any subsequent cross-origin request or navigation occurs on the page. Using GET for a state-changing, security-sensitive operation is itself a misconfiguration (GET requests are treated as idempotent/cacheable/prefetchable by browsers and intermediaries, and the operation is not protected by the same expectations as a POST). This is a classic case of sensitive authentication data being exposed through insecure transport-layer handling, distinct from encryption of the channel itself.

passwords.current, passwords.new and passwords.repeat are string-concatenated directly into a URL query string.

String concatenation continues: passwords.new is appended as the '&new=' query parameter and passwords.repeat as the '&repeat=' query parameter, completing the fully-built URL containing all three plaintext password values.
this.http.get(...) issues a GET request with the plaintext password values embedded in the URL, exposing them to browser history, server access logs, and proxy caches.

title: OAuth access token passed as URL query parameter to third-party endpoint
description: oauthLogin() forwards the caller-supplied accessToken by appending it directly to the Google userinfo API URL as a query parameter (`?alt=json&access_token=...`). Bearer/access tokens placed in URLs are routinely captured in server access logs, browser history, and can be exfiltrated via the Referer header on any subsequent navigation or embedded resource load from that page. The correct pattern is to send the token in an Authorization header rather than the URL. Because this token is what identifies/authenticates the user to the OAuth provider, its exposure in logs or history constitutes an authentication-credential exposure.

trace.description: oauthLogin(accessToken: string) receives an OAuth access token from a caller outside this file (e.g. the OAuth login callback component).
this.http.get(...) sends the access token as a plaintext URL query parameter to googleapis.com, exposing it to logging and history-based leakage.

title: Client marks user as authenticated before login request completes or succeeds
description: In login(), `this.isLoggedIn.next(true)` is invoked synchronously at line 45, immediately before the actual authentication HTTP POST request is even sent (line 46), and unconditionally regardless of whether that POST later succeeds or fails. Any component subscribed to getLoggedInState()/isLoggedIn (e.g. navigation guards, UI state toggles) will treat the user as authenticated the instant login() is called, not after the server has validated the credentials. If the subsequent POST fails (wrong password, account locked, network error), the application has already broadcast a successful-login signal. This is an authentication-outcome defect: the identity/authentication decision is made client-side ahead of, and independent of, server verification, which can drive downstream authorization/UI decisions on a false premise.

trace.description: login(params: any) is invoked by a caller outside this file (e.g. the login form component) with user-entered credentials.

isLoggedIn.next(true) fires unconditionally before the credential-verifying POST at line 46 is sent or resolved, causing subscribers to treat the session as authenticated regardless of the eventual server response.

title: Temporary 2FA authentication token stored in localStorage
description: The verify() method reads a temporary two-factor authentication token ('totp_tmp_token') directly from browser localStorage and submits it alongside the user-supplied TOTP code to complete authentication. localStorage is a JavaScript-accessible storage mechanism with no HttpOnly or SameSite protections, meaning any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the SPA (or a malicious browser extension/third-party script) can read this token and either replay it or exfiltrate it to an attacker-controlled server. Since this tmpToken represents a partially-authenticated state (password already verified, awaiting only the second factor), theft of this value lets an attacker who can also guess/brute-force or intercept a TOTP code (or who already controls the second factor via other means) complete the login as the victim, bypassing the intended security boundary the second factor is supposed to create. Using a non-JS-accessible mechanism (httpOnly cookie or a short-lived server-side session reference) would close this exposure.

trace.description: verify() is called by a caller outside this file (the 2FA login component) with the user-entered TOTP code.
The pending authentication token is read from localStorage, a storage area readable by any JavaScript running in the page (including injected XSS payloads).
The caller-supplied totpToken is merged into the same request body object alongside the localStorage-sourced tmpToken, forming the complete credential payload that will be sent.
The localStorage-sourced tmpToken is POSTed to /rest/2fa/verify to complete authentication, meaning any script/attacker able to read localStorage can hijack the in-progress 2FA login.

title: TOTP secret potentially returned by /rest/2fa/status outside of the setup flow
description: The status() method's response type (TwoFactorAuthStatusPayload) explicitly includes an optional 'secret' field that is passed through unmodified from the server response. If the backing endpoint returns the raw TOTP seed/secret in the status response (not exclusively during the one-time setup step), any authenticated request to this status endpoint would disclose the cryptographic seed used to generate one-time codes. Possession of this secret allows an attacker to generate valid TOTP codes indefinitely, permanently defeating the second factor without needing to intercept any individual code. The client code performs no restriction or stripping of this field before exposing it to calling components, so if the server is (or becomes) overly permissive about when it includes the secret, this file blindly propagates it to the UI/application state with no additional confidentiality control.

trace.description: status() is invoked by a caller outside this file to check the current 2FA configuration state.
GET /rest/2fa/status response is mapped straight into TwoFactorAuthStatusPayload, which declares an optional raw 'secret' field (see interface at line 24) with no filtering.

The response type declares an optional raw 'secret' field as part of the routine status payload, with no separate type/path reserved only for the initial setup step — the client accepts a secret in this same channel used for ordinary status checks.
The full payload, potentially including the plaintext TOTP secret, is returned to any caller that can invoke status(), with no check limiting exposure to the initial setup step.

title: No client-side logging/monitoring signal on failed 2FA verification or setup/disable attempts
description: All four operations (verify, status, setup, disable) use an identical catchError handler that does nothing but rethrow the error ('catchError((error) => { throw error })'). There is no logging, telemetry, or security-event emission on failed second-factor verification attempts, failed setup attempts, or failed disable attempts. Combined with the sensitivity of these operations (2FA verification is exactly the kind of event that should be monitorable for repeated-failure/brute-force detection, and disable/setup are privileged account-security state changes), the total absence of any client-side signal makes it impossible to correlate suspicious client behavior (e.g., rapid repeated TOTP guesses) with server-side telemetry from this layer, and provides no defense-in-depth alerting hook if the backend logging is itself incomplete.

trace.description: verify() (and similarly setup()/disable() at lines 48 and 56) is the client entrypoint for a security-sensitive 2FA state change or verification, invoked by a caller outside this file.
On failure, the RxJS catchError handler unconditionally rethrows the error with no logging, counting, or event emission of the failed security-sensitive attempt.

The same no-op catchError pattern is repeated for setup(), so a failed attempt to enable 2FA (e.g., wrong password or bad initial token) also produces no monitorable signal, reinforcing that this is a systemic gap across the service rather than one call site.
The same no-op catchError pattern is repeated for disable(), so failed attempts to remove a security control also generate no monitorable signal from this service.

title: Unthrottled challenge-verdict endpoint enables brute-force enumeration of correct answer
description: The check() method forwards an arbitrary caller-supplied 'key' and 'selectedLines' array directly to a server endpoint ('/snippets/verdict') that returns a boolean verdict. There is no client-side (nor any visible server-side, from this file's perspective) restriction on how many times this call can be made, nor any binding of attempts to a session/rate limit. Because the endpoint returns a direct true/false oracle for an arbitrary combination of selected lines, an attacker can script repeated calls that iterate through all possible line combinations to brute-force the correct answer to a security challenge without any genuine understanding of the underlying vulnerability, defeating the purpose of the check. This is a trust/design gap: the server is expected to gate on 'the user actually identified the vulnerable lines' but the design provides no mechanism (throttling, attempt caps, CAPTCHA) to prevent mechanical enumeration of the correct answer through this oracle.

Payload {key, selectedLines} is forwarded as-is to the backend verdict endpoint with no client-side throttling, caching of prior attempts, or limiting logic.
The caller-supplied key is embedded directly into the request body with no attempt-count association.
The caller-supplied selectedLines combination is embedded directly into the request body, allowing any combination to be tried without restriction.

.pipe(map(...), catchError(...)) only shapes/forwards the response or rethrows errors — no rate-limiting, delay, or attempt-cap logic is applied here either, so nothing in the response-handling chain impedes rapid repeated calls.
http.post(this.host, ...) issues the verdict check request; repeated automated calls with varying selectedLines can brute-force the correct answer since the response is a direct boolean oracle.

title: Errors from security-relevant verdict check are swallowed without logging
description: The catchError handler in the check() pipe simply re-throws the error ('throw error') without recording it anywhere (no console log, no telemetry call, no correlation identifier attached). Since this endpoint mediates a security challenge verification flow, failures here (e.g., malformed/oversized selectedLines from a scripted client, repeated invalid keys, or anomalous request patterns indicative of automated probing) are not captured or surfaced for monitoring. This makes it impossible to reconstruct or detect abusive/automated usage patterns (e.g., brute-force attempts described in the companion finding) purely from this client, and if this is the only place errors are observed client-side, no record of the failure reaches any monitoring system.

Error is rethrown with 'throw error' with zero record of the failed verdict-check request, so any anomaly (repeated failures, malformed payloads) leaves no trace for monitoring/alerting.

title: Unbounded selectedLines array forwarded to backend without size validation
description: The check() function accepts a 'selectedLines: number[]' parameter and forwards it verbatim in the POST body to the backend verdict endpoint. There is no validation of array length or element bounds before sending. While normal UI usage would only submit a small set of line numbers, any caller of this exported method (or a modified/scripted client bypassing the UI) can pass an arbitrarily large array, and this file performs no capping or truncation at any point during request assembly before dispatching it. If the backend also fails to bound the payload (unknown from this file), a large request body could be used to consume memory/CPU processing on repeated invocation. Even if the backend enforces limits, this file provides no defense-in-depth validation at the point where it receives external input.

title: Unvalidated, client-controlled financial payload forwarded to wallet balance endpoint
description: The WalletService.put() method accepts an untyped `params` object from whatever caller invokes it and forwards it verbatim as the body of a PUT request to /rest/wallet/balance, with no client-side validation of shape, bounds, sign, or amount, and no confirmation step for what is inherently a financial state-mutating operation. Because `params` is typed `any`, any caller in the Angular app (or any code that can reach this service, e.g. via browser devtools or a compromised/malicious component) can supply an arbitrary object — including negative amounts, oversized values, or unexpected fields — and it is sent to the server unmodified. This file establishes no rule about what a legitimate wallet update looks like; it simply passes caller-supplied data through to a monetary endpoint. If the server trusts this shape or performs incomplete validation, an attacker who can invoke this method with crafted params (e.g. via browser console or a modified request) can manipulate their own account balance. Even if server-side validation exists (outside this file), the design here provides no compensating control for an irreversible financial operation, which is a design gap independent of implementation bugs.

params is forwarded directly into the HTTP PUT body sent to the wallet balance endpoint with no bounds/type checks.
The destination base URL (hostServer) is read from environment configuration, contributing to the target the unvalidated params are sent to.
The target endpoint is the wallet balance resource; a client-controlled, unvalidated payload reaches it directly.

title: Wallet balance operation failures are swallowed without any logging or monitoring
description: Both get() and put() attach a catchError operator that simply re-throws the caught error (`catchError((err) => { throw err })`) with no logging, telemetry, or audit trail recorded for the failure. For a financial operation such as a wallet balance read/update, failed requests (which could indicate tampering attempts, authorization failures, or abuse) are not recorded anywhere in this service layer, making it impossible to reconstruct or detect a pattern of failed/malicious wallet manipulation attempts from this code path alone.

title: Unrestricted, untyped exposure of the native browser window object
description: WindowRefService.nativeWindow returns the entire global `window` object typed as `any`, with no restriction on which properties or methods of window may be accessed or mutated by consuming code. Because the return type is `any`, TypeScript's static type checking is disabled for every downstream use of this object, removing a compile-time safety net that could otherwise catch unsafe patterns (e.g., assigning attacker-influenced strings to window.location.href for open redirect, calling window.eval, reading/writing document.cookie, or using window.postMessage/window.opener without origin checks). This is a design choice rather than an implementation bug: the service was designed as a thin, unrestricted pass-through to the global object instead of exposing a narrow, vetted subset of window functionality (e.g., only location, only localStorage with validation). Any component or service in the Angular application that injects WindowRefService inherits full, unchecked access to the global browser object, and any misuse downstream will not be flagged by the type system because the return value is `any`. While the concrete exploit depends on how consumers use nativeWindow (outside this file), the design itself establishes no boundary or validation layer around a highly sensitive global object, which is the kind of missing compensating control the insecure-design class targets for inherently risky operations like arbitrary navigation, cross-frame messaging, or storage access.

The getter simply forwards the call to the internal getWindow() helper without any filtering, wrapping, or validation of what will be returned.

title: Client-controlled wallet balance value trusted without server-side re-derivation evidenced in test
description: The spec exercises WalletService.put() by passing an arbitrary numeric/object value directly ('put(1)' and 'put({amount: 1})') which is sent verbatim as the body of a PUT to /rest/wallet/balance. The test never exercises or asserts any client-side validation, bounds-checking, or server-derived recomputation of the wallet balance — the value the caller supplies is what is transmitted at every step: it is handed off to the mocked HTTP layer unchanged, the mock is only checked for HTTP method and response echo (not for any sanitization of the submitted amount), and the exact same unguarded pattern is repeated in a second, independent test with a different arbitrary value shape ({amount: 1}). If the backend mirrors this trust (accepting the client-supplied amount as authoritative rather than re-deriving the balance from a ledger of transactions), an attacker who can reach this endpoint directly (bypassing the Angular UI) could set their wallet balance to an arbitrary value — a classic 'trust assumption violation' where the client determines a value (money) that the server should independently validate/derive. This file cannot show the server-side handler, but it demonstrates the client design pattern of shipping a raw client-chosen amount to a financial mutation endpoint with no local validation layer at any point in the call chain.

title: Wallet balance endpoint hardcoded to plaintext HTTP, not HTTPS
description: All four test cases assert the WalletService issues requests to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/wallet/balance' using plain HTTP rather than HTTPS. The unencrypted URL is used consistently across every intermediate step of both the read and write flows — it is the literal string checked in the GET-path expectation, remains unencrypted as the flow proceeds through response flushing and assertions, and is used again unchanged when the PUT-path test sets up its own request expectation. This suggests the underlying WalletService implementation constructs requests against a non-TLS endpoint. Wallet balance is sensitive financial data; transmitting it (or accepting updates to it) over unencrypted HTTP would expose the balance value and any session/auth headers riding with the request to network-level interception or manipulation (missing transport-layer security enforcement, OWASP A05). This cannot be fully confirmed since environment-specific base URL configuration lives outside this file, but the literal string baked into the test at every step of both flows is unencrypted HTTP.

title: Password change transmitted via GET request with credentials in URL query string
description: The UserService.changePassword() client method (as verified by this spec) issues the password-change operation as an HTTP GET request with the current password, new password, and repeated password embedded directly in the URL query string (?current=foo&new=bar&repeat=bar) rather than in a POST/PUT request body. Placing credential material in a URL means it will be captured in browser history, server access logs, reverse-proxy/CDN logs, and can leak via the Referer header to third-party resources loaded on subsequent pages. This is a textbook cryptographic/authentication transport failure: sensitive authentication material is exposed through channels that are not designed to protect confidentiality (plaintext logs), independent of whether TLS is used for the connection itself. An attacker with access to any of these log stores (ops staff, compromised logging pipeline, browser history on a shared machine) can recover a victim's current and new plaintext passwords.

The test asserts the resulting HTTP call is made to a URL that embeds the credentials as query-string parameters (?current=foo&new=bar&repeat=bar).

title: OAuth access token sent as URL query parameter to third-party API
description: UserService.oauthLogin() sends the OAuth bearer access token as a GET query-string parameter (access_token=at) to the Google userinfo endpoint instead of using the standard Authorization: Bearer header. Tokens placed in URLs are routinely captured in server access logs, CDN/proxy logs, and can be exfiltrated via the Referer header when the response page subsequently makes further outbound requests. This is a recognized anti-pattern explicitly warned against by OAuth2 best practices (RFC 6750) because it increases the blast radius of token leakage well beyond the intended bearer-token lifetime and scope.

title: Unscoped 'authentication-details' listing endpoint with no per-user filtering
description: UserService.find() is confirmed by this spec to call GET /rest/user/authentication-details/ with no request parameters at all (the test explicitly asserts req.request.params.toString() is falsy). A GET endpoint named 'authentication-details' that accepts no identifying/query parameter and is invoked by a generic find() (no user id argument) suggests it returns authentication-related records for users in bulk rather than being scoped to the currently authenticated caller. If the underlying server endpoint does not itself enforce per-user or per-role authorization on this data, any authenticated (or, depending on server config, unauthenticated) caller could enumerate other users' authentication-related information via this client call — a Broken Object Level Authorization pattern. The full server-side authorization logic lives outside this file, so this is reported as the point where the file's own contract (no scoping parameter emitted) demonstrates the client never attempts to restrict the query to the caller's own identity.

The unscoped GET request targets /rest/user/authentication-details/, an endpoint whose name and lack of caller-derived identifier suggest it may return authentication-related data for multiple/all users without object-level authorization checks enforced by this client contract.

title: Stored XSS via explicit Angular sanitizer bypass on user-submitted feedback comment

title: Generic console logging of subscription errors without structured/security context
description: Both the application-configuration fetch (lines 68-73) and the feedback fetch (lines 105-112) catch errors and simply forward them to the browser console via console.error(err), with no structured logging, no correlation identifier, and no distinction between benign and security-relevant failures (e.g., repeated failures that might indicate probing of the config or feedback endpoints). Because this only writes to the client's own browser console, it has low direct security impact, but it means no server-side or centralized telemetry is generated from client-observed failures, and if the underlying HTTP error object carries backend details (stack traces, internal error messages) it is dumped as-is to the client console, potentially exposing internal implementation details to anyone with devtools access to that browser session.

title: Client trusts URL-supplied addressId for address lookup and update with no ownership check
description: The address-create/edit component reads an addressId directly from the Angular route parameter map and uses it, unvalidated, both to fetch an existing address (getById) and to persist changes to it (put). There is no code in this file that verifies the address identified by this attacker-controllable identifier actually belongs to the currently logged-in user before displaying its data in the form or submitting an update against it. Because the identifier used to determine both the 'edit' workflow and the target resource comes entirely from client-navigable URL state (e.g. /address/edit/<id>), a user can change the id in the browser address bar to attempt to view or overwrite another user's saved address (name, phone number, street, city, zip, country). Whether this is actually exploitable depends on whether the backend AddressService/API endpoint scopes the lookup and update by the authenticated user's id - that enforcement point is outside this file, but this file itself performs no defensive check and blindly trusts the route parameter as an authorization token, which is the classic BOLA client-side pattern combined with a design assumption that URL-derived identifiers imply ownership.

title: Business rules for address fields appear enforced only via client-side Angular form validators
description: The spec exercises Angular reactive-form Validators for the address form: mobile number must fall in the range [1111111, 9999999999] (lines 176-185), pin code capped at 8 characters (lines 152-162), and street address capped at 160 characters (lines 164-174). These tests confirm that AddressCreateComponent relies on client-side Validators (Validators.min/max/maxLength) to enforce these constraints before the value is sent through AddressService.save()/put() (exercised at lines 200, 211, 220, 229). Walking the full path shows the pattern is consistent across every save flow tested in this file: boundary values are checked only against the client FormControl's .valid flag (176-184), a translation message is generated purely client-side for the invalid case (187-192), and then, independently of whether any field constraint was actually enforced, component.save() is invoked (200, 211, 220) which forwards form values straight to the mocked AddressService.save/put and, on the mocked success or failure response, unconditionally calls resetForm()/ngOnInit() (201-204, 213-215) or shows a snackbar (222, 231). At no point does this spec assert that a value violating the range/length constraints is rejected by save() itself or by the service layer — the component and its tests treat the Angular Validators as the sole gate. Because Angular form validation runs entirely in the browser, an attacker who calls the underlying REST endpoint directly (bypassing the Angular UI and its FormControls) can submit a mobileNum, zipCode, or streetAddress value that violates these constraints unless the server enforces the same rules independently. This is a trust-assumption violation pattern (client controls a value the server should validate) if the backend does not duplicate this validation; that backend/service code is outside this file so it cannot be confirmed here, but the fact that this file's tests only assert client-side FormControl validity and unconditional save-then-reset behavior, never a validation-gated rejection at the save() boundary, is the visible symptom.

title: Component silently swallows configuration/feedback load errors via generic console.error with no structured/security logging
description: The tests at lines 157-164 and 198-206 confirm that when the application configuration load or feedback load fails, the component catches the error and calls console.error, then continues without throwing. There is no evidence of any structured logging, alerting, correlation ID, or monitoring integration — errors are only surfaced to the browser devtools console (client-side), which is not visible to any backend monitoring/alerting system. Both independent failure paths in this component (config retrieval and feedback retrieval) follow the identical pattern: catch, console.error, silently continue — confirming this is the component's uniform (and only) error-handling/observability strategy rather than an isolated oversight. If these failures are indicative of backend/API tampering, outages, or exploitation attempts (e.g. a malformed configuration response, or a feedback endpoint being abused), there is no server-side or centralized record of the event, only an ephemeral client console entry that most users never see. This is a logging-monitoring gap for what could be a security-relevant signal, though I cannot confirm from this file alone whether upstream logging/monitoring exists elsewhere in the app.

title: Client-supplied price/quantity accepted with only lower-bound clamping — no upper-bound or business-rule validation
description: The spec file documents the behavior of AccountingComponent.modifyPrice()/modifyQuantity(): whatever numeric value is passed in is forwarded essentially unchanged to productService.put()/quantityService.put(), with the only safeguard being that negative values are clamped to zero (lines 253-261). There is no upper bound, no comparison against the current stored price/quantity, and no re-derivation of the value on a trusted source — the client-supplied number is trusted almost entirely. The template-rendering tests (lines 346-368) confirm this value originates directly from a raw text <input matInput> bound in the UI and is passed straight into modifyPrice/modifyQuantity on button click, meaning whatever a user types into the input field becomes the new authoritative price/quantity for a product identified purely by an id parameter the caller also controls. A parallel test for arbitrarily large accepted values (line 195, price=100) shows the same absence of an upper bound. If this component is reachable by an authenticated non-admin user (a fact this file cannot confirm, but it establishes no defense-in-depth here), a user could set any product's price to 0 or an attacker-favorable value and then purchase it, or set stock quantity to an arbitrary large number — a textbook 'client determines a value the server should independently validate/derive' design flaw (OWASP A04).

title: Raw backend error payloads logged to the browser console instead of a secured audit/monitoring channel
description: Numerous tests assert that on any failed API call (product search, order history fetch, quantity fetch, price/quantity modification, delivery status toggle) the component calls console.log(error) with the entire raw error object/payload (e.g. lines 135, 142, 157, 164, 173, 182). This means whatever the backend returns as an error body (which could include stack traces, internal object structure, or other diagnostic detail in a non-mocked environment) is written directly to the end user's browser developer console — visible to that same user/attacker, not to any centralized, access-controlled security monitoring system. This is simultaneously a security-logging failure (no server-side/security-relevant audit trail is produced; the 'log' target is the attacker's own browser) and a misconfiguration (debug-style verbose error logging left active for what appears to be normal application flow, not a development-only code path).

title: Next-step gating never validates that an address was actually selected
description: The component exposes `showNextButton` to control whether the user may proceed to the next step of what is presumably a checkout/address-selection workflow. This flag is hard-coded to `true` at declaration (line 21) and is never re-evaluated or tied to the state of `addressId`. The only handler in the file, `getMessage(id)`, merely stores whatever value the child `AddressComponent` emits into `addressId` (lines 23-25) and does not flip `showNextButton` to `false` when no address has been chosen (addressId still `undefined`) nor validate that the emitted id corresponds to a real, owned address. `addressId` starts life as `undefined` (line 20), meaning the component's own declared state already represents 'no selection yet', yet nothing in getMessage cross-references that state against showNextButton when the id is written (line 24). If the surrounding template (not shown) uses `showNextButton` to gate a 'Next'/'Continue' control, a user can advance the checkout workflow without ever selecting a delivery address, because the enabling condition is a static value rather than a derived one based on `addressId` being set.

title: Untyped, unvalidated addressId accepted directly from child component and trusted downstream
description: addressId is declared as `any` (line 20) and is set verbatim from whatever the child AddressComponent emits (line 24), with no type check, no format validation, and no verification that the id refers to an address that belongs to the current user. Because Angular's type system is bypassed with `any`, any value (string, object, malicious payload, or an address id belonging to another user) can be stored and — presumably — later passed to a router navigation or an order-related API call made elsewhere in the checkout flow. This file establishes no rule that the client-supplied id must be re-validated by the server before being trusted as 'the selected address for this user', which is the kind of trust-assumption gap that enables IDOR-style abuse if the downstream consumer (outside this file) does not itself re-derive ownership. The entrypoint and sink for the eventual use of addressId are outside this file, so this is reported as a boundary/trust-assumption defect visible at the point this component accepts and stores the value.

While this is a frontend component and client-side logging is not typically security-critical on its own, if this selection feeds a security-relevant business flow (e.g., choosing the delivery/billing address used for an order), the absence of any client-side signal makes it harder to reconstruct which address a user selected during a session if a dispute or fraud investigation occurs later.

title: Privileged product/order mutation actions exposed with no in-component authorization check
description: AccountingComponent implements functions that perform highly privileged business mutations — modifyQuantity() changes stock quantity, modifyPrice() changes a product's price, and changeDeliveryStatus() toggles an order's delivered flag. None of these functions perform any check of the current user's role or permission before issuing the backend call; the component simply forwards whatever id/value it is given straight to the service layer. The component's only defense against unauthorized use is whatever route guard/backend authorization exists outside this file (not visible here). If that external control is weak, missing, or if the component's public methods are invoked directly (e.g., via Angular DevTools, browser console access to the component instance, or a compromised/omitted route guard), any authenticated (or even unauthenticated, depending on the guard) user could arbitrarily zero out or change product prices, restock quantities, or mark orders delivered — a classic broken function-level authorization pattern (API5) with real business impact (price manipulation, inventory fraud, fraudulent delivery marking). Because this file never re-derives or checks the caller's privilege before allowing these state-changing operations, it also represents an insecure design: the server-side privilege decision is fully outsourced to a control this file cannot see or enforce.

title: Unbounded fetch of full product catalog and full order history with no pagination request parameters

Both results are pulled entirely into client memory and only paginated client-side afterward via MatTableDataSource. If the catalog or order history grows large (or is deliberately inflated by an attacker who can create many products/orders), every load of this component forces the backend to serialize and the browser to hold the complete dataset, and this happens on every ngAfterViewInit invocation (line 58-61) with no caching or size cap. This is a resource-consumption risk for both the backend (unbounded query result) and the client (unbounded in-memory array), especially since these calls run automatically whenever the view initializes, without any rate limiting visible in this file.

title: Raw backend error text and unsanitized product name shown via snackbar notifications
description: In the error handlers for modifyQuantity/modifyPrice (and similarly changeDeliveryStatus), the raw err.error value returned from the backend is passed directly to snackBarHelperService.open() without any validation or sanitization (lines 134, 148, 160). Likewise, product.name — data originating from the product service — is interpolated directly into a template string shown to the user (lines 130, 144). If the backend echoes any caller-influenced content in its error body (a common pattern for validation error messages), or if a product name can contain attacker-supplied markup, and the underlying MatSnackBar/SnackBarHelperService renders this content in a context where markup or scripts can execute (e.g., via an innerHTML-based custom snackbar template), this becomes a reflected or stored XSS vector. This cannot be fully confirmed without seeing SnackBarHelperService's rendering implementation, but the data reaches the display layer with no encoding or sanitization performed in this file.

title: Component logs raw API error responses to browser console instead of a monitored security log
description: The specs at lines 107-113 and 115-121 assert that AddressComponent.ngOnInit() and deleteAddress() call console.log(error) directly with the raw error object/string returned by the AddressService HTTP calls when they fail (mocked here as throwError('Error')). This confirms the underlying component's error-handling path funnels backend/API failure information straight to the browser's developer console rather than to any structured, server-side security-monitoring or audit-logging mechanism. Because this is client-side console output, (1) it provides no server-side visibility into failed address lookups/deletions that could indicate probing or enumeration attempts (e.g., repeated failed deleteAddress calls against IDs the user does not own), and (2) if the underlying error object ever carries backend stack traces or internal details (common with unhandled Angular HttpClient error objects), that data is exposed in the end user's console, visible to anyone with access to the browser devtools or to third-party scripts that hook console output. There is no evidence anywhere in this spec of an alternative alerting/monitoring path (e.g., a call to a logging service) being exercised.

title: deleteAddress appears to operate on a bare numeric ID with no visible ownership check (inferred BOLA risk)
description: The tests at lines 115-121 and 123-130 call component.deleteAddress(1) with only a bare numeric address ID and assert that AddressService.del is invoked and the address list is subsequently reloaded. Nowhere in these specs is there any assertion, mock expectation, or setup that ties the deleted address ID to the currently authenticated user, nor any test verifying that deletion is rejected when the ID belongs to another user. The del and get mocks are configured generically (accepting/returning arbitrary values keyed only by id), and the post-delete reload (via load()/get()) fires unconditionally on success with no gating check observable in the spec. Because these are the only black-box tests exercising the deletion code path visible to this analysis, they do not exercise or prove the existence of a per-resource ownership check before the DELETE call is dispatched to the backend service. This is consistent with (but does not conclusively prove) an Object-level authorization gap in the underlying component/service where any authenticated user could invoke deleteAddress with an arbitrary ID belonging to another user, relying entirely on server-side enforcement that is outside the scope of this file. Flagged at reduced confidence since the actual authorization boundary (if any) lives in the AddressService/backend, not in this spec file.

expect(addressService.del).toHaveBeenCalled() confirms the delete call reaches the service layer keyed purely off the supplied numeric id, with no ownership check observable in this test suite.

title: Selected delivery address ID is trusted from client-side sessionStorage without server-side re-validation shown
description: The test at lines 132-137 shows that component.chooseAddress() writes the component's in-memory addressId property directly into sessionStorage via setItem('addressId', ...). The addressId value originates purely from client-side component state (e.g., set by clicking a radio button in the address table) and is persisted unencrypted/unsigned in sessionStorage, a location fully readable and writable by the end user via devtools. If a later step in the checkout/delivery workflow (outside this file) reads this sessionStorage value and trusts it as the authoritative selection for the order without re-verifying server-side that the referenced address actually belongs to the authenticated user, an attacker could tamper with the stored addressId to reference an address ID belonging to another account. This spec file only proves the write path exists and is unguarded; the read/trust path is outside this file's visibility, so this is reported as a design-trust concern rather than a confirmed exploit.

component.chooseAddress() is invoked, the method under test that persists the client-chosen id.

A spy is attached to Storage.prototype.setItem to observe the persistence call the chooseAddress method is about to make, confirming sessionStorage is the target sink for the unvalidated client-side id.

Assertion confirms setItem('addressId', 1) writes the client-controlled address identifier into sessionStorage, a value later presumably trusted by a downstream checkout step outside this file without visible re-validation.

title: Raw server error objects logged to browser console
description: When the address list fetch or address deletion request fails, the raw error object returned by the backend (err) is passed directly to console.log() in addition to being shown in a snackbar. Angular HTTP error objects frequently contain internal details (stack traces, backend messages, request URLs, sometimes validation details echoing submitted data). Logging this unfiltered object to the browser console persists it in the user's devtools history and can leak internal implementation details to anyone with access to that browser session (shared/kiosk machines, browser extensions with console access, screen-recording malware). This is a logging hygiene defect: sensitive/internal diagnostic data is emitted to a client-side log sink without redaction. The same pattern occurs twice in this file: once for the address-list fetch and once for the address-delete call.

Same pattern repeated in deleteAddress's error handler: console.log(err) after a failed delete request.

title: Selected address ID trusted from client-writable sessionStorage for checkout without re-validation
description: chooseAddress() takes this.addressId — a value populated purely from a UI selection event (emitSelectionToParent) — and persists it verbatim into sessionStorage under the key 'addressId', then immediately navigates to the delivery-method step. sessionStorage is fully writable/readable by the end user (via devtools or any script running in the page) and is not signed, encrypted, or bound to a server-issued session artifact. The only gate on whether addressId is set is a UI selection-model check (this.selection.hasValue()), which carries no ownership semantics whatsoever. If the downstream checkout/order-placement code (outside this file) reads sessionStorage.getItem('addressId') and uses it to resolve or attach a shipping address to an order without an explicit server-side ownership check tying that address id to the authenticated user, an attacker can simply overwrite the sessionStorage value (or manipulate the emitted selection) to reference another user's address id and have it accepted as their own delivery address — a classic client-controls-a-value-the-server-should-derive/verify design flaw feeding into a potential BOLA on order placement.

title: deleteAddress performs no local ownership check before issuing delete request
description: deleteAddress(id) forwards a caller-supplied numeric id directly to addressService.del(id) with no verification in this component that the id corresponds to an address actually present in this.storedAddresses (i.e., belonging to the currently authenticated user). While the UI normally derives id from rows rendered from the user's own address list, the id parameter itself is not cross-checked against storedAddresses before the delete call is issued, and the network request itself is fully attacker-controllable (e.g., via devtools or direct API call) regardless of what the UI displays. Whether this is exploitable depends entirely on whether the backend DELETE endpoint enforces per-resource ownership — that enforcement is outside this file and cannot be confirmed here, but this file itself adds no defense-in-depth check and blindly trusts the numeric id it is given, passing it straight into the outbound call with no intervening validation.

title: Admin user/feedback listing appears unbounded (no pagination/limit)
description: The tests exercise AdministrationComponent.findAllUsers() and findAllFeedbacks() with zero arguments, and assert that all mocked records returned by UserService.find()/FeedbackService.find() end up directly in the table data sources (component.userDataSource.data, component.feedbackDataSource.data). There is no test exercising a page size, offset, limit, or query filter being passed to find(), which indicates the underlying component methods call the backend service with no bounding parameters and simply dump whatever comes back into the UI data source. On the admin page (which typically surfaces the full user table and full feedback table), if the corresponding backend endpoints are equally unbounded, an admin - or anyone who can reach these methods - triggers retrieval of the entire Users/Feedback collections in one call, which is a resource-consumption risk that scales with data size and also an insecure-design gap since no upper bound was ever established for this operation.

Mocked UserService.find() returns an array with no pagination parameters observed or asserted, implying the real call is unbounded.

The injected UserService mock's find() is declared as a bare vi.fn() with no parameter contract enforced, so nothing in the test harness requires or validates a pagination/limit argument being passed by the component.

title: Admin error handling only logs to browser console, no security event logging or user feedback beyond raw error string
description: Multiple tests (for failed user lookup, failed feedback lookup, and failed feedback deletion) explicitly mock/suppress console.log before triggering the failure path, and then assert that component.error is set to the raw error value returned by the observable (e.g. the string 'Error'). This confirms the underlying component's error handling for these admin actions consists of console.log(err) plus storing the raw error text in a component property, with no indication of any server-side security logging, alerting, or structured audit trail for failed administrative operations (failed lookups, failed deletions). Because these are admin-privileged operations, failures (e.g., repeated failed feedback deletions, which could indicate probing or a broken permission check) are not tracked anywhere but the browser console, which is invisible to defenders and cannot be correlated with other events for incident detection.

title: Stored XSS via bypassSecurityTrustHtml() on user email in admin user list
description: findAllUsers() retrieves the full user list from the backend and, for every user, builds a raw HTML string that embeds the user's email address directly into a tag, then explicitly calls Angular's DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml() on it. bypassSecurityTrustHtml disables Angular's built-in output encoding and tells the framework to trust the string as safe HTML, which is then bound into the DOM (in the corresponding template, not shown in this file). Because the email field is attacker-controlled at registration time (Juice Shop places no HTML-safe restriction on the email field) and is never HTML-encoded before this call, an attacker can register an account with an email such as `@test.com` and have arbitrary script execute in the browser of any administrator who opens the Administration panel. This is a stored XSS that specifically targets the highest-privilege user (an admin), making the impact severe (session/cookie theft, full account takeover, or further admin-privileged actions performed on the attacker's behalf).

The subscription's next callback receives the raw users array from the backend response.

title: Stored XSS via bypassSecurityTrustHtml() on feedback comment in admin feedback list

An attacker can submit a feedback comment containing an HTML/script payload (e.g. ``), and when an administrator opens the Administration page, the payload executes in the admin's browser context, since bypassSecurityTrustHtml disables Angular's default output encoding for this value.

title: Admin-level user/feedback data and deletion actions invoked with no client-side authorization check
description: The AdministrationComponent unconditionally calls findAllUsers(), findAllFeedbacks() on init, and exposes deleteFeedback(id) for any feedback id, with no role/authorization check present anywhere in this file before issuing these privileged operations. If route-level guarding is weak or absent (not visible in this file), any authenticated user who can load this component can list every user's data and delete arbitrary feedback records simply by having the component instantiate and its methods invoked. Function-level authorization for these admin-only actions is not enforced here; it must rely entirely on a guard or server-side check outside this file, which cannot be confirmed from this component alone.

description: findAllUsers() and findAllFeedbacks() call userService.find() and feedbackService.find() with no arguments limiting result size (no page size, offset, or filter parameters). Pagination (MatTableDataSource + MatPaginator) is applied only client-side after the full result set has already been retrieved from the backend and held in memory in the browser. If the underlying service methods do not themselves enforce a server-side cap, this pattern causes the entire users or feedback table to be pulled into the client on every page load, which does not scale and can be leveraged for resource exhaustion as data grows (repeatedly reloading the admin page against a large table).

title: Client-controlled preference cookie set without secure attributes
description: toggleShowToolCalls() writes a persistent cookie ('show_tool_calls') via CookieService.put with only an 'expires' option; no 'secure', 'sameSite', or 'httpOnly'-equivalent restriction is configured. While this specific cookie only toggles a UI display preference (not a session/auth token), it is set without any transport or scripting restriction, meaning it can be sent over plain HTTP and is readable/writable by any script on the page. This is a minor misconfiguration in cookie handling that is worth remediating even though the immediate blast radius is limited to a UI setting.

title: Authentication state derived solely from presence of a 'token' key in localStorage, with no validation of the token's contents
description: The test suite for LoginGuard (lines 29-34, 36-41) demonstrates that canActivate() treats the user as authenticated purely because a localStorage entry named 'token' exists — the value used, the literal string 'TOKEN', is not even a well-formed JWT. There is no check for token format, expiration, or cryptographic validity before the guard grants access. Because localStorage is fully attacker/client-controlled, any script or manual browser console interaction that sets localStorage.setItem('token', <anything>) will satisfy this guard's authentication check. Since this is the only authentication gate demonstrated in the file, an attacker with local script execution (e.g. via any XSS elsewhere in the app) or simply by manually editing storage can force LoginGuard.canActivate() to return true without ever possessing a real, validly-issued credential.

guard.canActivate() is invoked with only this raw string present in storage.

Test asserts canActivate() returns true, confirming the guard's authentication decision is based only on key-presence, not on token validity.

title: Role-based authorization (Admin/Accounting/Deluxe guards) is driven by a JWT payload decoded without signature verification
description: The 'returns payload from decoding a valid JWT' test (lines 43-52) shows tokenDecode() simply base64-decodes the JWT payload segment and returns it as an object; the 'invalid JWT' test (lines 54-59) shows failure is only detected by malformed structure, not by signature mismatch. AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, and DeluxeGuard all base their entire authorization decision on `loginGuard.tokenDecode().data.role` (e.g. lines 100, 107, 115, 123, 160, 167, 175, 183, 219, 226, 233, 240) — i.e., on the unverified claims of a client-supplied token. Since the client never cryptographically verifies the signature before trusting the role claim, and the token itself lives in client-controlled localStorage, an attacker who can influence or forge the localStorage token (e.g., by constructing an unsigned/self-crafted JWT with `role: 'admin'` in the payload, since the decode logic shown here performs no signature check) can cause these guards to grant Admin/Accounting/Deluxe-level client-side access. This is both a broken function-level authorization control (privileged roles reachable via forged claims) and a crypto weakness (missing signature verification on a security-relevant token before trusting its claims for an authorization decision).

tokenDecode() returns the raw decoded payload object without any indication a signature check occurred.
AdminGuard.canActivate() consults `loginGuard.tokenDecode().data.role` to decide admin access, trusting the unverified claim.

The decoded object's fields (sub, name, iat) are asserted directly from the base64 payload, confirming the decode routine has no verification step interposed between decoding and returning the claims.

In the AdminGuard test module, LoginGuard.tokenDecode is stubbed as a bare mock function returning arbitrary data, mirroring the real contract observed above: tokenDecode is a pure decode-and-return call with no verification gate that AdminGuard could rely on.
AdminGuard instance is retrieved via injection, wired to the unverified-decode-producing LoginGuard mock.

title: Security-critical role/authorization decisions rely entirely on client-side Angular route guards without evidence of independent server-side re-verification
description: This spec file shows that all meaningful access decisions (login gate, admin-only, accounting-only, deluxe-only) are implemented as Angular CanActivate guards executing entirely in the browser, deriving their verdict from data (a JWT and its decoded role claim) stored in localStorage — data fully under the end-user's control. Angular route guards are a UX/navigation control, not a security boundary: a user can bypass them by calling backend REST endpoints directly, by manipulating localStorage, or by disabling/patching the guard in devtools. Nothing in this file (nor referenced by it) indicates that the corresponding backend endpoints independently re-check the caller's authenticated role using a properly verified credential before serving privileged data or actions. If the backend trusts the same unverified JWT decoding pattern demonstrated here (tokenDecode without signature check) for its own authorization, or if it assumes the frontend guard is the sole gate, this constitutes a design flaw: the app's only demonstrated authorization mechanism for admin/accounting/deluxe functionality is enforceable purely client-side.

trace.description: AdminGuard.canActivate() test shows role-gating implemented as an Angular route guard, a client-executed check.
The guard's verdict is driven entirely by locally decoded/mocked token data rather than a server round-trip confirming the role.

LoginGuard, the sole collaborator AdminGuard depends on for its role decision, is substituted with an in-memory mock object — demonstrating that AdminGuard's entire contract is `ask this one local object for a role and branch on it`, with no other dependency (e.g. an HTTP call) in its decision path.

An HttpClient is configured in the test bed alongside the guard, yet it plays no role in the canActivate() path exercised by these tests — no network round-trip to re-verify the role server-side occurs between token decode and the access decision.
AdminGuard instance obtained via injection, wired only to the local LoginGuard mock with no external verification step.
canActivate() returning true/false is the entirety of the enforcement demonstrated in this file for privileged routes, with no corresponding server-side authorization check visible or referenced.

title: Checkout authorization gate relies solely on presence of an arbitrary client-side token string
description: The test suite in this spec file demonstrates that BasketComponent.checkout() decides whether the user is allowed to proceed to the address-selection/purchase flow purely based on whether Storage.getItem(...) returns any truthy value. In the 'no auth token' test, getItem is mocked to return null and the component redirects to /login; in the 'auth token stored' test, getItem is mocked to return the literal string 'valid-token' (not a real JWT, not a signed/structured token) and the component immediately navigates to /address/select. This shows the component's security decision is 'is there *any* non-null string in storage under this key?' rather than 'is there a cryptographically valid, unexpired, signed token that this client can be trusted to have obtained legitimately?'. Since localStorage/sessionStorage is fully attacker/user-controlled in the browser, any script (XSS payload, browser extension, or the user themselves via devtools) can set an arbitrary string into this storage key and cause the client to treat itself as authenticated for the checkout navigation flow, without any signature, expiry, or format validation performed client-side. While the backend presumably re-validates on actual purchase/order APIs, this file's own tests establish that the client-side authentication gate for the checkout workflow step is a bare existence check on an unsigned string — a weak authentication check and a trust-assumption violation (client blindly trusts a value it itself stores) that skips a step of the intended workflow (real credential/session validation) for anyone able to write to storage.

component.checkout() is invoked; based on the null token it triggers navigation to /login with a redirectUrl.
In the second test, Storage.prototype.getItem is mocked to return the bare string 'valid-token' — an arbitrary, unsigned, unstructured value rather than a real credential/session artifact.

title: No security-relevant logging around checkout authentication gate (failed vs. successful auth check)
description: The tests show two distinct security-relevant outcomes of the checkout() flow: (1) a user without a stored auth token is silently redirected to /login (an authentication-required denial), and (2) a user with a token is allowed to proceed to checkout. Nowhere in the exercised behavior (nor inferable from these tests) is there any indication that either outcome is logged or reported for monitoring purposes — e.g., no call to a logging/analytics service is asserted or mocked in either test. Absence of logging for an authorization/authentication gate on a state-changing workflow (checkout) means repeated forged-token attempts or repeated unauthenticated checkout attempts (e.g., token stuffing, replay, or probing) would leave no trace for detection. This is inferred from the file's behavior surface; the actual component implementation is outside this file, so confidence is limited.

title: Checkout gate relies solely on client-side presence check of localStorage token
description: The checkout() method treats the mere presence of a value under the 'token' key in localStorage as proof of authentication (`localStorage.getItem('token') == null`). It does not validate the token's signature, structure, or expiration — it only checks that some string exists. Any user can open the browser console and run `localStorage.setItem('token','anything')` to satisfy this check and be routed straight into the address-selection/checkout flow (line 40) without ever having authenticated with the backend. Because this is the only gate present in this component before advancing the checkout workflow, it demonstrates both a broken/insufficient identity check (an authentication decision made from unauthenticated, attacker-controlled client storage) and a design flaw where the client is trusted to assert its own authentication state instead of the server deciding it. Real protection would have to come from server-side authorization on every subsequent API call, but this component's own gate is trivially bypassable and gives a false impression of enforcement to anyone reading or relying on this code path.

title: Client-controlled basket total persisted to sessionStorage for later checkout use
description: getBonusPoints() receives a [number, number] tuple from a child component and immediately writes the first element (item total) into sessionStorage as 'itemTotal', with no server-side derivation or validation. sessionStorage is fully accessible and editable via browser devtools by the end user. If any later step of the checkout/payment flow (outside this file) trusts this sessionStorage value rather than re-deriving the order total from server-authoritative data, a user could alter 'itemTotal' before proceeding, e.g. to reduce the amount charged. This is a classic 'client controls a value the server should validate/recompute' trust-boundary violation. The downstream consumer of 'itemTotal' is outside this file, so exploitability depends on how it is used later, but writing an untrusted, easily-tampered total into persistent client storage for reuse in a financial workflow is itself the design defect visible here.

title: No logging of unauthenticated checkout attempts / access-control denials

There is no call to any logging/monitoring service anywhere in this file.

title: API failures from challenge notification only logged to browser console, no server-side audit trail

This writes the error solely to the invoking user's local browser console. If this notification endpoint is being abused (e.g., repeated calls, malformed challenge names, or errors indicating backend issues/attack attempts), there is no way for defenders to detect, investigate, or reconstruct the event from server logs, because the failure never leaves the client. title: Authorization decisions based on client-controlled, unsigned-verification JWT payload
description: AdminGuard and AccountingGuard determine whether a user may access privileged routes by calling LoginGuard.tokenDecode(), which reads the 'token' value directly out of localStorage (fully writable by the client/attacker via devtools or any script) and passes it to jwt-decode. jwt-decode only base64-decodes the JWT payload; it performs no signature verification whatsoever. The decoded 'role' claim is then compared directly against roles.admin / roles.accounting to grant or deny access (lines 54, 70). Because the signature is never checked in this file, and the token source is a client-writable storage location, an attacker can craft an arbitrary JWT payload (e.g. {data:{role:'admin'}}), base64-encode it into a syntactically valid (but unsigned/invalid-signature) JWT, place it in localStorage, and the AdminGuard/AccountingGuard will treat the forged role claim as authoritative and unlock admin/accounting-gated client routes and UI. This is simultaneously a broken function-level authorization pattern (role claim trusted without server-verified proof), a cryptographic/authentication failure (signature verification omitted on the security-critical decision path), and an insecure design (the entire authorization decision is made from data the client fully controls, with no round-trip to a trusted server-side check).
