title: Raw backend error payload rendered to the end user without sanitization
description: On a failed password reset, the raw error.error value from the HTTP error response is assigned directly to this.error (and this.confirmation is cleared) with no filtering or generic-message substitution. If the backend returns a verbose error (e.g., stack trace fragment, internal validation detail, or other diagnostic content), this component will surface it verbatim to the user, which is a misconfiguration-style information disclosure risk if the upstream service is not itself disciplined about error verbosity. This file has no defensive normalization of the error message before display.

title: Authentication token persisted in localStorage, exposing it to theft via XSS
description: On successful login the JWT authentication token returned by the backend is written to localStorage (localStorage.setItem('token', authentication.token)). localStorage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the page's origin, so if any XSS vector exists elsewhere in the SPA (Juice Shop is known to have many), an attacker's injected script can read this token and impersonate the user (session hijacking / account takeover) without needing to intercept network traffic. Storing the same token in a cookie via cookieService.put right after (line 104) does not mitigate this because the token is still duplicated into a JS-readable storage location, defeating the protection that an httpOnly cookie would otherwise provide.

No secure, httpOnly, or sameSite flags are configured at this call site. Without an explicit secure flag the cookie can be transmitted over plaintext HTTP if the app is ever reached over http://, and without sameSite it is more exposed to CSRF-style cross-site delivery. This is a session-management misconfiguration on the credential-issuing code path.

title: TOTP temporary token stored in localStorage during MFA flow
description: When the backend indicates a TOTP (2FA) challenge is required, the temporary token used to complete the second factor is stored in localStorage (localStorage.setItem('totp_tmp_token', error.data.tmpToken)). Like the main auth token, this value is JS-readable and can be exfiltrated by any XSS payload running on the origin, allowing an attacker to hijack an in-progress MFA flow and potentially complete the 2FA step for a victim session, defeating the purpose of the second factor.

title: Google OAuth login uses deprecated implicit flow (response_type=token)
description: googleLogin() constructs the OAuth authorization URL with response_type=token, which is the OAuth2 Implicit Grant. This flow returns the access token directly in the URL fragment of the redirect, which can leak via browser history, referrer headers on subsequent third-party requests, and shared/proxy logs. Modern guidance (OAuth 2.1) deprecates the implicit flow in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE specifically because of this token-leakage risk. Because the client-side code hardcodes this flow choice, no server-side mitigation can compensate for it.

title: Client-side role/authorization decision trusts unverified decoded JWT payload (isAccounting)
description: The spec exercises NavbarComponent.isAccounting(), which is shown to derive an 'accounting' privilege purely from the object returned by LoginGuard.tokenDecode() (component.isAccounting() returns true when tokenDecode returns { data: { role: 'accounting' } }, false for 'customer', and falsy for undefined). The full path shows: the loginGuard collaborator is constructed with only a bare tokenDecode mock and a default observable-returning stub; a specific test then overrides that stub to synchronously return a plain decoded payload object (not an observable), which the component must therefore be calling and reading .data.role from directly and synchronously; the same call/return path is reused unchanged across the 'accounting', 'customer', and 'missing payload' test cases, showing isAccounting() has no other input than this single decoded value. No verification step (signature check, server round-trip) is exercised anywhere in this path before the role is trusted and returned to the caller. If tokenDecode merely base64-decodes the JWT payload without validating its signature, any user able to influence the decoded payload (e.g. a modified but unverified token) could flip this decision.

title: Authentication token persisted in localStorage (susceptible to XSS-based theft)
description: Multiple tests establish that the component's authentication state (isLoggedIn(), whoAmI on reload) is driven by an auth token stored in and read from browser localStorage under the key 'token'. The full path shows: the component's own beforeEach resets this same localStorage key before every test (confirming it is the component's persistent auth store); a test then populates it with a raw token string to simulate an authenticated reload, after which ngOnInit reads it to decide whether to call whoAmI and populate userEmail; a separate test reuses the identical key to drive component.isLoggedIn(), first removing it (falsy result) and then setting a literal token value 'abc', which isLoggedIn() returns verbatim. Storing bearer/session tokens in localStorage (rather than an httpOnly, SameSite-protected cookie) is a well-known session-management weakness: any XSS on the page can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token, giving full account takeover without needing to bypass any other control.

title: Raw backend error objects logged directly to browser console
description: Several tests confirm the component's error-handling design: on failures from AdministrationService.getApplicationVersion, UserService.whoAmI, and ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration, the component calls console.log(err) with the raw error value returned by the (mocked) HTTP-backed service, and the tests explicitly assert console.log was called with the literal 'Error' string/object. Tracing one instance in full: the whoAmI observable is stubbed to error; the test then swaps out the global console.log with a spy/stub, meaning the very next statement is what actually captures the value; ngOnInit() triggers the subscription whose error callback receives the raw error and forwards it into that console.log call; the assertion confirms the unmodified error value reached the console. This means any sensitive detail contained in a real backend error response (e.g., internal messages, exception text) would be written unfiltered to the browser's developer console, accessible to anyone with local access to the browser, malicious browser extensions, or console-log-scraping tooling, and provides no structured security-event logging (only ad-hoc error dumping) for these failure conditions.

title: NFT ownership verified by transmitting the raw private key to the server
description: The component's core workflow proves ownership of a crypto wallet/NFT by having the user paste their raw private key into a form field and sending it to the backend (keysService.submitKey). This is an insecure design: legitimate ownership-proof protocols use a challenge/signature scheme (server issues a nonce, client signs it with the private key locally, only the signature is transmitted) so the private key never leaves the client. Here the design requires the secret itself to cross the network and be evaluated by a remote service, meaning any interception (misconfigured TLS, malicious proxy, compromised backend, request logging middleware, error tracking tooling) exposes the user's private key outright, allowing full compromise of the associated wallet/NFT. This is a defect in the workflow's trust model, not a missing validation on one field — even a flawlessly implemented version of this design still requires trusting the network and server with the secret.

This is a missing compensating control for an inherently sensitive value — the design never establishes a rule that secret material must be purged after use.

title: NFT unlock flow submits raw wallet private key to backend server
description: The test file exercises a component workflow in which a user-supplied value bound to `component.privateKey` (a raw cryptocurrency wallet private key, per the property name and test literal 'test-private-key') is sent, unmodified, to `KeysService.submitKey()` on the backend via `component.submitForm()`. This is a fundamental insecure design: verifying blockchain asset ownership should never require a user to transmit their private key to any server. A private key is the sole secret that authorizes control of a wallet's entire holdings; any server that receives it (or any attacker who can intercept the request, compromise the KeysService endpoint, or view logs/error responses on the wire) gains full custody of the user's crypto assets. The correct design would use a signature-based challenge (server issues a nonce, client signs it with the private key locally, only the signature is transmitted) so the key never leaves the client. The pattern repeats identically across all three submission tests (success, failure, HTTP-error) — the same raw privateKey field is set and forwarded via submitForm() regardless of outcome, and the response (success flag or error.error.message) is consumed only after the key has already crossed the network boundary. Because this is the intended purpose of the form (not a bug in one field but the core mechanism the workflow is built around), it is a design-level trust violation: the client is asked to hand over a value the server should never see, and no compensating control (client-side-only signing, key derivation, etc.) exists in the flow exercised by these tests.

title: Unredacted error objects passed to console.error in NFT status/key-submission error handling
description: The test suite deliberately stubs out console.error (`vi.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {})`) specifically for the error-handling test of ngOnInit's NFT status check. This strongly implies the real component's error handler (in nft-unlock.component.ts, not visible here) logs the raw error/exception object to the browser console rather than a proper monitoring pipeline, and does so without stubbing in production. Additionally, the HTTP error test at line 88-93 shows the component extracts `error.error.message` directly from a failed submitKey call and surfaces it as errorMessage — if the same unredacted error object is also logged (as the console.error stubbing pattern in the ngOnInit test suggests is the component's habit), any sensitive details embedded in backend error responses (stack traces, internal identifiers, or partial key-validation feedback) would be exposed via the browser console, which is visible to anyone with dev-tools access or via error-monitoring integrations that scrape console output. This is a security-logging/monitoring gap: security-relevant failures (failed NFT verification, failed key submission) are only surfaced via console.error rather than any structured, centrally-monitored logging path, so there is no way to detect or alert on repeated failed private-key submission attempts (which would be a strong indicator of brute-forcing or credential-stuffing against the unlock mechanism).

title: NFT ownership confirmation renders a static hardcoded address rather than a verified per-user value

This suggests the component's success view is built around a fixed constant rather than a value returned by the backend for the currently-authenticated user. The intervening DOM assertions show the check is purely structural (form absent, owner-text present, anchor present) before the actual address content is verified, meaning nothing in the render path re-derives or binds the displayed address from a per-user server response — the same static markup renders for every user reaching successResponse = true. If confirmed in the actual component, the 'proof of ownership' UI is decorative rather than a genuine reflection of server-verified identity: the only thing driving the trust decision is the boolean successResponse flag, and the displayed 'owner' details are not derived from user-specific verified data. This is a trust-assumption weakness in the design: a single client-side boolean gates access to a UI state that visually implies specific, verified ownership data, when in fact that data is static and unrelated to the authenticated user's actual verification result.

title: OAuth-provisioned accounts use a predictable, email-derived password (base64(reverse(email)))
description: The spec explicitly asserts that when a user logs in via OAuth for the first time, the component creates a local account by calling UserService.save with password 'bW9jLnRzZXRAdHNldA==' — which is the base64 encoding of the reversed email address 'test@test.com' -> 'moc.tset@tset'. The same deterministic value is reused for UserService.login when the account already exists (line 98). Because the password is deterministically derived from public information (the user's email address) rather than being a securely generated random secret, any attacker who knows or guesses a victim's email address can compute this same password (reverse the email string and base64-encode it) and authenticate as that user through the normal /rest/user/login flow, completely bypassing the OAuth provider. This is a broken authentication design: the 'secret' credential is not a secret at all, it is a fixed, publicly-derivable transform of already-public data. It also constitutes a design flaw because the server never generates or requires a truly random credential for OAuth-provisioned accounts, and it directly enables unauthorized account access (an access-control consequence) for any account ever created via OAuth login.

Tokens placed in URLs are commonly leaked via browser history, proxy/server access logs, the Referer header when the page makes subsequent requests, and browser extensions — a well-known token-exposure weakness in OAuth implicit-flow style handling. While the actual component source is outside this file, this test's setup, wiring, and component bootstrapping are direct evidence of the design the component expects to receive its bearer token through.

title: Raw backend/API errors logged directly to browser console (client-side debug leakage, no monitoring)
description: The spec file explicitly tests and asserts that when the backend calls to ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() or TrackOrderService.find() fail, the component under test responds by calling console.log(error) with the raw error object/string returned by the observable. Walking the full path: the test first mocks console.log itself so the call can be observed, then invokes ngOnInit(), which drives the component's (externally defined) subscribe/error-handling logic to forward the raw error straight to console.log. The identical sequence is then repeated verbatim for the second backend dependency (trackOrderService.find), confirming this is the component's general error-handling strategy rather than an isolated test artifact. Two problems follow: (1) Logging-monitoring failure — failed lookups of configuration or order/tracking data (a security-relevant event, since it could reflect probing of the trackOrderService.find or configuration endpoints with invalid/out-of-scope order IDs) are never recorded anywhere the security team can see; console.log output is local to the end user's browser and is never captured, aggregated, or alerted on, so repeated failures leave no server-side trail. (2) Misconfiguration — dumping raw error objects to console.log is a diagnostic/debug behavior that should not be active in a production build; if the underlying error object from the HTTP client contains internal details (endpoint paths, stack traces, correlation identifiers), those are exposed in the browser console to any user, aiding reconnaissance.

title: Order details retrieved by client-supplied ID with no ownership/authorization check exercised in tests
description: MockActivatedRoute hardcodes a route parameter `id: 'ad9b-96017e7cb1ae7bf9'` that is fed into the component, which then calls trackOrderService.find() to retrieve order details (products, totalPrice, addressId, paymentId, eta, etc.). Tracing the full setup: the mock route instance is created and bound into the TestBed's providers so the component receives it exactly as it would receive a real ActivatedRoute derived from the URL; trackOrderService.find is defined as a bare mock function and, in both the shared beforeEach and the individual test, is configured to return complete order data unconditionally — its return value never varies based on the id supplied, nor is there any simulated rejection representing 'order not found for this user'. When ngOnInit() runs, the component's internal (external-to-this-file) logic pulls the id from the route and passes it to trackOrderService.find, then assigns the full response — including another customer's address and payment identifiers — directly onto component state that is asserted and presumably rendered to the page. None of the tests in this file ever verify that the returned order data is scoped to the currently authenticated user, nor do they simulate an authorization/ownership check being performed before displaying sensitive order/address/payment information. Because the test harness treats the id as the sole selector for which order's financial and address details are shown, and never once exercises a mismatched-user or rejected-ownership scenario, this is consistent with a broken object-level authorization / IDOR pattern: if the real backend endpoint behind trackOrderService.find does not itself enforce that the id maps only to an order owned by the caller, any user could substitute another customer's order id in the URL and view their order/address/payment summary.

The mocked ActivatedRoute is registered via Angular's dependency-injection providers array, so the component instance under test is constructed with this id-bearing route object, mirroring how the real component receives the URL-derived id.

Assertion confirms component.orderDetails.addressId — a customer-specific sensitive field — is populated directly from the mocked response tied only to the hardcoded route id, demonstrating that the object is exposed to the component/view without any test evidence that ownership of the id is verified.

Test confirms sensitive order fields (addressId, paymentId, totalPrice, products) are populated onto the component straight from the mocked backend response keyed only by the route id, with no ownership verification exercised anywhere in this suite.

title: Function-level authorization decision (accounting role) trusts unverified client-side JWT payload
description: isAccounting() decides whether the current user has the 'accounting' role by decoding the JWT stored client-side (via loginGuard.tokenDecode(), defined outside this file) and reading payload.data.role directly, with no signature verification performed in this file and no server round-trip to confirm the claim. Because the JWT itself lives in client-controlled storage (localStorage/cookie, see isLoggedIn()/logout()), and this component performs no cryptographic verification before trusting the 'role' claim, any code path that can alter the stored token payload (self-tampering, an XSS elsewhere in the app, or a forged/unsigned token) can make isAccounting() return true and unlock accounting-only UI. This is a classic authenticated-but-not-authorized / weak identity-resolution pattern: the component resolves 'who the caller is' (and what they may do) from an unverified claim rather than from a trusted, server-validated session.

payload.data.role is compared to roles.accounting with no signature/expiry validation performed here.
Return value of this comparison is used (from the template, outside this file) to gate accounting-only navigation/UI, making a security-relevant decision from an unverified claim.

title: Authentication state derived solely from unverified localStorage token
description: The component treats the mere presence of a value in localStorage['token'] as proof of authentication (isLoggedIn(), and the ngOnInit check at line 150) without any validation of the token's signature, issuer, or expiration. Combined with the fact the token is stored in localStorage (readable by any script in the page, unlike an httpOnly cookie), this is both a weak session-management pattern (crypto-auth: token exposed to XSS-class theft/tampering, no integrity check before trusting it) and a trust-assumption violation (insecure-design: the client is allowed to assert its own authentication state to itself rather than the server being the sole source of truth for what is essentially a client-side gate used to drive getUserDetails() and other authenticated UI). The same unverified-presence pattern is repeated in a second, parallel code path (the getLoggedInState() subscription), reinforcing that no point in this file ever validates the token itself before treating it as an authenticated session.

this.userService.getLoggedInState().subscribe((isLoggedIn) => { — a second, parallel authentication-state stream is wired up, forwarding the same trust decision reactively.
if (isLoggedIn) { — conditional gate that forwards the (equally unverified) logged-in flag to authenticated behavior.
this.getUserDetails() — second invocation site where the unverified auth state is acted upon, mirroring line 151.
return localStorage.getItem('token') — the predicate's implementation confirms it performs only a raw storage read, with no signature, expiry, or integrity check of the token value.
getUserDetails() (and other authenticated flows) are triggered purely on the unverified token presence, with no local validation of token integrity/expiry before treating the session as valid.

title: Unvalidated cookie value passed directly into translation loader without allow-listing
description: checkLanguage() reads the 'language' cookie value (client-controlled — settable by document.cookie, cookie-tossing from a related origin, or any script running on the page) and passes it straight into this.translate.use(langKey) before validating that it corresponds to a known/supported language. Only afterwards does the code attempt to look the key up in this.languages via .find(), and if the lookup fails the next line (.shortKey access on undefined) throws. The unvalidated value has already been used to trigger ngx-translate's resource-loading mechanism (which typically builds a fetch path such as assets/i18n/<langKey>.json) before any allow-list check occurs, meaning an attacker-controlled cookie value directly drives a dynamic resource-load path with no validation gate in front of it. The two occurrences of cookieService.get('language') (the condition check and the immediately following re-read) show the value is fetched twice from the same untrusted source without any sanitization introduced between them.

Raw cookie value assigned to langKey with no allow-list or format validation.
this.translate.use(langKey) is invoked with the unvalidated value, triggering resource loading before the subsequent .find() lookup (lines 207-208) even runs.

title: Security-relevant errors silently discarded to console with no monitoring/alerting
description: Multiple subscriptions to security/identity-relevant service calls (fetching application version, application configuration, current user identity via whoAmI(), and score-board/challenge status) handle errors solely via console.log(err), which is invisible to any server-side or centralized monitoring. Looking at the full whoAmI() subscription block, neither the success branch (which resolves and records the user's identity) nor the failure branch write to any logging/telemetry surface beyond the browser console: a successful identity resolution is stored silently in component state, and a failed one is discarded silently, so repeated identity-resolution failures (e.g., from token tampering or brute-force attempts against the whoAmI-equivalent endpoint) leave no trace an operator could use to detect abuse.

this.userEmail = user.email — successful identity resolution is recorded only into local component state, never logged as a security event (e.g. successful session confirmation).
Failure path terminates at console.log with no escalation, meaning repeated identity-check failures are unobservable to defenders.

title: Score Board link visibility enforced only client-side via cosmetic flag
description: getScoreBoardStatus() sets scoreBoardVisible purely to control whether the navbar renders a link to the score board, based on challenge completion. This is a UI-only gate: nothing in this file suggests the underlying route/page itself independently verifies the challenge is solved before rendering, so an attacker who simply navigates to the score board URL directly would bypass the 'discovery' workflow entirely. Tracing the full subscription shows the value travels through an Angular-zone re-entry wrapper purely for change-detection purposes, with no authorization check anywhere along the way — it is a display flag from entry to sink, not an access control.

No corresponding server-side or route-level enforcement is visible from this file; visibility is the only control shown.

title: Deterministic, email-derived password enables full account takeover via OAuth auto-registration
description: When a user completes OAuth login, this component derives the account's password purely as a deterministic function of the user's email address: the email string is reversed and base64-encoded (`btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join(''))`). This value is used both to auto-register the account (userService.save) and to subsequently log in (userService.login). Because this 'password' contains no randomness, no salt, and no server-held secret, anyone who knows a target's email address (frequently public, guessable, or harvested) can compute the identical value client-side and submit it to the normal (non-OAuth) email/password login endpoint to authenticate as that user. This completely undermines authentication: knowledge of an email address becomes equivalent to full account credentials, allowing pre-emptive account registration/takeover (attacker registers the account first using the derivable password before the legitimate user ever uses OAuth) or takeover of an already-OAuth-registered account. This is simultaneously a broken authentication/credential-generation defect (crypto-auth), an account-takeover / unauthorized access defect (access-control), and a fundamental design flaw in how OAuth identity is bridged to the password-based login system (insecure-design), since the design itself — not just an implementation bug — permits deriving valid credentials from public information.

This deterministic value is persisted as the account password via userService.save({ email, password, passwordRepeat: password }).

On successful save, the 'next' callback proceeds to call this.login(profile).

Even if save() fails (e.g., account already exists), the error callback still invokes this.login(profile), so the login attempt always proceeds regardless of registration outcome.
The login(profile) method definition receives the profile object from either call path.

The same deterministic password is recomputed and submitted to userService.login, establishing an authenticated session; any attacker who knows the victim's email can reproduce this exact value and log in through the standard login form.

title: Session token stored without secure cookie attributes and duplicated in localStorage
description: After successful login, the authentication token is stored in a cookie with only an `expires` option — no `secure`, `httpOnly`-equivalent, or `sameSite` attributes are set — meaning the cookie can be transmitted over plaintext HTTP and is fully accessible to JavaScript. The same token is then additionally written to `localStorage` (persistent, JS-accessible storage) and a session id (`bid`) is written to `sessionStorage`. Storing bearer tokens in JS-accessible storage significantly amplifies the impact of any XSS on the page (token theft/persistence), and the missing secure/sameSite cookie flags increase exposure to network interception and CSRF-style token leakage.

Token is set into a cookie via cookieService.put with only an expires option — no secure/httpOnly/sameSite flags configured.
A new Date object is created to compute cookie expiry.
Expiry is set 8 hours ahead, producing the options object used for the cookie.
The session bid is also written to sessionStorage, completing a pattern of session-identifying material duplicated across multiple JS-accessible, weakly-attributed storage locations.
Token is additionally persisted to localStorage, making it accessible to any script executing in the page context (XSS amplification).

title: Potentially sensitive error data logged to browser console
description: invalidateSession unconditionally logs the raw error object to the console on any OAuth/login failure, reachable from two separate error paths (the initial OAuth profile fetch and the subsequent login call). Depending on what the userService/HTTP layer attaches to error objects (response bodies, headers, or partial token data), this could expose sensitive authentication details in the browser console, which is accessible to any script with debugging access or to shared/kiosk-machine users, and complicates centralized security monitoring since these events are never sent anywhere for detection/alerting.

The oauthLogin subscribe 'error' callback receives an external error object from the OAuth login attempt.
login()'s own subscribe 'error' callback receives a second, independent error object from the login call.
invalidateSession(error) is called again from this second path, reinforcing that any failure funnels the error object to the same sink.

title: OAuth redirect handling lacks state/CSRF parameter validation
description: parseRedirectUrlParams extracts parameters from the URL fragment (e.g., access_token) and ngOnInit uses them directly to perform login, without validating any 'state' parameter that would tie the callback to a request the application itself initiated. Absence of state validation is the classic OAuth login CSRF pattern: an attacker can obtain a valid access_token/authorization artifact for an account they control and trick a victim into visiting the OAuth redirect URL carrying that artifact, causing the victim's browser to log into (or bind actions to) the attacker's identity, or otherwise manipulate the login outcome. This is a design gap — the workflow never establishes or checks a value that proves the callback corresponds to a session-initiated request.

Fragment is split into key=value pairs with no validation of an expected 'state' key or any anti-CSRF token.
The raw hash fragment is read from route.snapshot.data.params, entirely attacker-influenceable via a crafted redirect link.
The fragment is split into individual key=value segments by '&' with no expected-parameter allow-list.
An accumulator object is initialized to hold whatever parameters are present in the fragment.
Each segment is destructured into key/value with no validation of which keys are permitted.
The key/value pair is stored into the params object unconditionally.
The fully-populated, unvalidated params object is returned to the caller.
access_token is taken from the parsed params and used directly to perform oauthLogin without verifying the request originated from this client's own OAuth initiation.

title: Dynamic property assignment from untrusted URL fragment keys
description: parseRedirectUrlParams builds an object by assigning `params[key] = value` where `key` is taken directly from the untrusted URL fragment with no allow-listing of expected keys (e.g., 'access_token'). While a single-level assignment of `__proto__` to a string value does not by itself pollute Object.prototype in modern JS engines, the pattern of using attacker-controlled fragment text as an object key without restriction, applied across every parsed segment in the loop, is fragile and could become exploitable if the object is later merged, spread, or its keys iterated into another sensitive object elsewhere in the codebase not visible from this file.

Each fragment segment is split on '=' to derive an arbitrary key/value pair with no allow-list.

An empty accumulator object (params) is created to receive arbitrary keys.
The loop processes every attacker-controlled segment without restricting which segments are allowed to set properties.
The attacker-controlled key is used directly as a dynamic property name on the params object.

title: API failures are only dumped to the browser console with no security monitoring/alerting
description: The spec file explicitly asserts that when the OrderHistoryService.get() or ProductService.get() calls fail, the component's error handler calls console.log(err) with the raw error object and does nothing else (no re-throw, no reporting to a backend monitoring/logging service, no user-facing alert, no correlation ID). This is confirmed as the intended, tested behavior of the component (tests at lines 107-121 explicitly assert 'error from get order history/product API call' is logged 'directly to browser console'). Failed API calls — which can indicate broken access control, backend outages, tampering, or attempted exploitation of the order-history/product endpoints — are therefore never surfaced to any server-side or centralized logging/monitoring system; they only appear in an individual user's local DevTools console, which is invisible to defenders. This is a textbook A09 logging/monitoring failure: security-relevant failure events (failed data retrieval, which could stem from authorization failures or backend attacks) leave no auditable trail, and any sensitive error detail included in the thrown error object is exposed client-side rather than being sanitized and sent to a monitored logging pipeline.

title: Order confirmation PDF retrieved over an unauthenticated, potentially non-TLS host URL with no transport enforcement
description: The test wires basketService.hostServer to a plain 'http://host.example' value and confirms that component.openConfirmationPDF() builds a URL by directly concatenating this host with the order id and opens it in a new browser tab via window.open, with no scheme validation or enforcement of HTTPS. Because the component trusts whatever scheme is present in basketService.hostServer without normalizing or upgrading it to https, and order PDFs likely contain personal/order data (products, prices, delivery status), if hostServer is ever configured with an http:// origin in a real deployment, the confirmation PDF (and any session/host information implied by the request) is fetched over an unencrypted channel, enabling network-level interception/tampering (e.g., a MITM substituting a malicious PDF, or leaking order contents to network eavesdroppers). This reflects a design gap in this component: it never validates or upgrades the origin passed to window.open before navigating there, i.e., the client trusts a configuration value for a security-relevant transport decision (a scheme it should verify/redirect from http to https) without any check.

component.openConfirmationPDF('abc123') is called; internally the component concatenates basketService.hostServer with the order id to build the PDF URL with no scheme validation.

The mocked basketService object (carrying the unvalidated http:// hostServer value) is registered as the BasketService provider for the TestBed, so it is what gets dependency-injected into the component under test.

Test confirms window.open() is called with the resulting unvalidated URL 'http://host.example/ftp/order_abc123.pdf', demonstrating the component never enforces or upgrades the transport scheme before navigating the user to a resource that may carry sensitive order data.

title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on order confirmation PDF URL
description: openConfirmationPDF() builds the download URL for an order's PDF invoice by simple string concatenation of the backend host and the raw orderId, then opens it directly in a new browser tab. There is no client-side (and, as far as this file shows, no server-side) verification that the orderId being requested actually belongs to the currently logged-in user before the resource is fetched. Because the URL pattern `${hostServer}/ftp/order_${orderId}.pdf` is fully predictable/enumerable, any authenticated (or even unauthenticated, if the /ftp endpoint isn't itself protected) caller who learns or guesses another user's orderId can retrieve that user's invoice PDF, which typically contains PII (name, address, purchased items, prices). This is a classic BOLA pattern: the identifier is taken from data flowing through the client and used directly in a lookup/fetch operation with no visible per-user ownership check. It is also a design flaw in that the system relies on the obscurity of the orderId format rather than an explicit authorization check tied to the requesting user's session.

this.basketService.hostServer is injected/available as the backend host used to build the download URL; it is combined with the untrusted orderId with no per-user scoping logic in between.
The for-loop over the orders returned by orderHistoryService.get() begins; each order object (including its server-assigned orderId) is about to be processed.

description: trackOrder(orderId) forwards the caller-supplied orderId as a raw query parameter to the '/track-result' route without any validation or ownership check performed in this component. If the downstream track-result component/service resolves order details purely by this id (a pattern common in Juice Shop-style apps), a user could substitute another user's orderId to view someone else's order tracking/status information. The authorization check, if any, lives outside this file, but this file is the point where an arbitrary/unverified identifier is handed off toward that lookup.

title: Unbounded order history list fetched and iterated without pagination
description: ngOnInit fetches the full order history via orderHistoryService.get() and iterates over every order and every product within every order client-side, building a full in-memory array (this.orders) and a MatTableDataSource per order. There is no page size, limit, or cursor parameter passed to the service call. If a user (or an account with a very large historical order count) triggers this, the browser must materialize and render the entire order/product history in one pass, which can degrade client performance; more importantly, if the backing service also has no pagination, this same unbounded pattern likely exists server-side, risking excessive memory/CPU usage on repeated calls.

title: Unvalidated required @Input() 'passwordComponent' dereferenced without null/undefined check
description: The component declares passwordComponent: PasswordStrengthComponent as an @Input() with no default value and no runtime guard. In ngOnInit, the code unconditionally accesses this.passwordComponent.minLength (line 41) whenever minCharsCriteriaMsg is not explicitly supplied by the parent. If any consumer of this component fails to bind passwordComponent, this throws an uncaught TypeError at initialization. Because this component's sole purpose is to render the password-strength/complexity requirements that guide a user toward choosing a compliant password, a failure here silently breaks the only UI surface communicating the password policy to the end user (min length, character-class requirements) without any fallback or defensive default. The design never establishes a safe fallback for a missing/undefined password-policy source: the property is declared with a non-optional type but no initializer (lines 18-19), the guard condition that would otherwise gate the dangerous access only checks a different, unrelated input (minCharsCriteriaMsg, declared with no default at lines 36-37) rather than passwordComponent itself, and the lifecycle hook (line 39) proceeds straight into that inadequate guard (line 40) before dereferencing the unchecked value (line 41). So the component either fully renders the security guidance or crashes with no graceful degradation informing the user of password requirements.

ngOnInit checks only minCharsCriteriaMsg for falsiness, not passwordComponent itself, before proceeding to use it.
The property's type annotation (PasswordStrengthComponent) carries no initializer/default, so at runtime the field is simply 'undefined' until (and unless) a parent binds it.

title: Order details, address, and PDF retrieved via unvalidated order ID from route parameter (BOLA)
description: The component reads an 'id' route parameter directly from the URL (paramMap.get('id')) and uses it, unmodified, as the key to fetch order details (trackOrderService.find), the associated address (addressService.getById), and later to construct the URL for the order confirmation PDF (openConfirmationPDF). Nowhere in this file is there any check that the currently authenticated user actually owns the order identified by this ID. Because the identifier is taken straight from the browser URL, an attacker who is merely authenticated (or even unauthenticated, depending on the backing API) can substitute another user's numeric/string order ID and have this component render that user's order total, delivery price, promotional discount, product list, and shipping address, and can also open that user's order confirmation PDF by navigating to /order-completion/<victim-order-id> and clicking 'download PDF'. This is the classic BOLA pattern: authentication (if any) is verified elsewhere, but per-resource ownership is never re-checked before the lookup and render. The addressId used for the second lookup is itself extracted from the unverified order response and passed onward without any additional check, propagating the same unverified identity through a second resource fetch. The trust assumption that the client-supplied ID is 'the current user's order' is also a design-level flaw: the server-facing calls in this component never re-derive or restrict the ID to the authenticated user's own orders.

title: Security-relevant failures silently swallowed with console.log only
description: Every asynchronous call chain in ngOnInit (outer route-param subscription, order lookup, nested configuration fetch, nested address fetch) reports failures solely via `console.log(err)` / `console.log(error)` in the respective error callbacks. There is no structured logging, no correlation ID, no user-facing alert, and no upstream reporting mechanism anywhere in this component. If any of these lookups fail due to an authorization rejection from the backend (e.g., a 403/404 because the user tried to access someone else's order, tying into the BOLA issue above), that security-relevant event is discarded into the browser devtools console and never surfaces to any monitoring system. This pattern repeats at every nesting level of the subscription tree — the nested config-fetch error, the nested address-fetch error, the order-fetch error, and the outermost paramMap error — meaning the entire component has no path by which a failed/unauthorized lookup becomes visible to any monitoring or alerting layer.

trace.description: trackOrderService.find(this.orderId) call whose failure path is the security-relevant event (e.g., unauthorized/failed order lookup).
error: (err) => { console.log(err) } — the only handling of a failed order lookup; no structured log, alert, or reporting to any monitoring backend.
Within the successful order-fetch callback, a nested configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration().subscribe is issued, adding another async operation whose failure is also only console-logged.
error: (err) => { console.log(err) } — the nested configuration-fetch failure handler, no structured log or alert.
Also within the order-fetch success callback, addressService.getById(...) is issued as a further nested async operation.

title: Unencoded product name and social config concatenated into tweet text used for outbound share link
description: Product names returned from the order data (results.data[0].products) are concatenated directly into `this.tweetText` via string interpolation inside a for-loop, with no encoding or sanitization, and the twitterUrl from the application configuration is similarly appended raw. The only subsequent transformation applied, truncateTweet, merely measures length and takes a substring — it performs no character encoding or escaping of URL-special characters. `tweetText` is a public class field almost certainly consumed by the associated template (order-completion.component.html, not visible in this file) to build a Twitter share link/anchor. If product names are attacker-influenced (e.g., a maliciously named product added elsewhere in the system, or an admin-configured twitterUrl), unencoded control characters or URL fragments injected into `tweetText` could manipulate the resulting share URL/query string in the rendered link, enabling parameter injection or altering the destination of the generated tweet/share link. Because the actual DOM/URL sink lives in the companion template file, it is not visible here, but this file is the point where untrusted product-name text is merged into a URL-shaped string without any escaping or allow-listing.

const showDots = tweet.length > maxLength — only a length check is performed; no character escaping occurs at this stage either.

return `${tweet.substring(0, maxLength)}${showDots ? '...' : ''}` — the unescaped, only length-truncated string becomes the final public tweetText value exposed for use as a share-link/URL in the associated template; the actual render/href sink is outside this file.

title: PDF download URL built by concatenating service-provided host with unvalidated order ID and opened via window.open
description: openConfirmationPDF constructs a navigation target by string concatenation of `this.basketService.hostServer` and the client-held `this.orderId`, then calls `window.open(redirectUrl, '_blank')`. Neither the host component (hostServer, sourced from BasketService and not shown in this file) nor the orderId is validated against an allow-list or origin check before being used as a navigation destination. The method itself is a public entry point invoked from outside this file (bound to a template button/click handler not visible here), meaning the trigger for this concatenation-and-navigate sequence is external. If hostServer is derived from any user-influenceable source (e.g., a query parameter or configurable value elsewhere in the app, as BasketService is not visible here) or if orderId can carry additional URL-altering characters, this becomes an open-redirect-style sink: window.open navigates the browser to a fully attacker-influenced location. This is reported with lower confidence because the value and provenance of `basketService.hostServer` cannot be confirmed from this file alone; if it is a fixed, server-controlled constant, this reduces to a benign case, but as an unchecked navigation sink assembled from concatenated external-origin values it fits the SSRF/open-redirect pattern described in the guidance (destination assembled by concatenation, not compared to an allow-listed origin).

openConfirmationPDF() is a public method definition invoked from outside this file (a template button/click handler not shown here), forming the external trigger that reuses the stored orderId.

title: Password strength policy is weak and purely cosmetic, with no server-side enforcement visible in this trust boundary
description: This component computes a password 'strength' score used only to color a progress bar (get progressColor, lines 42-44). The underlying policy (calculatePasswordStrength, lines 30-40, and the five individual checks at lines 46-64) requires only: length >= 8 (hardcoded, ignoring the declared this.minLength field at line 20 which is never referenced), and the mere presence of one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter, one digit, and one special character anywhere in the string. There is no check against common/breached passwords, no entropy measurement, and no enforcement that a minimum score be reached before the password is accepted — the component only reports a percentage/label, it never blocks anything itself. If this client-side calculation is the design basis for what 'strong enough' means for the application (e.g., relied upon by a registration/change-password form elsewhere to gate submission), an attacker fully controls the client and can submit any password directly to the backend API regardless of the score shown here, and even a password that scores 'high' here (e.g., 'Passw0rd!') is trivially guessable. Because this file exposes no re-derivation of the rule on a trusted side and the policy itself is minimal (1 char per class, 8 char minimum), the design never establishes a real minimum-strength guarantee — it only establishes a UI hint. This is a design gap: the rule that passwords must be adequately strong is never actually enforced by (or traceable through) this component, only visualized.

trace.description: Component receives the candidate password from a parent component via @Input() password (caller/parent form is outside this file).
calculatePasswordStrength() runs five weak, easily-satisfied checks (length>=8, and presence-anywhere of one lower/upper/digit/special char) and reduces them to a percentage.
ngOnChanges lifecycle hook fires whenever the bound password Input changes.
Change is detected specifically on the password binding (changes.password), gating the recalculation.
passwordStrength field is reassigned to the result of calculatePasswordStrength(), the only place the score is (re)computed.
checks array is assembled from five getter references, defining the entire strength policy applied to the password.
checks.filter(x => x).length / checks.length * 100 reduces the five weak boolean checks to a single percentage score with no minimum threshold gating acceptance.

containAtLeastMinChars getter enforces only length >= 8, hardcoded rather than reading the declared this.minLength field (line 20), so the 'minimum length' rule is not actually configurable or centrally enforced.

containAtLeastOneSpecialChar (and the sibling lower/upper/digit getters at lines 50-59) each require only a single matching character anywhere in the string via an anchored lookahead, the weakest form of a complexity check.
progressColor only maps the score to a cosmetic UI color/label; no enforcement or blocking logic exists in this file to prevent acceptance of a weak password that nonetheless scores 'high'.

title: Raw HTTP error objects logged directly to browser console instead of being handled/reported securely
description: The test suite explicitly asserts that when AddressService.getById or PaymentService.getById error out, the component calls console.log(error) with the raw error payload from the HTTP layer (tests at lines 115-120 and 122-128). This confirms the production component's design: failed backend calls for address and payment data are routed straight to the browser devtools console rather than to a proper client error-handling/telemetry path, and there is no evidence of any security-relevant event being reported to a monitoring/logging backend when these lookups fail. In a real deployment this means (a) any sensitive detail contained in the error response (stack traces, internal service messages, user/account identifiers) is exposed to anyone with devtools open or to browser extensions/scripts that hook console output, and (b) repeated failures (e.g., an attacker probing paymentId/addressId values) generate no server-side audit trail, so such probing cannot be detected or alerted on. The pattern is repeated identically for the payment lookup path (lines 122-128), confirming this is a systemic component design choice rather than a one-off oversight.

The global console.log is replaced with a spy so the test can observe what the component actually writes to the browser console, confirming console.log is the real destination reached by the error value.

title: Order pricing/discount state trusted from client-writable sessionStorage without server-side re-validation
description: The test at lines 155-161 shows that component.getMessage() derives promotionalDiscount directly from a value the test placed in sessionStorage ('couponDiscount', '70'), and separately (lines 122-153) the component resolves which address, payment method, and delivery option to use for the order purely from sessionStorage keys ('paymentId', 'addressId' implied, 'deliveryMethodId') that are plain browser storage writable by any client-side script or by the user via devtools. Because sessionStorage is fully attacker/user-controlled, a user can set an arbitrary couponDiscount value (or an arbitrary paymentId/addressId/deliveryMethodId) before triggering checkout (basketService.checkout, exercised at line 164-171) and have that value flow into order totals/placement without the component re-deriving or validating it against a trusted server-side record. This is a client-trust design flaw: the server should be the sole authority for discount amounts and price computation, not a value copied out of client storage.

component.getMessage([100, 1]) is invoked; the component reads the sessionStorage-sourced discount and folds it into order state (itemTotal/promotionalDiscount/bonus) without any indication of server-side recomputation.

Test confirms component.promotionalDiscount equals the attacker-supplied sessionStorage value (70), demonstrating the untrusted client value is used directly as the applied discount that would subsequently feed checkout/placeOrder (line 166).

title: Order resource identifiers (paymentId, addressId, deliveryMethodId) sourced from client storage and looked up by ID with no visible ownership check
description: Across multiple tests (lines 122-128, 142-153) the component is shown to read 'paymentId' out of sessionStorage and pass it to paymentService.getById(id) to fetch payment method/card data; similarly address and delivery lookups are performed by ID (addressService.getById, deliveryService.getById). sessionStorage is writable client-side, so if these identifiers are sequential/guessable primary keys (as is typical for Juice-Shop-style REST APIs), a user could substitute another user's paymentId/addressId to have the component fetch and render that other user's saved payment/address record. Nothing in this file (nor inferable from the mocked service contracts, which are simple getById(id) calls) shows a per-user ownership check being applied before the fetched record is used. The pattern repeats with a different literal ID value ('wallet') in a second test, confirming the component treats whatever identifier is present in sessionStorage as authoritative input to the lookup call and to the resulting UI state, with no visible authorization gate in between. Because the actual authorization enforcement (if any) would live in AddressService/PaymentService or the backend API and is not visible in this spec file, this is reported as a plausible BOLA pattern rather than a confirmed one.

title: Resource identifiers for address/payment/delivery/basket are taken from client-controlled sessionStorage with no ownership verification in this file
description: ngOnInit() and placeOrder() read 'deliveryMethodId', 'addressId', 'paymentId' and 'bid' directly from sessionStorage and pass them straight into service lookups (deliveryService.getById, addressService.getById, paymentService.getById) and into the checkout call (basketService.checkout). sessionStorage is fully attacker-controllable client state (editable via devtools/console, or by any script that runs in the page, e.g. a stored XSS elsewhere in the app). Nothing in this component verifies that the addressId/paymentId/deliveryMethodId/basket id actually belong to the currently logged-in user before using them to fetch and display data or to place an order. If the backend endpoints behind AddressService/PaymentService/DeliveryService/BasketService perform lookup-by-id without a server-side ownership check (a common BOLA pattern), a user who changes these sessionStorage values (e.g. to another user's addressId or paymentId) will have that other user's PII/payment data fetched and rendered, or will place an order billed/shipped using another user's payment method or address. Even if the backend does enforce ownership, this file establishes an insecure design trust boundary: it treats client-side storage as an authoritative source of resource identifiers for both read (address/payment display) and write (order placement) operations, with the actual enforcement point invisible from this file.

title: Coupon/discount data protected only by Base64 encoding, not integrity-protected, before being sent to checkout
description: The coupon details used at checkout are taken from sessionStorage (set elsewhere, presumably after applying a coupon code) and merely Base64-encoded with btoa() before being sent to basketService.checkout(). Base64 is an encoding, not a cryptographic control — it provides no confidentiality or integrity guarantee and is trivially reversible/forgeable by anyone with access to the browser console. Because couponDetails originates from client-writable sessionStorage and is 'protected' only by btoa(), an attacker can fabricate or tamper with the coupon payload (e.g. forge a larger discount) before it reaches the checkout endpoint. Whether this succeeds depends on server-side validation not visible in this file, but the client-side design treats obfuscation as if it were a security boundary, which is the classic misuse-of-encoding-as-protection pattern.

placeOrder() reads 'couponDetails' from sessionStorage, another client-controlled value.

title: Raw backend error message surfaced directly to the user
description: On checkout failure, the raw server error message (err.error?.error.message) is passed unmodified to the snackbar helper for display to the user. The error object is first dumped to the console and then, without any sanitization, transformation, or generic-message fallback, its nested message field is handed to the UI notification component. If the backend returns verbose error details (stack traces, internal identifiers, database error text) in this field, it will be shown directly in the UI, leaking internal implementation details that aid an attacker in further probing the application.

title: Sensitive operation errors only logged to browser console with no structured/security logging
description: Errors from address lookup, payment lookup, and order placement are only sent to console.log with no structured logging, correlation ID, or reporting to any monitoring/telemetry service. Tracing each error path shows the same shallow pattern repeated three times in this file: the service call is made, and on failure the entire error object is dumped via console.log with no redaction, no severity classification, and no forwarding to any monitoring surface. This means failures during checkout (which can indicate abuse attempts such as tampered payment/address IDs or forged coupon data, see related findings) leave no server-visible or aggregable trail from the client side, and any sensitive fields inside the error objects are dumped to the browser console where they could be captured by browser extensions or shoulder-surfing.

title: Client-side-only file type validation used as a security control
description: The mimeType validator inspects the first 4 bytes of a user-selected File object in the browser and returns a validation result (null / {invalidMimeType:true}) that is consumed by an Angular reactive form. This check runs entirely client-side inside the user's browser, which the attacker fully controls. Nothing in this file (and nothing that can be seen from this file) guarantees the same check is independently re-applied and enforced on the server before the file is persisted or served. Because the validation logic, the file bytes, and the JavaScript runtime are all under attacker control, an attacker can trivially bypass this control by disabling JavaScript, editing the DOM, intercepting/modifying the XHR request, or simply issuing a raw HTTP POST directly to the upload endpoint (e.g. POST /profile/image/file or POST /rest/memories seen in the route inventory) with an arbitrary file and no magic-byte prefix at all. If the backend trusts that 'the frontend already validated the file type' and skips its own strict validation, this is a textbook trust-boundary violation: the client is allowed to assert a fact (file type/safety) that only the server can authoritatively determine. This is a design gap rather than an implementation bug — even a perfectly bug-free version of this exact validator can never be a real security boundary because it executes in the attacker's own environment.

control.value is cast to a File and read via FileReader entirely inside the client runtime.
First 4 bytes of the file are extracted and compared against a hard-coded whitelist of magic numbers, all client-side.

An Observable wraps the async FileReader-based check; the resulting verdict will later be exposed as the sole validation output to the Angular form, with no server round-trip.
A 'loadend' listener is registered so the verdict-computation logic runs only after the browser (attacker-controlled environment) finishes reading the file.
The extracted header is switch-matched against known signatures entirely within the browser context; the branch taken determines isValid.
The isValid flag computed purely client-side gates which verdict is emitted to the form, with no independent server confirmation of this decision.

title: Weak 4-byte magic-number check enables polyglot/spoofed file uploads
description: Even taken purely as a UX-level filter, the check only reads and compares the first 4 bytes of the uploaded file (line 20) against a small whitelist of PNG/JPEG signatures. It performs no further structural validation of the file (no full header/marker parsing, no dimension/codec sanity check, no rejection of trailing/embedded non-image data). This means any file can be trivially disguised as valid by prepending 4 bytes of a legitimate PNG/JPEG signature (e.g. 89 50 4E 47) to arbitrary payload bytes (HTML, SVG-with-script, polyglot JS/GIF, etc.). The validator will mark such a file 'valid' (isValid = true, line 28/35, observer.next(null) at line 42), even though the remaining content is attacker-controlled and potentially executable/malicious when later served or rendered by the application (e.g. as part of the photo-wall gallery). The design never establishes or enforces any check on the body of the file beyond 4 bytes, so this control provides only the illusion of type safety and can be defeated by a one-line file-crafting trick, independent of any implementation bug.

title: Client-side trust in promotional coupon validation allows forged discounts
description: The component maintains a hardcoded table of 'campaign' coupon codes with fixed validity dates and discount percentages (lines 84-94). When a user submits a coupon in applyCoupon(), the code computes the 'valid' date entirely from the browser's own clock (this.clientDate = new Date(), lines 154-158) and compares it against the hardcoded campaign.validOn value (line 163) purely in client-side JavaScript. If the comparison succeeds, showConfirmation() writes the resulting discount directly into sessionStorage('couponDiscount') (line 194) with no round-trip to the server for verification — unlike the non-campaign coupon path, which correctly delegates validation to basketService.applyCoupon() on the server (line 178). Because the date used for the check is taken from the client's own Date object, an attacker can trivially manipulate their system clock, or simply override window.Date / the couponControl value / sessionStorage via devtools/console, to force the equality check to pass for any campaign code and obtain a 40-75% discount that was never approved server-side. This discount value then flows into totalPrice computation in initTotal() (lines 140-144), a business-critical monetary value, without the server ever re-deriving or re-validating it in this component. This is a textbook trust-boundary violation: a security/business decision (is this coupon currently valid, and what discount does it grant) is made entirely on the untrusted client rather than being authoritatively decided by the server.

title: Session/auth token persisted to client-accessible storage without protective flags
description: After a successful deluxe-membership upgrade, the server-issued token (data.token, obtained from userService.upgradeToDeluxe()'s response) is stored both in localStorage (line 232) and via cookieService.put() (line 233) with no options supplied for secure, sameSite, or any equivalent protections. Because both writes happen from client-side JavaScript, the token is necessarily JS-readable (cookies set via document.cookie/client libraries cannot be marked HttpOnly), meaning any XSS on the origin can exfiltrate the authentication token directly from localStorage or the cookie. This is a session-management weakness under OWASP A07 (missing secure/HttpOnly flags on session tokens) and simultaneously a misconfiguration, since a security-sensitive value is persisted through a call site with no hardening options configured despite the library exposing such options in most cookie-service APIs.

The subscribe next callback receives the response object 'data' (containing the token field) from the server call
cookieService.put('token', data.token) sets the session token cookie from client-side code with no secure/sameSite options specified, leaving it readable by JavaScript and unprotected

title: Raw backend error objects logged directly to browser console (client-side sensitive data exposure)
description: Two spec tests explicitly assert that when the backend call fails, the component reacts by calling console.log with the raw error value returned from the (mocked) backend/service call, rather than a sanitized message or a proper monitoring/telemetry call. 'component.load()' on a failed paymentService.get() call results in console.log(error) being invoked with the raw error value, and 'component.delete()' on a failed paymentService.del() call does the same. Since paymentService.get/del wrap real HTTP calls to the backend in production, any error payload (which can include internal messages, stack traces, or other backend-supplied content) ends up printed verbatim to the browser's developer console. This is a logging/monitoring anti-pattern: security-relevant failures (failed card retrieval, failed card deletion) are only 'logged' to a client-side console that is not centrally collected, not alertable, and can expose backend internals to anyone with access to the browser (shared machines, browser extensions capturing console output, screen-sharing, etc.), while providing no server-side audit trail of the failure.

title: Credit card number stored/validated as JavaScript number, risking silent precision loss for a financial field
description: The component's numberControl accepts 16-digit credit-card numbers as a JavaScript 'number' type rather than as a string. The spec file itself acknowledges the danger with explicit 'eslint-disable-next-line no-loss-of-precision' comments around the boundary test values. JavaScript numbers only safely represent integers up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991); 16-digit values such as 9999999999999999 and 1234567887654321 used in these 'valid' test cases already exceed that safe-integer boundary. The test walks the validator through a below-range value, an above-range (17-digit) value, and then two accepted 16-digit values that are both already beyond safe-integer precision, and asserts they are VALID card numbers. This means the design accepts and processes a financial identifier in a numeric representation that can silently lose precision (i.e., the value bound to the form/model may differ from what the user actually typed) before being sent to the save() call and persisted via PaymentService.save. This is a design flaw: the field should never have been typed/validated as a plain number for a value whose exact digit sequence must be preserved, and it constitutes a data-integrity risk for a financial field.

title: No test coverage for throttling/duplicate-submission protection on card save/delete operations
description: The spec suite exercises save() and delete() only for single, isolated invocations (success/failure) and never verifies any protection against rapid repeated submissions (e.g., double-click submitting the same card twice, or repeated delete calls). Because save()/delete() ultimately call an external PaymentService (whose real HTTP implementation is outside this file), the complete absence of any test asserting debounce, submit-button disable-after-click, or rate-limiting behavior is a weak signal that the component/business logic may allow unrestricted repeated card-mutation requests. The submit-button-disabled test ties the button's enabled/disabled state purely to form-control validity, never to an in-flight/submitting request state, so nothing in the tested behavior would stop a user (or script) from firing save() or delete() repeatedly in quick succession. This is inferred only from the absence of such tests in this file and cannot be confirmed without seeing the component implementation or server-side controls.

title: Component swallows configuration-fetch errors via console.log instead of structured logging or user/security alerting
description: This spec explicitly asserts (lines 62-67) that when ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() errors, PrivacyPolicyComponent.ngOnInit() responds by calling console.log(error) with the raw error object/string. This test locks in the production component's error-handling behavior: failures are only written to the browser devtools console, with no structured/security logging, no telemetry/monitoring hook, and no compensating control (e.g., user-visible error state, retry, or reporting to a backend logging endpoint). Because this is the *only* observable behavior on failure, an attacker or automated tooling causing repeated configuration-fetch failures (e.g., via a misbehaving/compromised backend, network tampering, or malicious extension) would leave no server-side or centralized trace — only a console entry visible to whoever has devtools open on that specific browser session. This is both an absence of security-relevant logging (A09) and a design gap: no monitoring signal is ever generated for a failure condition on a security-adjacent endpoint (application configuration), and errors are silently discarded from the user's perspective with no confirmation or fallback for a broken configuration state that other components may depend on for security-relevant settings.

title: Deluxe-membership token persisted in localStorage and JS-writable cookie
description: The spec verifies that when the deluxe-upgrade API call succeeds, the component takes the returned authentication/session token and stores it both in the browser's localStorage and in a cookie set via CookieService.put() (Angular code calling cookieService.put can only ever set a JS-accessible, non-httpOnly cookie). Persisting a bearer/session token in two JS-readable browser storages means any XSS on the page (or any script able to run in the page context) can read document.cookie or localStorage and exfiltrate the token, fully impersonating the user. This is a session/token-handling weakness: the design never places the token behind an httpOnly, non-JS-readable mechanism.

title: Raw backend error objects logged unredacted to the browser console instead of structured security logging
description: Across multiple tests, the PaymentComponent's error-handling paths (configuration load, wallet-balance load, deluxe-status load, coupon/campaign param subscription, deluxe-upgrade) are verified to call console.log() directly with the raw error value/object returned by the backend/service call, with no sanitization, categorization, or routing to any monitoring/telemetry layer. This establishes that the underlying component has no security-relevant logging strategy (e.g., distinguishing an auth failure from a generic API error, no correlation ID, nothing sent to a backend logging/alerting service) and instead dumps whatever the backend returned straight to the client-side console, which is visible to anyone with access to devtools or via any injected script. Because the console.log target is verified with the literal error content, any sensitive detail present in a real backend error payload would also be surfaced this way. The pattern repeats identically in five separate flows, showing it is systemic rather than incidental.

title: Backend wallet-charge error message surfaced verbatim to end user and console without sanitization
description: The test for the wallet-charge failure path mocks walletService.put to reject with a nested backend error object ({ error: { message: 'Wallet down' } }) and then asserts both that console.log was called and that the SnackBarHelperService displays the raw internal message ('Wallet down') directly to the end user. If a real backend error ever contains internal details (stack fragments, service names, infra hints), this design leaks them straight to the browser UI/console.

title: Wallet-balance sufficiency check enforced client-side against locally cached component state
description: The 'choosePayment edge cases' test shows that whether a wallet payment proceeds is decided entirely by comparing component.walletBalance to component.totalPrice — both plain client-held fields set directly in the test (in production these come from an earlier walletService.get() call cached on the component and from totalPrice computed/stored client-side). When the comparison fails, the code blocks by simply not calling setItem for paymentId and shows a snackbar, without any indication in this file that the eventual charge request itself is re-validated authoritatively server-side within this flow. Because the gating decision is made purely from client-held state that can be stale (fetched earlier) or tampered with via browser devtools before choosePayment() runs, the design pattern trusts the client to prevent overspending rather than having the server be the sole source of truth for the balance check at charge time. This is a trust-boundary/business-logic design concern rather than an implementation bug, and its exploitability depends on whether the server-side wallet-charge endpoint independently re-validates balance — which cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: Payment card deletion executed without confirmation or compensating control
description: The delete() method immediately invokes the backend deletion call for a stored payment card as soon as it is invoked, with no confirmation step, undo window, or re-authentication check visible in the component logic. Deleting a saved payment method is an irreversible action from the user's perspective (the card data, e.g. full number, is not re-enterable from the UI afterwards without re-adding it). The only gate that exists anywhere in this component before delete() can be reached is the client-side allowDelete flag, which merely controls whether a 'Remove' column/button is rendered at all — it is not a confirmation step, and once the button is shown, clicking it (or triggering the handler by any other means, e.g. via devtools) deletes the card immediately with only a fire-and-forget subscribe/reload afterwards.

title: Full backend error objects logged to browser console instead of structured, sanitized logging
description: Both the card-list load failure and the card deletion failure handlers dump the raw error object to console.log. Error objects surfaced by HTTP clients frequently include response bodies, status text, or backend stack/error details. Logging these unfiltered to the browser console exposes potentially sensitive backend information to anyone with access to the browser's devtools (including via malicious extensions or shoulder-surfing on shared machines), and provides no structured, centrally-monitored security event trail (e.g., no distinction between an authorization failure and a network error) that could be used to detect or investigate abuse of the payment endpoints. The same unsafe pattern is repeated verbatim in a second, independent network call in the same component, showing it is a systemic choice rather than an isolated typo.

title: Unsanitized server error message rendered directly in UI notification
description: On a failed card save, the raw error message returned by the backend (err.error?.error) is passed directly to snackBarHelperService.open() for display to the user, with no validation or encoding applied in this file. The request that produces this error is built directly from user-entered form fields (name, card number, month, year) with no server-independent sanitization performed client-side first. If the helper inserts the string into the DOM in a way that is not context-safe (e.g., via innerHTML rather than Angular's default text interpolation — the helper's implementation is outside this file and cannot be confirmed here), and if the backend ever echoes attacker-influenced content back in its error field (for example a validation error that includes a submitted value), this becomes a reflected/stored XSS sink. Even absent that specific echo behavior, passing untrusted backend-derived strings into a UI toast/snackbar without any allow-list or encoding step in this component is a weak control.

title: Client-supplied card id forwarded to deletion endpoint with no client-side ownership check
description: delete(id) accepts an identifier and forwards it verbatim to paymentService.del(id) with no verification in this component that the id belongs to the currently authenticated user's own card list. The only condition anywhere in the component related to this action is the allowDelete UI flag, which controls visibility of the delete button but performs no per-resource ownership check on the id itself. This component assumes the backend enforces per-resource ownership on the DELETE endpoint; if that server-side check is weak or missing (not visible from this file), an id manipulated outside the normal UI flow (e.g., via a modified request replaying a different numeric id) would be accepted by this code path without any additional client-side gate. This is reported as a low-confidence observation since the authoritative check must exist server-side and is outside this file's visibility.
