title: Stored XSS via unsanitized caption/username concatenation rendered on Photo Wall
description: Memory captions are free-text values (see form control at line 42, which applies only a `required` validator and an async MIME-type validator — no output encoding or sanitization) that are submitted via `addMemory()` and later retrieved via `photoWallService.get()`. When memories are received in `ngOnInit`, the component builds a new caption string by concatenating the raw `memory.caption` value with `memory.User.username` using a template literal (line 65), with no HTML-encoding or sanitization applied to either field. The resulting string is pushed into `slideshowDataSource` (line 67), which is bound for display in the companion template (photo-wall.component.html), a file not visible here. Because neither `caption` nor `username` is sanitized at this construction point, if the rendering template does not apply context-appropriate escaping (e.g. if it uses `[innerHTML]` rather than plain interpolation), an attacker who controls either their own caption text or their own username can have arbitrary markup/script persist and execute in the browser of every user who views the Photo Wall — a classic stored XSS. The persistence/assembly point is in this file; the actual render sink is outside it, so exploitability there cannot be fully confirmed from this file alone.

title: Client-side authentication check trusts mere presence of a localStorage token
description: isLoggedIn() determines the user's authenticated state solely by checking whether a 'token' key exists in localStorage (line 126), without validating the token's signature, structure, or expiration. Any code in the surrounding template that gates UI functionality (e.g., showing the upload form) on this method's return value will treat a stale, expired, or manually-fabricated non-empty localStorage value as proof of a valid session. While actual authorization must ultimately be enforced server-side on the backend calls this component makes, this local trust decision is not itself an authentication check (it does not verify the token content), and using it as the sole gate for UI-level access to sensitive functionality is a weak identity-verification implementation.

title: Photo upload lacks any client-side size cap, and file-type enforcement relies solely on a bypassable client-side async validator
description: The upload form (line 40-43) validates the 'image' control only with `Validators.required` and the `mimeType` async validator; there is no maximum file size constraint anywhere in the component, and the MIME-type check is a client-side Angular validator that can be trivially bypassed by calling the underlying API directly (the entrypoint for this data is outside this file, in PhotoWallService.addMemory). The selected file flows from the raw DOM file input, through form state, through the only validation step present (an async MIME-type check with no size bound), and directly into the upload call with no intervening size cap. Because the design never establishes or enforces a bound on upload size before invoking `save()` → `addMemory()` (lines 111-112), a malicious or careless client is not prevented, at the level this file controls, from attempting arbitrarily large uploads, and the only file-type gate present is a soft client-side check offering no real security guarantee if the corresponding server endpoint does not independently re-validate.

title: Errors from configuration fetch are only console-logged with no security monitoring or structured logging
description: The subscription to getApplicationConfiguration() defines an error handler that does nothing but `console.log(err)`. There is no structured/centralized logging, no correlation ID, and no alerting mechanism tied to this failure path. If the configuration endpoint is unreachable, tampered with, or returns an error indicating backend compromise or a blocked/failed request (e.g., due to a proxy/CORS misconfiguration or an attacker intercepting the request), this security-relevant signal is silently dropped into the browser console where it is visible only to the end user and never reaches any monitoring/alerting system. Additionally, if the underlying HTTP client surfaces response bodies or headers inside the error object (common with Angular's HttpErrorResponse), those details are printed to the browser console, which is a plaintext log sink that could include internal implementation details useful to an attacker or accidentally exposed sensitive data.

title: Server configuration response consumed without any validation and trusted implicitly
description: The component types the configuration payload as `config: any` and directly assigns nested fields (config.application.name, config.application.privacyContactEmail) to component state without any schema validation, type checking, or sanitization. This is a trust-assumption violation: the client blindly trusts whatever shape/content the configuration service returns and propagates it into the UI-bound fields `applicationName` and `privacyContactEmail`. If the configuration source is ever compromised, proxied through an untrusted intermediary, or manipulated (e.g., via a misconfigured/insecure config endpoint elsewhere in the app), arbitrary attacker-controlled strings can be pushed into displayed identity fields (site name, contact email) with no server-side or client-side validation ever performed on this data before use.

Response is typed as `any` with no schema/shape validation applied before use.
Only an existence check (config?.application?.name) gates the assignment — the content/value of `name` itself is never validated or sanitized, only its presence.

title: Fallback privacy contact email derived from unvalidated client-side hostname
description: When the server-provided configuration lacks a privacyContactEmail, the component falls back to constructing one from `this._document.location.hostname` (the browser's current hostname) rather than a hardcoded, trusted organizational default. In deployments where the hostname can be influenced by the client's request (e.g., app served behind a misconfigured reverse proxy that reflects an arbitrary Host header, or via DNS rebinding / alternate domain binding), this design causes the application to synthesize and display a plausible-looking but attacker-influenced contact email address (e.g., donotreply@attacker-controlled-domain). This is a weak default that assumes the browser-observed hostname is always trustworthy for constructing security/contact-relevant content, without any allow-list or server-side canonical value being enforced.

title: Client-side authentication gate relies on mere presence of a localStorage token, not its validity
description: The test suite documents that PhotoWallComponent.isLoggedIn() simply returns the raw value of localStorage.getItem('token') (line 226-232, any string such as 'abc' is treated as a valid logged-in state). This value then gates rendering of the privileged 'share-a-memory' form and its submit button (lines 280-290). Because localStorage is fully attacker/script controllable (e.g. via XSS elsewhere, browser extensions, or simply manual devtools manipulation) and no signature/expiry/format validation of the token is performed before granting UI access to the memory-upload flow, this is a weak, forgeable authentication check pattern. While the backend addMemory endpoint presumably re-validates the token server-side (not visible in this file), the client-side authorization decision itself is based on an unauthenticated, unverified value, which is the core weak-session-token pattern (no signature check, no expiry check) combined with a broken function-level access decision made purely on the client.

title: API and configuration errors are only logged to the browser console with no security monitoring or user-facing handling
description: Across multiple tests (get() failure, addMemory() failure, getApplicationConfiguration() failure), the component's only observable error-handling behavior is `console.log(error)` (verified at lines 120, 128, 174). This means failures of authenticated actions (e.g., a failed memory submission, which could reflect an authorization failure or blocked request) are not reported to any centralized logging/monitoring/alerting mechanism, are not surfaced to the user in an actionable way, and are only visible transiently in the client browser console. Security-relevant failures (e.g., repeated denied uploads, malformed responses) would be undetectable to defenders, preventing incident detection and response for this feature.

description: The test at lines 177-181 shows that when a memory record contains a caption and an associated User.username (both attacker-influenced values coming from a stored memory / uploader profile), the component builds a new display string via concatenation: `caption + ' (© ' + username + ')'` (observed result 'Hi (© alice)'). This assembled string is then rendered into the photo grid tiles, as shown by the later template-rendering tests (lines 244-254) that assert one '.container' tile per memory. This spec file cannot show the actual template binding (interpolation vs. innerHTML) used to render `slideshowDataSource[*].caption`, so if the component or its template inserts this concatenated string via an unescaped HTML sink, it constitutes stored XSS carried through the caption/username fields. title: Client-side image upload handling has no observable file size restriction before reading into memory
description: The onImagePicked() handler (exercised at lines 200-224) reads a selected file entirely via FileReader.readAsDataURL with no test coverage or evidence of a maximum file size check before the read occurs. If the underlying component does not enforce a size cap (not shown to exist here), a user (or malicious script driving the file input) could select an extremely large file, causing the browser to attempt to load and base64-encode the entire file into memory as a data URL, potentially freezing or crashing the tab, and subsequently submitting a very large payload to the addMemory upload endpoint.

title: Component relies on client-side console.log for error handling instead of proper security logging/monitoring
description: The spec file explicitly tests and asserts that when the ProductReviewService.patch() call fails, the component under test (ProductReviewEditComponent) logs the raw error directly to the browser console via console.log(err), rather than reporting it to any server-side logging/monitoring facility or a structured error-handling service. This test (lines 88-96) locks in that behavior as expected/required. Because the failure path only writes to the browser's local console, there is no server-side record of the failed review-update attempt, no correlation ID, and no mechanism for security operations to detect repeated failures (which could indicate probing, tampering with review IDs, or abuse of the patch endpoint). Additionally, logging raw caught error objects to the console is a pattern that can leak internal error details (stack traces, backend messages) to anyone with access to the browser devtools, and the test does nothing to constrain what is logged, so if a future/backend error object contains sensitive data (e.g., validation details, IDs, tokens embedded in error responses) it would be exposed the same way. This is a genuine security logging/monitoring gap: failed mutation attempts against the review-edit API are only observable client-side and never reach a monitorable, auditable channel.

title: Stored XSS: unsanitized review text persisted without any output-encoding contract
description: addReview() takes the raw value of a native HTMLTextAreaElement (not even routed through the reviewControl validator declared on line 49) and sends it verbatim as the review 'message' field to productReviewService.create(). There is no sanitization, encoding, or allow-listing of the text before it is persisted. Juice Shop's review list renders review messages elsewhere (outside this file) typically via a template that may not always context-appropriately encode rich content, and this is the canonical Juice Shop 'Five-Star Feedback' / persisted XSS pattern. Even if the rendering sink is not visible in this file, the persistence point is here: a free-form text field accepted from the DOM with zero validation or encoding before being written to the backend is where the stored-XSS vulnerability is introduced. Any other client (or admin panel) that renders this review message without escaping will execute attacker-supplied markup/script in the victim's session.

title: Client-side authentication decision based solely on localStorage token presence
description: isLoggedIn() determines the user's authenticated state purely by checking whether a 'token' key exists in localStorage, with no validation of the token's structure, signature, or expiration, and no server round-trip. An attacker with access to the browser (or via any injected script, e.g. from the stored-XSS finding above) can set an arbitrary non-empty value under localStorage['token'] via devtools/console and cause isLoggedIn() to return truthy, flipping any UI logic in the associated template that gates review-authoring controls or other functionality on this method. This is a client-controlled identity signal being treated as an authentication/authorization decision; it establishes both a broken function-level check (UI elements gated by unverifiable client state) and an authentication weakness (identity/session state decided from unverified client storage rather than a verified token).

title: No client-side or design-level control preventing repeated/duplicate 'like' actions on a review
description: likeReview() fires productReviewService.like(review._id) every time it is invoked, with no check for whether the current user has already liked this review, no debouncing, and no rate limiting on repeated clicks. If the backend does not independently enforce one-like-per-user-per-review (which cannot be confirmed from this file), a user can call this repeatedly (e.g., by scripting rapid calls or holding down the UI action) to arbitrarily inflate a review's like count, an economic/reputation-integrity imbalance the design here does nothing to prevent. Even setting aside server-side enforcement, the design leaves the like operation entirely unthrottled from the client, and a scripted/automated caller reaching the like() sink could trigger unbounded repeated calls with no cool-down.

title: Security-relevant failures are only logged to the browser console, never reported to a backend monitoring system
description: The spec explicitly asserts that when UserService.whoAmI() fails (line 123-129) or ProductReviewService.create() fails (line 131-143), the component's error handling calls console.log(error) and nothing else. This confirms the production component's behavior: authentication/identity lookup failures and failed review-submission attempts (both security-relevant events — one is an auth-adjacent failure, the other a failed write operation) are surfaced only to the end user's local browser console. There is no call to any telemetry, error-reporting, or backend logging service visible from these tests. As a result, an operator/security team has no way to detect patterns of failure (e.g., repeated whoAmI failures indicating session/token issues, or repeated review-post failures potentially indicating abuse or backend errors) because the only record of the event exists in the individual user's browser, which the server-side team can never see. This is a textbook absence of security logging/monitoring for events that should be reported to a central system. The same console-only pattern is independently re-confirmed for the review-creation failure path (lines 133-141), showing this is the component's consistent, deliberate error-handling design rather than an isolated oversight.

title: Free-form review text is submitted verbatim with no client-side sanitization before persistence
description: Multiple tests (e.g. lines 99-106, 113-121, 137-141, 151-156) show that whatever raw string is placed into the review textarea's `.value` (user-controlled input) is passed unmodified as the `message` property of the object handed to `ProductReviewService.create()`. No encoding, stripping, or allow-listing of the textarea content is performed by the component before the request is dispatched — the test only checks that the exact string 'Great product!' is forwarded unchanged, and the assertions on the call's arguments (id and payload shape) confirm the value is passed through the submit handler with no intervening transformation step. Since this is a review 'message' field that will be persisted server-side and later re-rendered to other users viewing the product page (the review list, exercised elsewhere in this same spec via productReviewService.get), any HTML/script content typed here would flow through unsanitized at the point of submission. This file establishes the persistence-point half of a potential stored XSS: user text goes straight from the DOM input into the outbound create() call without any sanitizing transformation. The actual encoding (if any) occurs either in ProductReviewService, on the backend, or in whatever component renders review.message later — none of which are visible in this file, so this cannot be confirmed complete or ruled a false positive from here alone.

title: Review edit resource ID trusted from client-supplied dialog data with no ownership check
description: The component receives reviewData (including the review's _id) via Angular's MAT_DIALOG_DATA injection token, which is populated by whatever calling component opened this dialog. The editReview() method then submits a patch request using this._id id directly to the backend (productReviewService.patch) without this component performing, or being able to verify, any check that the currently authenticated user actually owns the review being edited. The component simply trusts that the ID it was handed corresponds to a review the current user is allowed to modify. If the parent component (or any code path that opens this dialog) can be induced to supply an arbitrary review _id — e.g., via manipulated UI state, a modified API response, or a compromised parent component — this component will happily submit an edit request for a review belonging to another user, relying entirely on an unseen server-side check to reject it. Because the authorization boundary the design depends on (server-side ownership validation on PUT/PATCH review-by-id) is not visible from this file, and this component performs zero defense-in-depth validation of its own, this is a trust-assumption violation typical of BOLA-enabling client design.

This value is taken directly from user input and sent verbatim to the backend via productReviewService.patch() in editReview(). Per standard guidance for persisted user text, the defect should be reported at the persistence point since the rendering sink lives in a different file/component not visible here. Length caps and required/minLength validators are input constraints, not sanitizers, and do not prevent HTML/script content from being submitted and stored.

This is an uncontrolled/verbose client-side logging of security-relevant failure data rather than a structured, minimized log entry. The two lines are directly consecutive in the error callback, so there is no intermediate transformation of the error value before it is logged.

title: Basket operations trust a client-controlled basket ID (bid) from sessionStorage, enabling BOLA on another user's basket
description: When a logged-in user adds a product to the basket, the component reads the target basket's identifier directly from `sessionStorage.getItem('bid')` and uses it both to look up the basket (line 71) and to construct the payload sent to the server when creating a new basket item (line 137, inside the `.save(...)` call at lines 134-139). sessionStorage is fully attacker/user controllable via browser devtools or a script, so a logged-in attacker can simply overwrite the 'bid' value with another user's basket ID. The subsequent `basketService.find(...)`, `basketService.get(...)`, `basketService.put(...)`, and `basketService.save(...)` calls all operate on whatever basket ID is supplied, with no ownership check performed in this file before the requests are issued (and, given the values are the sole identifiers sent for these operations, the server-side handler in Juice Shop's basket API is only prompted with this attacker-suppliable ID). This is the classic Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) pattern: the client is trusted to supply the resource identifier for a resource it does not necessarily own, and this component's design does not derive the basket ID from any server-verified session state, only client-stored data. An attacker who can view or guess another user's basket ID can view its contents (line 72-73), modify existing item quantities (line 84), or add products directly into someone else's basket (line 135-139).

title: Basket identity trusted from client-controlled sessionStorage ('bid') with no visible per-user ownership check
description: The spec repeatedly seeds sessionStorage with a basket id ('bid') immediately before invoking component.addToBasket(...), e.g. sessionStorage.setItem('bid', '4711') followed by component.addToBasket(1). This reveals that the production ProductComponent (not visible in this file) resolves which basket to read/mutate from a value stored in client-side sessionStorage rather than from a server-derived, session-bound identifier. The subsequent assertions confirm the full path: basketService.find is invoked (implicitly keyed on the sessionStorage-derived context) to look up the basket, productService.get is invoked to resolve the product being added, and basketService.save is invoked to persist a new basket item — all without any test ever exercising or requiring a check that the resolved basket id belongs to the currently authenticated user. If the actual component simply forwards this client-supplied 'bid' to the backend basket endpoints, an attacker can overwrite the sessionStorage value with another user's basket id and add/update items in someone else's basket (BOLA), and the design itself never establishes a rule that the server must re-derive the basket id from the authenticated session rather than accepting the client's value. Because the real sink (the component's addToBasket implementation and the BasketService HTTP calls) lies outside this file, this is reported at the boundary where the spec demonstrates the client-controlled input feeding basket lookup and mutation calls.

trace.description: Test seeds sessionStorage key 'bid' with a raw value, simulating the client-controlled basket identifier that the (external) ProductComponent implementation reads to determine which basket to act upon.

component.addToBasket(1) is invoked; the production implementation (not present in this file) is expected to use the sessionStorage 'bid' value to locate the basket via basketService.find, without any ownership verification visible in the test expectations.

expect(basketService.find).toHaveBeenCalled() confirms the internal flow forwards the bid-derived basket context into the basket lookup call, with no assertion anywhere in the suite that this lookup is scoped or validated against the authenticated user's own basket.

expect(productService.get).toHaveBeenCalled() shows the flow continuing to resolve the product tied to the unverified basket/product association returned from the prior lookup, still without any ownership check having been introduced.
basketService.save is asserted to have been called, confirming the basket mutation proceeds using the client-supplied 'bid' with no test coverage of an ownership/ownership-mismatch rejection path.

title: Failed basket/product operations are only surfaced via client-side console.log, with no server-side security audit trail
description: Multiple tests in this file assert that when basketService.find, basketService.get, basketService.put, basketService.save, or productService.get fail, the sole observable handling behavior is a call to console.log with the raw error (e.g. expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')). Tracing one representative case end to end: the failure is injected into basketService.find, a basket-id context is established via sessionStorage exactly as in the normal-path tests, the console.log spy is installed to observe the component's error handler, the component method is invoked to actually trigger that handler, and the resulting assertion shows the handler's only action is a console.log call. This confirms the production component's error-handling design: failures during basket operations — including failures that could indicate abuse such as repeated failed attempts to access/modify a basket a user does not own — are logged only to the end-user's local browser console and are never reported, forwarded, or logged to any backend/security-monitoring mechanism. There is no evidence in any of these test cases of a security event log, correlation id, or alerting path being exercised. Because browser console output is neither centrally collected nor monitored, an operator has no way to detect brute-forced basket ids, repeated authorization failures, or anomalous add-to-basket activity from this code path.

trace.description: Test simulates a basketService.find failure (throwError) representing a real failure condition the component must handle.
console.log is stubbed and component.addToBasket(2) is invoked; the component's only observable error-handling action is a console.log call, per the spy setup.
sessionStorage.setItem('bid', '815') establishes the basket-id context under which the failing operation occurs, identical to the successful-path flow, before the error handler is exercised.
component.addToBasket(2) is invoked, driving execution into the production error-handling branch reached after the basketService.find failure.

expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error') confirms the failure is logged solely to the browser console with no server-side or centralized logging/alerting evident anywhere in this suite (repeated at lines 185, 194, 212, 246, 276 for other failure paths).

title: Security-relevant basket errors are logged only to the browser console, never surfaced to a monitoring/alerting system
description: The spec repeatedly confirms that when BasketService calls fail (find(), del(), get(), put()) the component's only response is a console.log(errorMessage) call — no server-side audit trail, no alerting, and no user-visible error state is asserted. Six separate tests (lines 122-127, 201-206, 225-230, 240-246, 248-255, 283-289, 291-298) mock console.log and assert it was called with the raw error, confirming this is the sole error-handling path implemented in the component under test. Failed basket loads, failed quantity mutations, and failed deletions are all security/business relevant events (e.g., could indicate broken authorization, tampering attempts, or backend rejection of an operation) but leave no trace anywhere the operations team could review, and repeated failures (e.g., automated probing of basket item IDs) would never trigger any alert.

basketService.find() failure is fed into component.load(); the only asserted side effect is a console.log call, shown again for del/get/put failures at lines 226, 241, 251, 284, 294.
console.log is spied on and silenced ahead of time, implying the component's internal error handler for this path calls console.log directly.
component.ngOnInit() is invoked, triggering the internal handler that consumes the whoAmI failure.
The only externally observable effect asserted is userEmail falling back to '(anonymous)'; no alert, re-throw, or server-side report is asserted or implied.

Test asserts `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')` — confirming the component's error handling terminates at a client-side console.log with no server-side logging, alerting, or audit record.

title: Authentication state derived solely from presence of a client-readable localStorage token
description: The test harness establishes 'authenticated' behavior purely by writing a token value into localStorage (`localStorage.setItem('token', 'token')`) and 'unauthenticated/guest' behavior purely by removing that key (`localStorage.removeItem('token')`). The component under test (per lines 129-137) branches its entire behavior — whether to call userService.whoAmI at all, whether to use the authenticated basket vs. the guest basket — based only on whether this key exists in localStorage, not on any validation of the token's authenticity or expiry from within the component. This mirrors a known weak session-management pattern: bearer tokens held in localStorage are readable by any script (XSS-exploitable, unlike httpOnly cookies), and client-side code trusts mere key presence to decide the user's authentication tier for UI/data-fetching purposes.

trace.description: Test setup writes an auth token directly into localStorage under the plain key 'token' to simulate a logged-in user for the component under test.
A separate test removes the same localStorage key to simulate a guest; component.ngOnInit() is then called and its behavior changes based purely on key presence.
TestBed.createComponent constructs the component while the localStorage token is present, priming the component's construction-time state.
fixture.detectChanges() runs initial change detection, driving the component's lifecycle hook that reads the localStorage token's mere presence to decide authentication tier.
userService.whoAmI mock is cleared beforehand so the subsequent assertion can isolate whether the component still attempts server-side identity resolution.
component.ngOnInit() is explicitly invoked, re-evaluating authentication state purely from local token presence/absence.

component.userEmail (and the resulting authenticated/guest UI and basket behavior) is set purely from the client-controlled, XSS-readable localStorage flag rather than a server-verified session, completing the authentication-tier decision without any signature/validity check performed in this file.

Assertion confirms userService.whoAmI is skipped entirely when the localStorage token key is absent — the component's authentication-tier decision is made from a client-controlled, XSS-readable localStorage flag rather than a server-verified session.

title: Basket item mutation methods accept caller-supplied numeric IDs with no visible ownership scoping
description: component.delete(id), component.inc(id) and component.dec(id) are exercised throughout the spec purely with arbitrary numeric literals (e.g., delete(1), inc(1), dec(1), delete(42)) and directly forward that ID to basketService.del/get/put without any assertion that the ID is checked against the current user's own basket contents before the mutating call is dispatched. If the backing BasketService/API does not itself re-verify basket-item ownership server-side (not visible from this file), a logged-in user could invoke inc()/dec()/delete() with another user's basket-item ID and have the request dispatched unconditionally by the client, which is the classic BOLA precondition (client performs no per-resource ownership check before calling the mutating operation).

trace.description: component.delete(1) is called with a bare numeric basket item id supplied by the test (standing in for a caller-controlled value reaching the component from outside this file, e.g. a template click handler bound to a rendered row).
component.inc(1) is shown forwarding the id straight into basketService.get(1) and basketService.put(1, {quantity}) with no intervening ownership check asserted anywhere in the surrounding test.
A second test seeds basketService.find so a BasketItem with id 1 is treated as the 'current' item, establishing the id that subsequent mutation calls will target.
basketService.get is mocked to return the item matching id 1 with no user/ownership-scoping represented in the lookup.
Assertion confirms basketService.get was called with the raw id unchanged — the id flows straight through the component with no ownership check applied anywhere in the traced path.
basketService.put is called with (id, {quantity}) to perform the mutating write, completing the id-driven request dispatch with no ownership verification anywhere in the traced path.

Assertion confirms basketService.del was called with the raw id (1) directly, evidencing the component performs the mutating call without any client-side verification that the id belongs to the current user's basket.

title: Negative/tampered basket quantities are silently corrected client-side rather than rejected, indicating the invariant is not enforced upstream
description: Two tests (lines 308-315 and 317-324) show that when basketService.get() returns a BasketItem with a negative quantity (-100), component.dec()/inc() simply clamp the outgoing value to 1 and proceed with the update. This demonstrates the application's data model permits basket item quantities to reach invalid/negative states in the first place (otherwise there would be nothing to correct), and that the client component is the layer papering over that invariant violation rather than the value being validated/rejected at its source. Because the quantity used server-side ultimately comes from a client-controlled request (put(id, {quantity})), an attacker bypassing this UI path (e.g., calling the underlying API directly) could submit arbitrary negative or unbounded quantities without a corresponding invariant enforced by this component or, as far as can be seen here, elsewhere.

component.dec(1) is invoked against this tampered/invalid quantity value.
basketService.find is mocked to return a BasketItem with quantity -100, the invalid value entering the component's dataSource.
basketService.get is mocked to return the same invalid quantity when the component looks up the item to mutate it.
basketService.put is mocked to return a 'corrected' quantity of 1, standing in for the backend accepting whatever quantity the client ultimately sends.
Assertion confirms basketService.get was called with the raw id, i.e., the invalid quantity was read directly by the component with no upstream rejection of the negative value.

basketService.put is called with a clamped quantity of 1 — confirming the invalid quantity state was reachable and is only corrected client-side per this UI action, not prevented by a server-enforced invariant visible in this trace.

title: Basket identifier read from client-controlled sessionStorage enables BOLA on basket contents and mutations
description: The component determines which basket to load, and which basket item ids are subsequently deleted or quantity-modified, entirely from the client-controlled sessionStorage value 'bid'. load() calls basketService.find(parseInt(sessionStorage.getItem('bid'), 10)) with no server-side ownership re-derivation visible in this file, then populates dataSource with the returned basket's products. The row-level id values coming from that basket are then passed straight through to delete(id) and addToQuantity(id, value), which invoke basketService.del(id), basketService.get(id) and basketService.put(id, ...) i.e. mutating operations keyed purely by an id sourced from client state. Because sessionStorage is fully writable by the browser/user (e.g. via devtools or a script), an attacker can overwrite 'bid' with another user's basket id. If the backing API (outside this file) does not independently verify that the authenticated caller owns the requested basket id, this yields Broken Object Level Authorization: the victim's basket contents can be viewed, its items can be deleted, or quantities can be changed, all driven by values this file trusts without any ownership check. The authorization decision is delegated entirely to a value this file never validates.

trace.description: load() reads the basket id straight from client-controlled sessionStorage ('bid') and uses it as the resource identifier for basketService.find(), with no ownership check performed in this file.
The returned basket's Products (potentially belonging to another user if 'bid' was tampered with) are assigned directly to dataSource and rendered/operated on.
delete(id) forwards the row id, sourced from the loaded basket, straight into basketService.del(id) with no re-verification that the id belongs to the current session's own basket.
The subscribe next handler receives the basket object returned for the (possibly attacker-substituted) bid, beginning to process it as if it were the current user's own basket.
delete(id) receives a row id that originates from the dataSource populated from the possibly-foreign basket, with no re-check against the authenticated user's own basket.
The guest-vs-authenticated branch check lets execution continue to the real deletion call for any authenticated session, regardless of whether the id actually belongs to that session's basket.
addToQuantity(id, value) similarly receives a row id sourced from the same possibly-foreign dataSource, with no ownership re-check.
The guest-vs-authenticated branch check lets execution continue to the real quantity-update path for any authenticated session using the untrusted id.
basketService.get(id) is called using the untrusted id to fetch the basket item to be modified, with no verification that it belongs to the caller's own basket.
The subscribe next handler receives the basketItem for the untrusted id and proceeds to compute an updated quantity for it.
newQuantity is derived from the fetched (possibly foreign) basketItem's quantity plus the requested delta, continuing to treat the untrusted id as if it were owned by the current user.

addToQuantity(id, value) calls basketService.put(id, {...}) to mutate the quantity of a basket item identified only by an id that traces back to the client-controlled 'bid' lookup, with no ownership check visible in this file.

title: Deluxe pricing entitlement determined and applied entirely on the client
description: Whether a basket item is charged at the discounted 'deluxePrice' versus the normal price is decided purely client-side by this.isDeluxe() (backed by DeluxeGuard, whose state ultimately derives from client-held token/claim data). In both load() and loadGuestBasket(), if isDeluxe() returns true the component overwrites product.price with product.deluxePrice before computing itemTotal and bonus, which are then emitted to the parent component via sendToParent()/emitTotal. The server-authoritative price is never re-derived here; the price used for the displayed (and potentially checkout-bound) total is a value this file itself substitutes based on a client-evaluated boolean. If the guard's deluxe determination can be influenced by client-held state (a token claim, local flag, or similar) without a corresponding server-side re-validation at the point of purchase, an attacker can obtain deluxe pricing without actually holding deluxe status - a trust-boundary violation where the client, not the server, decides an economically significant price outcome.

trace.description: Client-side isDeluxe() check (delegated to DeluxeGuard, driven by client-held auth state) gates which price is applied to every basket product.
product.price is unconditionally overwritten with product.deluxePrice for every item in the basket based solely on the client-side deluxe flag.
itemTotal is computed using the client-substituted price value, with no server-side recomputation performed in this file.
basket.Products.forEach begins iterating every product in the basket to apply the client-decided pricing to each one.
dataSource is assigned from basket.Products after the client-side price substitution, so all downstream calculations operate on the client-decided price.
bonus is likewise computed from the client-substituted price, compounding the reliance on the unverified client-side pricing decision.
sendToParent(this.dataSource.length) is invoked, initiating the hand-off of the client-computed totals to the parent component.
sendToParent() packages the client-derived itemTotal and bonus for emission, without any point at which a server-verified price is substituted.

The client-computed itemTotal/bonus (derived from the client-decided price) is emitted to the parent component via emitTotal, presumably feeding downstream checkout/total display without independent server verification visible in this file.

title: Guest basket load issues unbounded parallel product requests driven by client-controlled storage
description: loadGuestBasket() maps every item in the guest basket (sourced from basketService.getGuestBasketItems(), which is backed by client-writable local storage) into an individual productService.get() HTTP call, then fires all of them concurrently via forkJoin. There is no cap on the number of guest basket items processed this way. Because the guest basket contents are entirely client-controlled, a user (or a script acting on their behalf) can inflate the guest basket with a very large number of distinct product ids, causing this component to issue a correspondingly large burst of concurrent requests to the backend product endpoint every time the basket view loads, with no batching, pagination, or throttling control in this file.

trace.description: guestBasketItems is read from client-controlled storage via basketService.getGuestBasketItems(), with no size limit enforced here.
Every guest basket item is mapped to its own productService.get() call with no batching or cap on the number of items processed.
Each item triggers its own productService.get(item.ProductId) call, so the number of outbound requests scales linearly and unboundedly with the attacker-controlled guest basket size.
Each request's result is piped through map() to pair the product with its quantity, continuing to process every item regardless of how many there are.
catchError absorbs individual request failures without aborting or throttling the overall batch, allowing the full unbounded set of requests to proceed.
guestProductRequests is finalized as an array whose length is exactly the unbounded, client-controlled item count.
forkJoin fires all generated product requests concurrently with no throttling, so an inflated guest basket produces an unbounded burst of simultaneous outbound requests.
